title: Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback
authors: Long Ouyang et al.
summary: InstructGPT aligns GPT-3 to follow instructions through a three-step pipeline: supervised fine-tuning on labeler demonstrations, a reward model trained on labeler rankings, and PPO optimization against that reward model. A 1.3B InstructGPT is preferred to 175B GPT-3, with better truthfulness, fewer hallucinations and a small alignment tax that PPO-ptx reduces. Alignment is to the aggregate preferences of a small labeler group, not to individual users. The paper does not study per-user adaptation, interaction decisions or adaptation over time, so it serves as the outcome-averaged baseline for USIL.
user_evidence: labeler demonstrations and rankings
usil_relation: InstructGPT is the canonical outcome_averaged baseline that USIL contrasts against. It trains one reward model on rankings from about 40 labelers and optimizes the policy with PPO. Section 5.2 raises conditioning on group preferences as future work, which is a step toward personalization [personalization].
open_question: Can the RM-plus-PPO pipeline be conditioned on or fine-tuned from sparse signals of a single user (edits, approvals, takeovers) to learn procedural preferences (when to ask, confirm or defer) rather than output-quality preferences? How should that be evaluated when labelers are not the users who wrote the prompts?
evaluation_scale: About 40 contracted labelers rating outputs on held-out customer prompts, plus a held-out labeler group; no end-user study.

title: Personalizing Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback with Variational Preference Learning
authors: Sriyash Poddar, Yanming Wan, Hamish Ivison, Abhishek Gupta, Natasha Jaques
summary: Variational Preference Learning (VPL) extends RLHF to multi-modal preferences by inferring a user-specific latent from a few preference comparisons and conditioning reward models and policies on it. The authors derive an ELBO and add likelihood-based reward scaling, active query selection, and an LLM architecture with data augmentation. In simulated control tasks and synthetic LLM datasets (Pets, UltraFeedback-P), VPL beats BTL and DPL in task success and reward accuracy, matches BTL in unimodal settings, and active querying halves queries needed. Evaluation uses only simulated users, with no temporal adaptation. It personalizes outputs rather than interaction policy, but it is a clear predecessor for few-shot user latents.
user_evidence: few pairwise preferences per user
usil_relation: VPL infers a per-user latent z from a few preference annotations and conditions reward models and policies on it, which is the z_u = g(h) decomposition of USIL. Its active query selection, which decides which questions to ask a user, resembles the asking part of USIL.
open_question: VPL personalizes what is preferred (reward over outputs), not how the agent works. Can a latent like z be inferred from implicit signals such as edits, takeovers and approvals to condition when to ask, confirm or defer, evaluated with real users over sessions and with drift?
evaluation_scale: Simulated and synthetic users only: control tasks (Maze, Ravens, Habitat) with up to 100 users and 10 modes; LLM experiments on Pets and UltraFeedback-P with 2-4 synthetic users; 3 seeds for GPT2, 1 for Llama; no real humans.

title: FSPO: Few-Shot Optimization of Synthetic Preferences Personalizes to Real Users
authors: Anikait Singh, Sheryl Hsu, Kyle Hsu, Eric Mitchell, Stefano Ermon, Tatsunori Hashimoto, Archit Sharma, Chelsea Finn
summary: FSPO reframes LLM personalization as meta-learning over users. A model trained on synthetic preference data infers a user's reward function in context from a few labeled preference pairs, optionally predicting a natural-language user description first (RAT). On synthetic benchmarks (Reviews, ELIX, Roleplay with up to 1,500 personas), FSPO reaches about 87% win rate, and RAT nearly matches an oracle persona. A 50-person human study shows 68-72% win rates over base and SFT, and PRISM reward accuracy is 82.8% vs 61.7% for IPO. It personalizes outputs only; interaction decisions and temporal drift are not studied.
user_evidence: few labeled preferences per user
usil_relation: FSPO treats each user as a task instance and meta-learns over users to adapt from few-shot evidence, with in-context latent user inference and a natural-language user description (RAT). This is the few-shot user adaptation machinery USIL would reuse for procedural preferences.
open_question: Can FSPO-style meta-learning over users infer per-user interaction preferences (when to ask, confirm, or defer) from sparse signals such as takeovers and approvals, rather than output style preferences from pairwise labels, and does it hold up as preferences drift across sessions?
evaluation_scale: Synthetic benchmarks with up to 1,500 LLM-generated personas (ELIX 550 users, Roleplay 1,500), judged by GPT-4o; Prolific human study with 50 users and 11 questions; PRISM reward-accuracy check.

title: Principles of Mixed-Initiative User Interfaces
authors: Eric Horvitz
summary: This 1999 CHI paper proposes 12 principles for mixed-initiative user interfaces, illustrated with LookOut, an Outlook add-in that assists with calendaring. A linear SVM infers the probability that an email implies a scheduling goal. An expected-utility framework then chooses among acting, engaging in dialog, or doing nothing, with thresholds that depend on the user's focus and the costs of mistaken action. A timing model of dwell time versus message size controls when service is offered, and life-long learning refines the models over time. The paper reports no formal evaluation, only a sigmoid dwell-time finding from sample data from one user.
user_evidence: inferred user goals
usil_relation: LookOut's expected-utility choice among acting, dialog, and waiting, with thresholds shifted by user focus, is the classic population-level form of USIL's when-to-ask-or-act policy. Its optional custom timing model learned from watching one user, and its user-specifiable utilities, point toward per-user adaptation of interaction behavior.
open_question: Can the per-user timing model and utility thresholds be learned from sparse, evolving implicit signals (dwell time, manual invocation, hesitation sounds) and shown to improve ask/act/defer decisions for individual users over a default population policy, and do they transfer across tasks?

title: Levels of Autonomy for AI Agents
authors: K. J. Kevin Feng, David W. McDonald, Amy X. Zhang
summary: This conceptual paper argues that agent autonomy is a design decision separate from capability and environment. It defines five levels by the role the user takes: operator, collaborator, consultant, approver and observer. For each level it gives illustrative scenarios, must-have controls and open questions. It applies the levels to autonomy certificates for governance and proposes a user-assisted evaluation in which user involvement is raised until a task-performance threshold is met, so autonomy can be measured apart from capability. There are no experiments, no learning and no per-user adaptation. Personalization, such as consultant-level training periods and user-set approval conditions, is only mentioned conceptually.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned from data. This is a conceptual framework of five autonomy levels defined by user role (operator, collaborator, consultant, approver, observer), with autonomy certificates and a proposed assisted-evaluation protocol.
user_evidence: n/a
usil_relation: The five user-role levels (consultant, approver, observer) give a vocabulary for the autonomy dimension of a user-conditioned interaction policy. The L4 idea that users pre-specify approval conditions and the L3 'training period' hint at user-specific adaptation [personalization].
open_question: How could a per-user autonomy level be learned and updated from approvals, takeovers and interruptions, rather than fixed at design time or certified for an average user? And would the assisted-evaluation protocol work with individual users whose preferred level changes by task and stakes?

title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
authors: Shunyu Yao, Noah Shinn, Pedram Razavi, Karthik Narasimhan
summary: τ-bench is a benchmark for tool-agent-user interaction. A language agent holds multi-turn conversations with an LM-simulated user while calling domain API tools and following written policies, in retail (115 tasks) and airline (50 tasks) customer service. Success is judged by comparing the final database state to a unique ground truth. The paper also proposes pass^k, the chance that all k i.i.d. trials of a task succeed. Even gpt-4o with function calling succeeds on under 50% of tasks, and pass^8 falls below 25% in retail. The paper trains nothing, uses no per-user personalization, and runs no cross-domain transfer experiment.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned. This is an evaluation benchmark for off-the-shelf LM agents (function calling, ReAct, Act-only) interacting with an LM-simulated user and API tools under domain policies.
user_evidence: simulated user dialogue
usil_relation: The agent decides each turn whether to message the user or call a tool, and policies require explicit user confirmation before database writes, so the benchmark touches procedural behavior (ask, confirm, act). It also uses pass^k to measure reliability across repeated trials, a population-level analogue of consistency [interaction_decisions][claimed_contribution].
open_question: Could τ-bench's simulated users be given persistent, differing procedural preferences (for example confirmation tolerance or verbosity) across repeated sessions, and would per-user pass^k then distinguish agents that adapt to an individual from agents that follow one generic policy?
evaluation_scale: LM-simulated users (gpt-4-0613) on τ-retail (115 tasks) and τ-airline (50 tasks), at least 3 trials per task, about 12 LMs

title: Delegating or Doing? Understanding User Behavior in Hybrid Human-Agent Interfaces
authors: Gavin Dizon, Tyrone Justin Sta Maria, Jordan Aiko Deja, Yasuyuki Sumi
summary: This between-subjects study (N=73) compares Traditional-Only, AI-First, and Hybrid interfaces for CRUD tasks in a CMS with an MCP-based Gemini chat assistant. Task time did not differ by condition, but AI-assisted modes reduced clicks and page navigations. In the Hybrid condition, delegation (measured by chat turn counts) was not tied to operation type, and about half of its variance was at the participant level (ICC=.50). The authors recommend keeping the assistant always available so users can settle at their own level. The study has no learning or personalization component, and it is limited by a homogeneous student sample, a coarse delegation measure, one app, and one model.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned. This is an empirical behavioral study of how users split work between direct GUI manipulation and delegation to an LLM chat agent. It reports that delegation varies by participant (ICC=.50) rather than by CRUD operation type.
user_evidence: per-user choice to delegate vs. directly manipulate, interaction logs (clicks, navigation, scrolling), task outcomes
usil_relation: It gives empirical evidence that the choice to delegate or act directly varies more across users (ICC=.50) than across CRUD task types, which supports treating the individual user as a unit for procedural interaction decisions [key_results]. The authors recommend letting each user settle at their own level of assistant use, but this is a design suggestion and not a tested personalization mechanism [personalization].
open_question: Can per-user delegation tendencies be inferred from a few logged chat-versus-GUI choices and used to predict or adapt the agent's ask/act/defer behavior in later tasks, sessions, and applications? This paper tests one session, one app, and one model, and has only coarse chat-turn counts without trust or self-report measures.
evaluation_scale: 73 undergraduate students in a between-subjects study (Hybrid 25, AI-First 25, Traditional 23), each completing 16 fixed-order CRUD tasks

title: Assistant or Actor? Student Trust, Control, and Delegation Regret When Using a General-Purpose AI Agent
authors: Shiva Pochampally, Shengwei An, Yan Chen
summary: A within-subjects lab study in which 20 AI-literate CS students delegated five everyday academic tasks to the OpenClaw general-purpose agent. Trust was calibrated per task rather than per agent. Participants granted wide autonomy for advisory and low-stakes tasks but demanded confirmation for irreversible, externally visible actions such as emailing a professor. All 20 flagged the missing confirmation step even when output quality was fine, which the authors call 'delegation regret'. They propose action-boundary displays, per-task autonomy policies and advisory/action separation, but do not evaluate them. The sample is small and homogeneous, task order was fixed, and results are averaged across users.
what_is_learned: No model is trained. The paper empirically characterizes how students' trust, supervision and approval preferences vary by task (privacy, stakes, reversibility), and identifies 'delegation regret' (dissatisfaction from unauthorized action despite adequate output) as a failure mode.
user_evidence: user study observations
usil_relation: Shows that approval preference for confirmation is highest for irreversible, externally visible actions (email, M = 4.65) and that all 20 participants flagged the missing confirmation step even though output was rated adequate. This supports the claim that procedure, not just outcome, drives dissatisfaction, and it suggests the task-level factors (reversibility, visibility) that a user-conditioned confirmation policy would need.
open_question: Do individual users differ stably in their confirmation and autonomy thresholds across tasks and over time, so that per-user interaction policies would outperform the task-level averaged policy implied here? The study reports only group-level statistics from one session and does not test the proposed per-task autonomy policies.
evaluation_scale: 20 undergraduate CS students at a single institution, 5 tasks in a fixed order, ~45-minute session, selected from a 64-person screening survey

title: Modeling Distinct Human Interaction in Web Agents
authors: Faria Huq, Zora Zhiruo Wang, Zhanqiu Guo, Venu Arvind Arangarajan, Tianyue Ou, Frank Xu, Shuyan Zhou, Graham Neubig, Jeffrey P. Bigham
summary: The paper introduces the task of modeling human intervention in collaborative web agents. It collects CowCorpus, 400 real-user trajectories from 20 participants with interleaved human and agent actions, and clusters users into four interaction styles (Takeover, Hands-on, Hands-off, Collaborative) using behavioral features. Fine-tuned multimodal LMs predict at each step whether the user will intervene, beating prompted closed models on Perfect Timing Score. Style-conditioned models mostly perform best on their own cluster. PlowPilot, an intervention-aware agent that prompts only when intervention is likely, was rated 36.8% more useful in a small user study (n=16). The paper does not implement adaptation over time or test transfer.
user_evidence: intervention traces
usil_relation: Predicts at each agent step whether the user will intervene, which drives when the agent asks or continues, and conditions this on four clustered user interaction styles (Takeover, Hands-on, Hands-off, Collaborative), so it is a group-level proxy for per-user procedural adaptation [what_is_learned][personalization][user_representation].
open_question: Can the style-level intervention models be turned into truly individual, online-updating policies that adapt to a single user's drift across sessions, given that Takeover users had only 11 intervention steps and no temporal adaptation was implemented? Can they transfer to unseen tasks or users?
evaluation_scale: 400 trajectories (over 4,200 actions) from 20 participants doing 20 tasks each; offline split of 1,247 train and 251 test steps; live user study with 16 participants (4 returning, 12 new) rating on a 7-point Likert scale

title: Personalized Benchmarking: Evaluating LLMs by Individual Preferences
authors: Cristina Garbacea, Heran Wang, Chenhao Tan
summary: The paper introduces personalized benchmarking of LLMs. Using Chatbot Arena votes from 115 active users, it computes per-user ELO and Bradley-Terry model rankings and shows they diverge sharply from the global ranking (mean Spearman 0.432 for ELO, 0.043 for BT). It characterizes users by topic mixtures and writing style, and shows that a 778-dimensional topic+style feature vector predicts a user's model ratings better than a mean-predictor baseline (MAE reduced 35% for ELO, 12% for BT) on 18 held-out users. It argues for personalized benchmarks, but studies only output preferences, with no interaction policy and no longitudinal adaptation.
user_evidence: individual preference ratings
usil_relation: It makes the individual user the unit of evaluation, showing that per-user rankings from 115 Chatbot Arena users diverge from global ones (mean Spearman 0.043 for BT). Its target is outcome preference (which model is better), not interaction procedure. This is the outcome_individual counterpart to USIL's argument against averaging.
open_question: Does the same divergence appear for procedural preferences, such as when users want clarifying questions, confirmations, or autonomy, and can topic and style profiles from a few queries predict those per-user interaction policies?
evaluation_scale: 115 Chatbot Arena users with at least 25 battles (about 59 queries each), from 13,383 users in the dataset; regression trained on 97 users and validated on 18

title: Comparing Human Oversight Strategies for Computer-Use Agents
authors: Chaoran Chen, Zhiping Zhang, Zeya Chen, et al.
summary: This paper compares four human oversight strategies for web computer-use agents: Action Confirmation, Risk-Gated, Supervisory Co-Execution, and Structurally Enriched. In a within-subjects study with 48 Prolific participants (192 live sessions, plus 10 interviews), the strategies differ in when control returns to the user. Users blocked only 21% of problematic actions that reached execution, and this did not differ by strategy. Plan-based strategies mainly reduced occurrence upstream, by 76% in odds. Failures came from mistimed authority, procedural rather than content checking, and plans that reduced scrutiny. No strategy was best subjectively. The oversight designs are fixed and not personalized, and the study is short-term.
what_is_learned: No model is trained; the agent is a fixed off-the-shelf LLM (Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite). The paper produces empirical findings about how oversight strategies affect problematic-action occurrence, intervention, and user behavior.
user_evidence: interventions/corrections during execution, exposure to risky actions, trust and subjective ratings, qualitative interviews
usil_relation: It compares oversight/confirmation timing and control-return strategies for web computer-use agents, which are the procedural decisions (confirm, defer, return control) USIL wants to learn per user. It treats them as fixed, population-level designs.
open_question: Could per-user signals such as Approve Similar use, approvals made without inspection, and takeovers be used to learn when each individual needs re-entry points or plan scrutiny, given that fixed strategies only block about 21% of problematic actions?
evaluation_scale: 48 Prolific participants, four live sessions each (192 sessions), plus 10 follow-up interviews

title: Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance
authors: John D. Lee, Katrina A. See
summary: A multidisciplinary review and conceptual model of how trust in automation mediates reliance. It links context (individual, organizational, cultural), the bases of trust (performance, process, purpose), analytic, analogical and affective processes, and display features to the dynamics of trust and reliance. It introduces calibration, resolution and specificity as criteria for appropriate trust and gives tentative design, evaluation and training guidance, including 'design for appropriate trust, not greater trust'. It runs no new studies and learns nothing from data. It treats individual differences conceptually and offers no per-user adaptation method. It is useful background for USIL's autonomy and reliance constructs.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned from data. This is a conceptual review and dynamic model of how trust mediates reliance on automation. Its only quantitative element is a cited first-order differential equation of trust change from Lee & Moray, 1994.
user_evidence: n/a
usil_relation: Its dynamic model of trust and reliance, with temporal specificity and trust that tracks changes in automation capability, parallels the USIL concern with when a user hands over or retains control. Its guidance to design for appropriate rather than greater trust, and its calibration, resolution and specificity metrics, could act as evaluation constructs for per-user autonomy policies.
open_question: Can calibration, resolution and temporal specificity of trust be estimated for each individual from interaction signals such as takeovers, approvals and delegation, and used to set a per-user autonomy or confirmation policy? The paper offers only population-level, qualitative constructs and no individualized estimation method.

title: BusyBody: Creating and Fielding Personalized Models of the Cost of Interruption
authors: Eric Horvitz; Paul Koch; Johnson Apacible
venue: Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Computer Supported Cooperative Work (CSCW)
summary: BusyBody is an onboard system that learns personalized Bayesian network models of a user's cost of interruption. It intermittently asks for busy/not-busy self-assessments and logs desktop events, calendar, wireless location and conversation detection. It retrains periodically and exposes expected interruption cost, which can set a threshold for alerting versus journaling messages. In a field trial with four participants over several weeks, per-user classification accuracy on a random 80/20 split ranged from 0.70 to 0.87. Learned networks differed across users, and participants found the probes somewhat annoying. Transfer across users and a larger study are left as future work. No baselines are reported.
usil_relation: BusyBody learns a per-user model of interruptibility from each user's own labels and sensed activity over weeks, and uses it to decide when to alert or defer notifications. This is an early individual-level procedural model of when to interrupt. It is the closest historical precedent for the USIL claim that interaction timing should be learned per user.
open_question: Can per-user interruption-cost models be learned from implicit signals (dismissals, takeovers, ignored alerts) rather than intrusive self-assessment probes? Do they transfer across tasks, contexts and users, and do they track drift in preferences over time? The paper leaves all of these open, with no baselines, no per-user transfer results, and only four participants.
evaluation_scale: 4 participants (program manager, team lead, two developers) over several weeks; 470 to 2365 cases each

title: The Off-Switch Game
authors: Dylan Hadfield-Menell, Anca Dragan, Pieter Abbeel, Stuart Russell
summary: The Off-Switch Game formalizes why a rational robot would allow a human to switch it off. A robot that is uncertain about the utility of its action, and treats the human's press or non-press of the off switch as evidence, has a non-negative and typically positive incentive to defer. The paper analyzes a rational human, a noisily rational human, and Gaussian beliefs, and shows that more robot uncertainty increases the incentive to defer but lowers the value generated. The analysis is one-shot and analytic, with no learning, personalization or user studies. It offers a theoretical basis for deference but not for per-user adaptation.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned from data. The paper derives analytically the robot's incentive to defer to a human off-switch. The robot holds a belief over the human's utility for its action and treats the human's press or non-press as evidence about it.
user_evidence: n/a
usil_relation: The game gives a formal account of deference: an agent uncertain about the human's utility should let the human veto its action. The incentive Δ depends on the robot's belief and the human's policy (rational vs noisily rational) [key_results][user_representation]. This is the theoretical basis for learning when to defer or return control.
open_question: How could the robot's belief over Ua and the human's rationality parameter β be learned per user from takeovers and approvals over repeated interactions? Would the resulting user-specific deference policy still give a positive incentive to preserve the off switch when the human model is misspecified?
evaluation_scale: Analytical proofs and numerical plots with Gaussian beliefs, plus a simulated designer scenario with a Gaussian customer population; no real users.

title: AI Alignment with Changing and Influenceable Reward Functions
authors: Micah Carroll, Davis Foote, Anand Siththaranjan, Stuart Russell, Anca Dragan
summary: This ICML 2024 paper introduces Dynamic Reward MDPs (DR-MDPs) to formalize AI alignment when human preferences change over time and the AI can influence them. It shows that static-preference alignment methods such as RL recommenders, RLHF and TAMER can implicitly reward undue influence, and that longer horizons can increase the incentive for it. It compares eight alignment objectives analytically on toy examples and finds that all either permit undesirable influence or are overly conservative. Nothing is learned, there are no user data or empirical evaluation, and reward functions and dynamics are assumed known. It is relevant to USIL for its treatment of preference drift and influence.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned from data. The paper is a formal analysis (DR-MDPs) of which alignment objective to optimize when human reward functions change over time and can be influenced by the AI. Reward functions and dynamics are assumed known.
user_evidence: n/a
usil_relation: Models the user as an evolving cognitive state θ that parameterizes the reward function and can be influenced by the AI, with a no-op baseline and conservative ParetoUD objectives. This bears on whether an agent should shape user preferences and on how to treat drift [user_representation][temporal_adaptation].
open_question: How could an agent learn per-user preference dynamics and susceptibility to influence from sparse real interaction data, and then use them to set individualized limits on influence and autonomy, given that DR-MDPs assume known reward functions and dynamics?

title: When Should Users Check? Modeling Confirmation Frequency in Multi-Step Agentic AI Tasks
authors: Jieyu Zhou, Aryan Roy, Sneh Gupta, Daniel Weitekamp, Christopher J. MacLellan
summary: The paper asks when an agent should ask users to confirm during long multi-step tasks. A formative study identifies the Confirmation–Diagnosis–Correction–Redo (CDCR) pattern. The authors build a dynamic-programming model that places checkpoints to minimize expected user time. In a 48-participant within-subjects study across simulated shopping, image-editing and Overcooked tasks, intermediate confirmation cut completion time by 13.54% against confirm-at-end, and 81% of participants preferred it. Gains were largest for early errors and slightly negative for late ones. The model is population-level, time-only and untested for adaptation. Personalization and online belief updates are deferred to future work.
user_evidence: task error model
usil_relation: It is a procedure-level confirmation-scheduling model (when to check in multi-step agent tasks) with a CDCR cost decomposition. This is the procedure_averaged cell that USIL targets for individualization. The authors name hierarchical per-user timing parameters and online accuracy updates as future work [personalization] [temporal_adaptation].
open_question: Can per-user t_confirm and t_diagnose, and user-specific error beliefs, be learned from sparse logs so that individualized checkpoint schedules beat the population schedule? Does this hold when users' expertise or perception of task difficulty conflicts with the model-prescribed frequency, and when preferences drift over sessions?
evaluation_scale: 48 participants in a within-subjects lab study over 3 simulated domains. Also an 8-participant formative study, a 10-participant pilot, and 5,000-run appendix simulations.

title: Value of Information: A Framework for Human–Agent Communication
authors: Yijiang River Dong, Tiancheng Hu, Zheng Hui, Caiqi Zhang, Ivan Vulić, Andreea Bobu, Nigel Collier
summary: This paper proposes a parameter-free, inference-time Value of Information framework for deciding whether an LLM agent should ask a clarifying question or commit to an action under underspecified requests. The LLM estimates belief distributions over latent user intents, simulates answers to candidate questions, and asks only while net VoI, expected utility gain minus linear question cost, is positive. Tested across four domains (20Q, medical, flight preference, WebShop) with two LLMs and simulated users, it matches or beats tuned baselines in 18 of 20 conditions. It trails at high cost, calibration is weaker in medical diagnosis, and it has no persistent per-user learning or human study.
what_is_learned: Nothing is trained. A pretrained LLM is prompted at inference time to estimate belief distributions over latent intents or preferences, simulate answers, and compute Value of Information. Net VoI drives a clarify-or-commit policy with no learned parameters.
user_evidence: task uncertainty
usil_relation: The net-VoI stop/ask rule with a per-question cognitive cost is a decision-theoretic mechanism for when to ask versus act. A USIL policy pi_u could build on it. The FlightPref task also infers a per-user latent reward from choice history within an episode.
open_question: Can the fixed, uniform linear per-question cost c be replaced by a cost learned per user from interruptions, corrections and takeovers, and can that user-specific cost persist across sessions to change when the VoI agent asks, with real users validating it?
evaluation_scale: Four tasks (20Q animals, medical, FlightPref, ambiguous WebShop), two LLMs (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash), costs c=0.01 and 0.05 plus a 0.01–0.20 sweep; simulated users, no human study.

title: Agents that Reduce Work and Information Overload
authors: Pattie Maes
summary: This 1994 CACM article argues for interface agents that act as personal assistants under an indirect-management metaphor, in which user and agent both initiate communication, monitor events and perform tasks. It identifies competence (deciding when, what and how to help) and trust (the user's comfort delegating) as the key problems. It claims a novel approach in which the agent gradually becomes more effective by learning the user's interests, habits and preferences, and those of the user's community. Prototypes cover meeting scheduling, email handling, news filtering and entertainment selection. The excerpt gives no mechanism, evaluation or results.
usil_relation: Frames the agent's competence as learning when, what and how to help a particular user from that user's habits and preferences, plus delegation and trust. This is the closest early statement of a user-conditioned interaction policy [research_question][what_is_learned].
open_question: The excerpt gives no concrete learning mechanism, evidence signals, or evaluation. Do the prototype agents (meeting scheduling, email, news, entertainment) actually learn per-user decisions on when to act versus ask, and does that transfer across tasks or hold as preferences change?

title: User–interface agent interaction: personalization issues
authors: Silvia Schiaffino, Analía Amandi
summary: This 2004 survey of 42 users examines how interface agents should personalize interaction in mixed-initiative settings. Participants answered questionnaires on assistant type, allowed assistance actions, interruptions, error tolerance, feedback and autonomy. Preferences differ widely: 12% want a collaborative agent, 40% a background agent, and 48% an agent that acts in certain situations. 76% accept interruptions only when the situation is relevant, and 90% tolerate errors early but not later. The authors propose a user interaction profile of situation-action-probability tuples and interaction style. The profile and learning algorithms are not implemented or evaluated.
user_evidence: observed user reactions and explicit feedback
usil_relation: It is an early conceptual predecessor of USIL. It argues that procedural interaction preferences (interruptions, autonomy, notify-before-suggest, feedback willingness, error tolerance) vary by individual, and it proposes a per-user profile of <Situation, Action, Probability> tuples [personalization][user_representation].
open_question: Can per-user profiles of situation-action acceptance probabilities actually be learned from sparse implicit feedback, and do they improve interruption and autonomy decisions over a population-level policy? The paper never implemented or tested its profile, and it does not address drift beyond noting that error tolerance shifts over time.
evaluation_scale: 42 survey participants (ages 21-50, varying expertise), one-off questionnaire; descriptive percentages only

title: Personalizing User–Agent Interaction
authors: Silvia Schiaffino; Analía Amandi
summary: This 2006 paper presents WoS, an association-rule-based learning algorithm for interface agents. It learns, for each user and problem situation, whether the user wants a suggestion with justification, only a warning, or no assistance. It mines hypotheses from the user's implicit or explicit reactions to the agent's actions, promotes them to facts when they are well supported, and revises facts periodically. In a study with 30 agenda-system users, the agent with WoS made more correct assistance actions than the same agent without it. Results are shown only as a graph. Transfer, interaction costs and temporal weighting are left unaddressed or as future work.
usil_relation: WoS is an early instance of a per-user interaction policy: it learns from user reactions when to suggest, warn, or stay silent in each situation in an agenda agent [personalization][interaction_decisions]. This matches USIL's procedural, individual cell.
open_question: Does WoS-style per-user assistance-type learning transfer across tasks and contexts, handle genuine preference drift versus noise, and account for interaction costs and stakes? None of these is established, and the evaluation is a small 30-user study with graph-only results.
evaluation_scale: 30 agenda-system users, half with WoS and half without; precision averaged per session over about 30 actions

title: Building respectful interface agents
authors: Silvia Schiaffino, Marcelo Armentano, Analía Amandi
summary: Proposes respectful interface agents whose user profile extends the classic profile with user intentions and an interaction profile of assistance and interruption preferences. Intentions are recognized by a Bayesian intention graph with context nodes and fading evidence. WATSON learns when a user wants a warning, suggestion, action, or nothing, and IONWI learns whether to interrupt or notify, both as association rules with certainty degrees. A decision algorithm uses these to pick assistance type and modality. On tourism datasets (15 users) precision rose from 70% for the confidence-based baseline to 87% (WATSON) and 90% (WATSON+IONWI). Datasets are small, and transfer between users or domains is not studied.
user_evidence: user reactions to interruptions
usil_relation: It is an early, explicit per-user learner of procedural preferences (when the user wants a warning, suggestion, or action, and whether to interrupt) from implicit and explicit feedback, which is the USIL central object. The decision algorithm conditions on the user's learned profile [what_is_learned][interaction_decisions][personalization].
open_question: Do per-user assistance and interruption preferences learned with association rules transfer across tasks, applications, or users, and can they track drift? The paper excludes cross-agent transfer, has no explicit preference-drift handling, and reports only averaged precision on 15 users in small tourism datasets [transfer][limitations].
evaluation_scale: 30 tourism datasets from 15 users (20-45 interactions each); results compared with earlier calendar-management experiments

title: Human-Robot Mutual Adaptation in Shared Autonomy
authors: Nikolaidis, Stefanos; Zhu, Yu Xiang; Hsu, David; Srinivasa, Siddhartha
venue: Proceedings of the ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction (HRI)
summary: The paper proposes a human-robot mutual adaptation formalism for shared autonomy. A bounded-memory model of human adaptability is integrated into a MOMDP, so the robot keeps a joint belief over the user's goal and their adaptability α. The robot guides adaptable users toward a better goal and complies with stubborn users to keep their trust. In a 51-participant between-subjects table-clearing study, mutual adaptation beat one-way adaptation on team performance, 9/16 users switched to the optimal goal, and trust matched one-way adaptation and exceeded no-adaptation. Adaptation is within-session only, adaptability is assumed fixed, and transfer is untested.
usil_relation: The robot infers a per-user adaptability α within a session and uses it to choose between complying with the user and guiding them, which is an individualized autonomy and deference policy conditioned on user history. This is close to the USIL pi_u(a|s,h^u) with a latent user variable.
open_question: Can adaptability or stubbornness be learned and carried across sessions and tasks, rather than assumed fixed within one table-clearing task with a hand-specified model? Would it transfer to other interaction decisions such as asking or confirming?
evaluation_scale: 51 participants in a between-subjects study (16 mutual-adaptation, 17 one-way, remainder no-adaptation), 3 trials each; plus simulated users with varying α

title: Aligning LLM Agents by Learning Latent Preference from User Edits
authors: Ge Gao, Alexey Taymanov, Eduardo Salinas, Paul Mineiro, Dipendra Misra
summary: PRELUDE is a framework for aligning LLM agents by learning from the edits users make to agent outputs. CIPHER, its algorithm, infers a natural-language description of the latent preference from each edit, stores it with a context embedding, and retrieves and aggregates preferences from the k nearest contexts to guide later generation. The LLM stays frozen. In simulated GPT-4 user environments for summarization and email writing, CIPHER gets the lowest cumulative edit distance, cutting edits by 31% and 73%, at modest token overhead. A small human study agrees. Preferences are stationary, and no interaction-policy decisions or transfer are studied.
user_evidence: user edits
usil_relation: CIPHER learns from user edits as implicit feedback, with no explicit ratings, and keeps an editable natural-language preference memory retrieved by context. This is close to the USIL evidence-to-profile pipeline, with edit cost as an effort metric. But it targets output style, not interaction policy.
open_question: Could PRELUDE/CIPHER-style edit inference be extended to infer procedural preferences, such as when this user wants confirmation or clarification, and be tested on multiple distinct users with drifting preferences rather than one simulated GPT-4 user per source?
evaluation_scale: Simulated two-stage GPT-4 user over 200 rounds, 5 summarization and 4 email document sources, 3 seeds; small human study with 7 evaluators for win rate and 3 users for edits.

title: Creating General User Models from Computer Use
authors: Omar Shaikh, Shardul Sapkota, Shan Rizvi, Eric Horvitz, Joon Sung Park, Diyi Yang, Michael S. Bernstein
summary: This paper introduces General User Models (GUMs): per-user collections of confidence-weighted natural-language propositions learned from unstructured computer-use observations such as screenshots, notifications and emails. A Propose-Retrieve-Revise architecture with a privacy Audit module builds and updates the model using open LLMs and VLMs. Applications include LLM contextualization, notification filtering, and the Gumbo proactive assistant, which uses expected utility to decide whether to interrupt or execute suggestions. In an email study (N=18) the full GUM was better calibrated and ranked higher than ablations, though accuracy was similar. In a 5-day deployment (N=5), propositions were 79% accurate. Limitations include privacy, injection attacks and execution failures.
user_evidence: passive screen/computer-use observations
usil_relation: GUM is a persistent per-user natural-language model learned from implicit computer-use signals, and Gumbo uses it for expected-utility decisions on when to interrupt or act autonomously. This is the closest existing instance of a user representation z_u feeding an interaction policy.
open_question: Does the interruption/autonomy policy actually adapt per user? The expected-utility costs and benefits are LLM-elicited from the GUM, and the paper does not test whether proactive-assistance behavior transfers to new tasks or users, or whether it learns per-user procedural preferences such as when to ask versus act.
evaluation_scale: 18 participants in an offline email study (200 emails each, 30 propositions judged); 5 participants in a 5-day Gumbo deployment (24-hour burn-in, 4 days active use)

title: CollabLLM: From Passive Responders to Active Collaborators
authors: Shirley Wu, Michel Galley, Baolin Peng, et al.
summary: CollabLLM trains LLMs for long-term multiturn collaboration instead of next-turn rewards. Multiturn-aware Rewards are estimated by forward-sampling simulated conversations with an LLM user simulator, scoring task success, efficiency and interactivity. A Llama-3.1-8B policy is fine-tuned with SFT, DPO and PPO. It learns to ask clarifying questions and offer suggestions, beating baselines by 18.5% on task performance, 13.3% on efficiency and 46.3% on interactivity in simulation. A 201-person study shows 17.6% higher satisfaction and 10.4% less time. It transfers zero-shot to Abg-CoQA. It does not model individual users or adaptation across sessions; the authors flag personalization as future work.
user_evidence: Simulated user responses over future turns (rollouts) scored for task success, efficiency and engagement; no real per-user data in training
usil_relation: CollabLLM trains an interaction policy (when to ask clarifying questions, when to answer, when to suggest) from simulated user feedback with forward-looking Multiturn-aware Rewards, so it covers the procedural, population-level cell (procedure_averaged) that USIL contrasts itself with. Its zero-shot transfer from BigCodeBench-Chat to Abg-CoQA and its sim-to-real user study give evidence on generalization of interaction behavior.
open_question: Can the Multiturn-aware Reward be conditioned on a user-specific history, for example simulators with distinct interaction styles, so the ask/answer/suggest policy adapts per user across sessions? Would that outperform the averaged policy for individual users who differ in their tolerance for clarifying questions?
evaluation_scale: 201 MTurk participants (document writing, at least 8 turns each) plus simulated benchmarks with a GPT-4o-mini user simulator: 100 documents, 600 coding problems, 200 math problems

title: Towards Optimizing Human-Centric Objectives in AI-Assisted Decision-Making With Offline Reinforcement Learning
authors: Zana Buçinca, Siddharth Swaroop, Amanda E. Paluch, Susan A. Murphy, Krzysztof Z. Gajos
summary: The paper proposes offline reinforcement learning to learn AI-assistance policies for human-AI decision-making that optimize human-centric objectives such as immediate accuracy and learning. Using data from 142 participants on an exercise-prescription task, it learns tabular Q-learning policies over a 64-state space that includes binary Need for Cognition, AI correctness, and concept/task knowledge. Actions are four assistance types. Two online studies (N=316, N=964) show accuracy-optimized policies beat baselines and reach complementarity. Learning-optimized policies only partly succeeded. Personalization is by NFC group within a session, with no longitudinal or cross-task transfer test.
user_evidence: logged decisions and outcomes under different assistance types, user traits (e.g., need for cognition), task features
usil_relation: It learns an assistance policy with offline RL from participant data, conditioned on a user trait (NFC) and running per-concept knowledge. It decides when and how the AI intervenes (withholding help, giving explanation only, or on demand) and optimizes human-centric objectives beyond accuracy [what_is_learned][personalization][interaction_decisions].
open_question: Can the NFC-binned, within-session tabular policy be replaced by individually learned policies that persist across sessions and adapt as a user's reliance and expertise drift? Would the learning-objective gains, which were weak and inconsistent, appear with richer per-user evidence and tasks other than exercise prescription?
evaluation_scale: Data collection N=142; evaluation studies N=316 (3 policies) and N=964 (6 conditions) on Prolific/LabInTheWild, between-subjects

title: Robot Behavior Personalization from Sparse User Feedback
authors: Maithili Patel, Sonia Chernova
venue: IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (DOI 10.1109/LRA.2025.3550833); arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.19219
summary: TAACo is a robot framework that learns an individual older adult's preferred manner of assistance (do now, do later, remind, no action) for open-set household tasks from sparse feedback. It uses GPT-4 to score tasks against abstract concepts, expanded per user from feedback and explanations, and a per-user transformer that predicts the adaptation and attends to concepts for explanations. On interview data from five older adults, it reaches 0.71 accuracy with 40 samples (oracle 0.89), beating few-shot GPT-4 and a rule-based baseline, and gives better explanations. Preference change, lifelong learning and user-specific commonsense are left to future work.
user_evidence: Sparse user feedback on preferred assistance mode for household tasks
usil_relation: It learns individual users' procedural preferences about who acts and when (do now, do later, remind, no action) from sparse verbal feedback, and generalizes them to unseen household tasks through concept representations. This is close to USIL's P1 and P2 for a per-user interaction policy on a robot.
open_question: Can the concept-based per-user preference model handle drift and longitudinal feedback, and learn when to ask for feedback or confirm, rather than only predicting allocation from a fixed offline interview dataset? Does it transfer across users or sessions?
evaluation_scale: Interview dataset from 5 older adults (65-85) covering 74-85 tasks each (173 distinct tasks), with per-person k-fold cross-validation and 10-40 training samples; plus a qualitative robot demo

title: Towards Automating Data Access Permissions in AI Agents
authors: Yuhao Wu, Ke Yang, Franziska Roesner, Tadayoshi Kohno, Ning Zhang, Umar Iqbal
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P) 2026 (accepted); arXiv preprint arXiv:2511.17959
summary: This paper proposes automating data-access permissions for AI agents, so that a permission assistant learns from a user's decision history and decides on their behalf. A vignette study with 205 US participants covers 8 domains and 21 tools, and it identifies the factors that drive permission decisions. A hybrid predictor, combining o3-mini in-context learning with LightGCN collaborative filtering, reaches 85.1% accuracy overall and 94.4% at 25.9% coverage for high-confidence predictions. Uncertain cases are deferred to the user. Accuracy falls for high-variance users and sensitive data types. Preference drift, real deployment and interaction cost are untested. Data and code are released.
user_evidence: Past allow/deny permission decisions, demographics, self-reported privacy and AI attitudes, and other users' decisions (collaborative filtering)
usil_relation: It learns a per-user predictor of permission decisions from each user's own history and defers low-confidence cases to the user. This is a concrete per-user autonomy and deference policy, a form of procedure_individual, in which the agent learns when it may act on its own and when it must ask. Hybrid LLM in-context learning plus collaborative filtering gives cross-user and cross-domain transfer.
open_question: Do these predictions hold with real, longitudinal agent use rather than stated vignette decisions, including preference drift, and does automating permissions actually reduce interruptions and prompt fatigue or change trust? Neither was measured here. Can the confidence threshold be learned per user and per stakes level, rather than fixed globally?
evaluation_scale: 205 Prolific participants in the US (181 after filtering), 7,563 always/never permission decisions from vignettes, offline 5-fold cross-validation

title: PrefIx: Understand and Adapt to User Preference in Human-Agent Interaction
authors: Jialin Li, Zhenhao Chen, Hanjun Luo, Hanan Salam
summary: PrefIx is a configurable simulation environment for evaluating how LLM agents interact, not only what they accomplish. It treats interaction behaviors as structured tool calls (Interaction-as-a-Tool). It also provides a taxonomy of 14 preference attributes (31 settings), a preference-guided LLM user simulator, and a multi-judge LLM evaluation across seven UX dimensions. In tests on BFCL multi-turn tasks with four LLMs, prompting agents to infer preferences from an interaction history raised UX by 7.6% and preference alignment by 18.5%, while mostly preserving tool-use accuracy. Users are all simulated and nothing is trained. Transfer and long-term adaptation are not tested.
user_evidence: interaction preference annotations
usil_relation: PrefIx evaluates whether agents infer a user's implicit procedural interaction preferences (confirmation frequency, transparency, pacing, error handling) from interaction history and adapt which interaction tools they call. This is close to the USIL target of procedure-level personalization, and it adds a UX-focused evaluation beyond task success.
open_question: Do agents learn per-user interaction policies from real users' sparse, evolving, possibly conflicting signals (takeovers, corrections) over many sessions, rather than inferring one of 31 fixed LLM-simulated preference settings from a single prompted history? Will the gains transfer to new tasks and real people?
evaluation_scale: GPT-4.1 simulated users across 31 preference settings and 283 BFCL tasks per condition, four LLM agents and four LLM judges; human validation by 5 volunteers rating 20 interactions

title: Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models
authors: Belinda Z. Li, Alex Tamkin, Noah Goodman, Jacob Andreas
summary: This paper introduces Generative Active Task Elicitation (GATE), in which a language model interviews a user with free-form questions, yes/no questions or generated edge cases to elicit task preferences. It then predicts that user's labels from the transcript. No model is trained: GPT-4 is prompted both as the questioner and as the predictor. In a pre-registered study with 388 participants across email validation, content recommendation and moral reasoning, GATE usually beats no elicitation and often beats user-written prompts, supervised learning and pool-based active learning. Users report equal or lower mental demand. The paper studies one session only, with no cross-session or cross-task transfer, and the elicitation policy is not optimized.
what_is_learned: No model is trained. GPT-4 is prompted as an elicitation policy that asks questions or generates edge cases, and as a predictor conditioned on the individual user's elicitation transcript. The per-user specification is the transcript itself.
user_evidence: answers to questions
usil_relation: GATE has an LM ask questions adaptively, conditioned on a single user's transcript, to learn that user's individual task preferences. It is evaluated with 388 real participants and a measured effort cost. This is close to USIL's ask/clarify decisions and user-evidence framing. What it learns is the user's task preferences (the outcome side), not how the agent should interact.
open_question: GATE elicits what a user wants for a task within one session using a fixed prompted question policy. Can an agent learn per-user procedural preferences, such as how much questioning each user tolerates and when to stop asking, and carry them across sessions and tasks?
evaluation_scale: 388 human participants (Prolific and university), 20-30 per domain-method cell, 3 domains, 5-minute elicitation each; supplementary LM-persona model-model study

title: Modeling Future Conversation Turns to Teach LLMs to Ask Clarifying Questions
authors: Michael J. Q. Zhang, W. Bradley Knox, Eunsol Choi
summary: The paper trains LLMs to ask clarifying questions for ambiguous queries by labeling preferences with simulated future turns rather than single-turn quality. Each distinct gold answer in NQ-Open/AmbigQA defines a simulated user, and a user simulator answers the clarifying question. Responses are ranked by whether the final answer matches that user's expected answer, then used for SFT and DPO. Double-turn labels improve answer F1 by about 5% across three base LLMs. A clarify-or-answer model improves direct-answer accuracy while using fewer turns. Limitations: simulated users, short factoid QA, and at most two turns. It does not address persistent per-user personalization.
user_evidence: Annotated/simulated user answers to clarifying questions and resulting final-answer quality across multiple annotated interpretations
usil_relation: The Clarify-or-Direct-Ans DPO policy learns when to ask a clarifying question versus answer directly, and favors direct answers on ties to limit turns. This is the procedure_averaged baseline that USIL would individualize. Simulated users each hold a different intended interpretation of an ambiguous query.
open_question: Could double-turn preference labels be made user-conditioned, so that the ask-or-answer threshold adapts to a persistent user's history, such as tolerance for questions or how often their query interpretations repeat, rather than being averaged over simulated annotators on NQ-Open/AmbigQA?
evaluation_scale: AmbigQA test set (1,960 questions) with a GPT-4 user simulator; one simulated user per gold answer; three base LLMs (Llama2-7b, Gemma-7b, Llama3-8b); significance tested over 10,000 samples

title: MultiSessionCollab: Learning User Preferences with Memory to Improve Long-Term Collaboration
authors: Shuhaib Mehri, Priyanka Kargupta, Tal August, Dilek Hakkani-Tür
summary: MultiSessionCollab is a benchmark for whether conversational agents learn user interaction preferences across 20 sessions and use them to improve collaboration. Preference-driven simulated users enforce preferences, and effort is counted as the number of enforcements. The authors build a reflection-based memory agent that keeps per-user natural-language notes. They also train reflection generation with SFT and GRPO, using rewards from simulator behavior. Memory improves task success, effort, and conversation length, and it beats Mem0. A 19-person human study shows fewer turns and higher satisfaction, but weak cross-domain transfer. Preferences are explicit and static, and no interaction policy is learned.
user_evidence: multi-session interaction feedback
usil_relation: Learns per-user interaction preferences (formatting, communication, and clarification style) as persistent natural-language memory across 20 sessions, and measures user effort as preference-enforcement count rather than task success alone. This is close to the USIL idea of learning how the agent works for each user.
open_question: Can the memory move from static, explicit, simulator-stated preferences to implicit, evolving, context-dependent procedural preferences, and then drive a learned per-user policy for when to ask, confirm, or defer? Cross-domain transfer, which the human study found weak, also needs work.
evaluation_scale: 100 LLM-simulated user profiles × 20 sessions (10,000 sessions per agent) with Llama-3.3-70B as simulator; plus a 19-participant human study with three sessions in single- and mixed-domain conditions

title: Learning Personalized Agents from Human Feedback
authors: Kaiqu Liang, Julia Kruk, Shengyi Qian, Xianjun Yang, Shengjie Bi, Yuanshun Yao, Shaoliang Nie, Mingyang Zhang, Lijuan Liu, Jaime Fernández Fisac, Shuyan Zhou, Saghar Hosseini
summary: PAHF is a framework for continual agent personalization that pairs explicit per-user natural-language memory with proactive pre-action clarification and reactive post-action feedback. A ReAct-prompted GPT-4o agent retrieves notes, asks at most one question when memory is empty and the task is ambiguous, acts, and updates memory from corrective feedback. A four-phase protocol (learn, test, drift, adapted test) on embodied and shopping benchmarks with simulated personas shows PAHF beats no-memory and single-channel baselines; pre-action-only is brittle under drift. The paper does not train an interaction policy, uses no real users, and does not test transfer across users.
user_evidence: answers to clarifying questions; post-action feedback
usil_relation: PAHF is a near neighbor of USIL: it keeps per-user memory, learns online from clarification answers and post-action corrections, tests preference drift, and decides when to ask using that memory. However, what is learned is mostly outcome-level content preference (which item or location). Asking is a fixed rule rather than a learned per-user interaction policy.
open_question: Can the ask/act/confirm decision itself become user-specific, for example learning from real users that one person wants a question while another wants the agent to act, instead of the fixed 'ask once if memory is empty and the task is ambiguous' rule? Can that be evaluated with real users and cross-user transfer?
evaluation_scale: LLM-simulated personas: 40 users × 30 scenarios per phase (embodied, 1,200 per phase) and 20 users × 45 scenarios per phase (shopping, 900 per phase), across four phases

title: Training Proactive and Personalized LLM Agents
authors: Weiwei Sun, Xuhui Zhou, Weihua Du, et al. (incl. Graham Neubig, Maarten Sap, Yiming Yang)
summary: The paper introduces UserVille, an environment with preference-aware LLM user simulators that rate the effort of each agent question, and PPP, a multi-objective RL framework that jointly optimizes Productivity, Proactivity and Personalization. Seed-OSS-36B agents trained with PPP on SWE and deep-research tasks learn to ask on vague prompts, keep questions low-effort and follow one of 20 stated interaction preferences. They beat GPT-5 by about 16.7 points on average, generalize to unseen preferences, other simulators and SWE-Full, and score 3.75 in a 33-person user study. Preferences are fixed and given, with no cross-session learning.
user_evidence: simulated user answers to questions, user-centric feedback on preference adherence and effort, task outcome
usil_relation: PPP trains an ask-or-act policy that is conditioned on a stated user interaction preference and rewarded for low user effort. This is close to a user-conditioned interaction policy pi_u(a|s,h), but the preference is given to the agent as a discrete label rather than learned from user evidence.
open_question: Can the agent infer a user's interaction preferences (question effort, format, ask frequency) from sparse corrections and answers across sessions, instead of being told one of 20 fixed preferences, and does the learned policy hold up when real users' preferences drift or conflict?
evaluation_scale: LLM-simulated users (GPT-5-Nano) with 20 preferences (12 seen, 8 unseen) on SWE-Bench Verified (488 instances) and BrowseComp-Plus (100 test); Prolific study with 33 programmers on 100 SWE tasks (300 evaluation tasks).

title: Hedwig: Dynamic Autonomy for Coding Agents Under Local Oversight
authors: Tanjal Shukla, K. J. Kevin Feng, Leijie Wang, Mohammad Rostami, Amy X. Zhang
venue: ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems (CAIS 2026), demo; arXiv preprint arXiv:2605.11495
summary: Hedwig is a local CLI coding agent that learns when to check in with the developer instead of relying on static permissions or instruction files. It scores each proposed action with a per-repository online logistic regression over 13 action features, trained on approvals, denials and corrections. Hard constraints sit above the learned policy. Actions either proceed silently, proceed with a post-run flag, or trigger a live check-in with an explanation. Retrieved text snippets add guidance. On synthetic cautious and permissive personas, Hedwig had higher check-in recall than Claude Code with CLAUDE.md rules but more false positives for the permissive persona. The evaluation is a single illustrative run with no user study.
user_evidence: Developer approval/oversight decisions and feedback during coding sessions
usil_relation: Hedwig learns a per-repository, trust-based autonomy policy from approvals and denials to decide when a coding agent checks in, which is close to a user-conditioned interaction policy pi_u. It is a near-direct instance of procedure_individual learning.
open_question: Do learned check-in policies hold up with real developers over weeks, including preference drift, transfer across repositories and to higher-risk operations, and measured interruption burden and trust? The current evidence is a single run on seeded synthetic personas.
evaluation_scale: 2 synthetic personas (cautious, permissive), 20 seeded decisions replayed 3x, 2 backend tasks (11 write ops), single run; formative survey of 21 developers only for motivation

title: Getting Better at Working With You: Compiling User Corrections into Runtime Enforcement for Coding Agents
authors: Yujun Zhou, Kehan Guo, Haomin Zhuang, et al. (incl. Nitesh V. Chawla, Xiangliang Zhang)
summary: The paper identifies an access-compliance gap in coding agents: storing a user's correction in memory does not ensure the agent follows it later. Trace is a drop-in skill-layer pipeline that detects corrections in chat and compiles them into a per-user library of atomic rules, each with an applicability check, behavior instruction, and verifier. A lifecycle resolver handles repeated, refined, or contradicting preferences, and verifiers gate task completion. On ClawArena and MemoryArena-derived tasks with simulated users, Trace lowers violation rates (to 2.0% OOD on ClawArena) and user turns versus memory baselines. Evaluation is frozen, uses simulated users, and does not test cross-user transfer.
user_evidence: natural-language corrections in chat (anonymized real-user cases)
usil_relation: Trace turns each user's corrections into a persistent per-user library of enforceable behavioral rules (what files to leave behind, which commands to run, when to ask before modifying state). These are procedural preferences learned from user-specific edits and corrections across sessions, which is close to USIL's per-user interaction policy.
open_question: Can compiled rules cover when to ask, confirm, or defer, rather than only enforcing fixed constraints at termination? Do they hold up with real users whose preferences drift, with online updating at test time, and with cross-user or cross-task transfer? The main experiments use simulated users and the real-user diagnostic is a single researcher.
evaluation_scale: Simulated users profiled from one researcher's history. ClawArena has 62 scenarios (32 ID, 30 OOD) and MemoryArena-derived tasks, across 4 agent models. The diagnostic uses 32 transcripts, 142 correction-conflict records, 19 tasks, and 6 models.

title: KnowU-Bench: Towards Interactive, Proactive, and Personalized Mobile Agent Evaluation
authors: Tongbo Chen, Zhengxi Lu, Zhan Xu, et al.
summary: KnowU-Bench is an online benchmark for personalized, proactive mobile GUI agents in a reproducible Android emulator with 23 apps. It has 42 general, 86 personalized, and 64 proactive tasks. Agents see only behavioral logs, clean or noisy, while a GPT-4o user simulator holds a hidden profile for one of four roles. Agents must infer preferences, ask clarifying questions, and decide whether to act, seek consent, stay silent, or stop after rejection. Hybrid rule and LLM-judge scoring is used. Across 11 models, the best (Claude Sonnet 4.6) reaches 60.4% overall but 44.2% on hard personalized tasks. Failures stem mainly from preference acquisition and intervention calibration rather than GUI navigation.
what_is_learned: Nothing is trained. This is a benchmark that tests whether existing mobile GUI agents can infer hidden user preferences from behavioral logs and clarification dialogue, and whether they choose well among acting, asking for consent, staying silent, and stopping after rejection.
user_evidence: behavioral logs, answers to clarification questions, consent and rejection responses
usil_relation: KnowU-Bench evaluates the full proactive decision chain (act, ask consent, stay silent, stop after rejection) against hidden user profiles in a live Android environment. This is the closest benchmark to USIL's when-to-ask/act/defer decisions, with user-specific preference inference from logs and clarification [interaction_decisions][user_evidence].
open_question: Does an agent improve its ask/act/silent calibration for a specific user across repeated sessions as preferences drift? KnowU-Bench uses only four synthetic roles, static logs, and a single GPT-4o simulator, with no longitudinal adaptation, per-user interaction-policy learning, or transfer to new users.
evaluation_scale: GPT-4o-simulated users with 4 synthetic role profiles; 192 tasks (42 general, 86 personalized, 64 proactive) across 23 apps; 11 models; judge validated by 4 human experts on 26 trajectories

title: VitaBench 2.0: Evaluating Personalized and Proactive Agents in Long-Term User Interactions
authors: Yuxin Chen, Yi Zhang, Zhengzhou Cai, et al.
summary: VitaBench 2.0 is a benchmark of 56 users and 819 temporally ordered tool-using tasks across delivery, in-store, and travel domains. User preferences are hidden in noisy dialogues and behavior logs and drift between tasks. Some tasks are proactive, requiring the agent to ask or explore when context is missing. An extensible UPDATE/RETRIEVE memory interface compares full context, agentic memory, and RAG. About 25 LLMs reach only ~0.5 Avg@4 and ~0.3 Pass^4. Memory often hurts relative to full context, performance falls with task index, and proactive tasks are harder than personalization. Users are synthetic and no transfer experiment is reported.
what_is_learned: No learning is proposed. VitaBench 2.0 is an evaluation benchmark that measures whether LLM agents can extract, use, and update implicit user preferences from long-term histories, using LLM-driven agentic memory rewriting, RAG memory, or full context. These memory mechanisms are evaluated, not trained.
user_evidence: Longitudinal per-user interaction histories with scattered, evolving preferences
usil_relation: VitaBench 2.0 builds per-user temporally ordered task sequences with implicit preferences, noisy histories, and injected drift, and an interface for comparing memory architectures. This is the closest benchmark for longitudinal personalized agent evaluation. Its proactive tasks (ask when context is missing) touch on when to ask, but they are scored by task rubrics rather than as a user-specific interaction policy.
open_question: Can proactive ask-or-act behavior be evaluated as a per-user procedural preference, where users differ in how much clarification or autonomy they want, rather than as a fixed rubric of when to ask? Do the results hold with real users and with cross-domain transfer, given that preferences are synthetic and no transfer experiment is reported?
evaluation_scale: 56 curated/synthetic users, 819 tasks, ~2,286 preference annotations, GPT-4.1 user simulator, ~25 LLMs, 4 runs each

title: Direct manipulation vs. interface agents
authors: Ben Shneiderman, Pattie Maes
summary: This 1997 interactions debate transcript has Ben Shneiderman argue for direct manipulation, with its predictability, user control and responsibility, and Pattie Maes argue for software agents that learn a user's interests and act proactively. Maes describes agents such as Letizia, Yenta, Firefly and Kasbah that learn from browsing, email and files, and says users must be able to bypass them. The two partly converge: agents may operate beneath a predictable, visible interface, and both stress user understanding and control. No empirical results are reported, and the discussion of costs, errors and risk is qualitative. Shneiderman urges rigorous user evaluation.
usil_relation: The Maes-Shneiderman debate frames the autonomy-versus-control tension that USIL treats as learnable: proactive agents that know the individual user's habits [personalization] against predictable, controllable interfaces, with Maes insisting users can bypass the agent [interaction_decisions].
open_question: Can the per-user choice of when an agent should act proactively versus defer to direct control be learned from one user's corrections, takeovers and bypass behavior, and evaluated with the scientific user studies Shneiderman requests?

title: Know Me, Respond to Me: Benchmarking LLMs for Dynamic User Profiling and Personalized Responses at Scale
authors: Bowen Jiang, Zhuoqun Hao, Young-Min Cho, et al. (incl. Lyle Ungar, Camillo J. Taylor, Dan Roth)
summary: PersonaMem is a benchmark for dynamic user profiling and personalized responses. It uses simulated multi-session user-chatbot histories for 20 personas, with timestamped preference changes and reasons across 15 topics, at 32k to 1M tokens. Seven in-situ query types test fact recall, tracking of preference evolution, applying the latest situation, and generalizing to new scenarios. In a multiple-choice format, 15 LLMs reach only about 50% accuracy overall, and struggle most to incorporate users' latest situations. RAG and Mem0 improve results, with RAG ahead on most question types. No model is trained and no interaction decisions are studied. The data are synthetic.
what_is_learned: Nothing is trained. The benchmark tests whether off-the-shelf LLMs, with optional RAG or Mem0 memory, can use multi-session histories to pick the response that fits a persona's current traits and evolving preferences.
user_evidence: long multi-session conversation histories with preference changes over time
usil_relation: PersonaMem tests whether LLMs track evolving per-persona preferences across long multi-session histories and transfer them to new tasks, which is the longitudinal, individual-level evaluation USIL calls for. It covers only response content, not interaction behavior.
open_question: Can a PersonaMem-style timelined persona benchmark be extended to procedural preferences, such as when a user wants clarification, confirmation, or autonomy, and to real users rather than synthetic personas, with per-user results?
evaluation_scale: 20 synthetic personas, 180+ simulated histories (32k/128k/1M tokens), about 6k query-response pairs, 15 LLMs; human validation of 90 pairs

title: Collaborative Gym: A Framework for Enabling and Evaluating Human-Agent Collaboration
authors: Yijia Shao, Vinay Samuel, Yucheng Jiang, John Yang, Diyi Yang
summary: Collaborative Gym (Co-Gym) is an open framework for enabling and evaluating human-agent collaboration. It offers dual-control task environments, a non-turn-taking protocol of collaboration acts and notifications, and an evaluation suite covering outcomes and process. Agents are prompted ReAct LMs, some with situational planning that decides whether to act, message, or wait. Experiments cover travel planning, related-work writing, and tabular analysis with simulated users and 99 real participants. Collaborative agents beat autonomous ones in win rate (66-86%), though delivery rates are lower. Communication and situational-awareness errors are common. Nothing is learned per user or across sessions.
what_is_learned: No model is trained. Agents are prompted ReAct LMs with an in-session scratchpad and an optional situational-planning step. The paper contributes a collaboration framework, benchmark comparisons, an error taxonomy and collaboration patterns rather than a learned component.
user_evidence: real and simulated users
usil_relation: Co-Gym evaluates process-level collaboration (initiative balance, communication and situational-awareness errors, Personalization as an error category at 16% of real cases) with 99 real participants. It also tests a 3-way act/message/wait decision. This is the procedure-focused, human-in-the-loop evaluation infrastructure that USIL would need.
open_question: Can Co-Gym's real and simulated environments be extended to multi-session, per-participant studies in which an agent learns each user's preferred asking/acting/waiting balance, and are the Initiative Entropy and Overall Satisfaction metrics reported per user instead of averaged?
evaluation_scale: 99 participants contributing 150 real trajectories (50 per task); 312 simulated task instances with an LM user simulator; 20 Upwork professionals in the ablation

title: Learning to Summarize User Information for Personalized Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
authors: Hyunji Nam, Yanming Wan, Mickel Liu, Jianxun Lian, Peter Ahnn, Natasha Jaques
summary: PLUS (Preference Learning Using Summaries) personalizes RLHF reward models by learning natural-language summaries of each user from past conversations and preference examples. An RL-trained summarizer and a summary-conditioned reward model are trained jointly, with the summarizer rewarded by the reward model's loss. PLUS improves reward accuracy over BTL by 11-77% on synthetic benchmarks, stays above 90% on out-of-distribution Pets topics and users, and gives modest gains on PRISM, though held-out-user transfer is weak. Summaries can also personalize GPT-4o/4.1 judgments and responses without fine-tuning. It addresses output preferences, not interaction decisions, drift, or live users.
user_evidence: user preference data
usil_relation: PLUS learns an individual, human-readable user summary from past conversations and preference examples and conditions a reward model on it, matching USIL's optional z_u = g(h). The summaries also transfer to GPT-4o/4.1 prompts without fine-tuning. This is the outcome_individual cell.
open_question: Could PLUS-style summaries encode procedural preferences (when to ask, confirm, or defer) learned from takeovers and corrections, and would they track preference drift across sessions and generalize to held-out users, where PRISM transfer was poor?
evaluation_scale: Offline evaluation with synthetic users (Pets, UltraFeedback-P2/P4) and PRISM dataset (1,000 training users, 308 held-out users); 3 seeds for some settings, otherwise one; no live human study

title: Robust AI Personalization Will Require a Human Context Protocol
authors: Anand Shah, Tobin South, Talfan Evans, Hannah Rose Kirk, Andrew Trask, E. Glen Weyl, Michiel A. Bakker
summary: This position paper argues that robust AI personalization needs a Human Context Protocol (HCP): a user-governed, portable layer that stores natural-language preferences and shares them across AI systems. An intermediary LLM interprets requests and discloses only scoped, minimal context to downstream models. The paper gives design attributes, an example architecture, a minimal open-source prototype (web app with MCP server, no orchestrating LLM), and responses to counterarguments on adoption, incentives, and high-stakes use. It includes clarification protocols and user-chosen ask-first tiers for sensitive categories, but nothing is learned or empirically evaluated. Benchmarks and metrics are left to future work.
user_evidence: user-stated preferences
usil_relation: The HCP's user-owned, portable natural-language preference store with provenance, versioning, and time-indexed profiles is an architectural counterpart to USIL's user representation z_u. Its user-set ask-first tiers for high-stakes categories also touch the question of when an agent should ask or defer.
open_question: Could an HCP-style portable store hold learned procedural preferences (when to ask, confirm, or hand back control), inferred from edits, takeovers, and approvals rather than only explicit statements, and would those preferences transfer across providers and tasks?

title: Autonomy Reshapes How Personalization Affects Privacy Concerns and Trust in LLM Agents
authors: Zhiping Zhang, Yi Evie Zhang, Freda Shi, Tianshi Li
summary: This paper reports a 3×3 between-subjects experiment (N=450) crossing agent autonomy (none, risk-contingent, full) with personalization (none, privacy-aware, full) for an LLM agent that speaks on a user's behalf in group chats. Full personalization raised privacy concerns and lowered trust. Risk-contingent autonomy, where the agent asks for approval only when a detector flags sensitive content, attenuated these effects, with perceived control as the mediator. Full autonomy showed no significant effects. No model is trained and no per-user adaptation is studied. The study covers a single session and two scenarios. It offers population-level evidence that confirmation and return-of-control policies shape trust.
what_is_learned: No model is trained. The paper estimates empirical effects (mixed-effects regression, moderated-mediation SEM) of agent autonomy and personalization on privacy concern, trust, and willingness to use. The agent uses prompt-based personalization and an LLM-as-judge sensitivity detector that triggers a confirmation request.
user_evidence: self-reported privacy concern, trust, perceived control, willingness to use
usil_relation: Risk-contingent autonomy is a confirmation and return-of-control policy that depends on the stakes of the content (sensitive vs. not). The user's self-marked sensitive items also define a personal data-flow boundary [user_signals][interaction_decisions]. This is close to USIL's idea of deciding when to confirm or defer.
open_question: Could the sensitivity threshold and confirmation policy be learned per user from approvals, edits, and self-marked boundaries over repeated sessions, rather than fixed for everyone? Would the gain in perceived control hold given individual differences in AI literacy and agency, and given decision fatigue?
evaluation_scale: 450 valid Prolific participants (of 538) in a 3×3 between-subjects online experiment, 50 per condition; the detector was evaluated on 2,250 messages

title: Position: A Roadmap to Pluralistic Alignment
authors: Taylor Sorensen et al.
