summary: This ICML 2024 position paper offers a conceptual roadmap for pluralistic alignment of LLMs. It formalizes three kinds of pluralistic models (Overton, steerable, distributional) and three kinds of benchmarks (multi-objective, trade-off steerable, jury-pluralistic). A small offline experiment uses GlobalOpinionQA and MPI survey distributions. It finds that post-alignment models (Alpaca, Tulu, LLaMA2-Chat, Gemma IT, GPT-3.5) have higher Jensen-Shannon distance from human answer distributions and lower entropy than pre-aligned base models. No personalization method is implemented or tested, and no individual user data or interaction decisions are studied. Its relevance to USIL is as a framing for individual-level evaluation of outputs.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned as a method. The paper defines Overton, steerable and distributional pluralistic models and multi-objective, trade-off steerable and jury-pluralistic benchmarks. Its only experiment compares pre- vs post-alignment LLM answer distributions to human survey distributions.
user_evidence: n/a
usil_relation: Steerable pluralism for customization and jury-pluralistic benchmarks that model individual jurors' utilities (per-juror reward models) conceptually anticipate individual-level evaluation [personalization][user_representation]. They concern outputs and values, not interaction procedure.
open_question: Can the jury-pluralistic benchmark idea, with per-person utility functions, be extended from output preferences to per-user procedural preferences such as when to ask, confirm or defer, and be evaluated longitudinally?

title: Learning to Clarify: Multi-turn Conversations with Action-Based Contrastive Self-Training
authors: Maximillian Chen, Ruoxi Sun, Tomas Pfister, Sercan Ö. Arık
summary: ACT (Action-Based Contrastive Self-Training) is a quasi-online DPO method that teaches LLMs to implicitly choose between asking a clarifying question and answering under ambiguity. It builds action-contrastive preference pairs and uses on-policy sampling with LLM-simulated user replies to evaluate multi-turn trajectories. The paper also introduces AmbigSQL, an ambiguous text-to-SQL task. Tuned on as few as 50 conversations, ACT beats SFT and IRPO on action recognition and trajectory quality across tabular QA, reading-comprehension QA, and SQL. Users are simulated and there is no personalization or adaptation over time, so it is a population-level clarification policy.
user_evidence: Small sets of conversations with implicit action labels plus simulated user replies during self-training
usil_relation: ACT learns a clarify-vs-answer decision policy from preference optimization over action-contrastive pairs and simulated trajectories. This is the procedure-averaged counterpart to USIL's pi_u, covering the 'when to ask' decision for a population.
open_question: Could ACT's action-contrastive DPO be conditioned on a per-user interaction history, so the clarify/answer threshold adapts to each user's tolerance for questions? Could it be evaluated with real users rather than LLM simulators, and with an explicit cost for interruption?
evaluation_scale: LLM (Gemini Ultra) user simulator; Zephyr 7B-β tuned on 50/100/250 conversations per task across PACIFIC, Abg-CoQA, and AmbigSQL

title: Bayesian Preference Elicitation with Language Models
authors: Kunal Handa, Yarin Gal, Ellie Pavlick, et al.
summary: OPEN combines Bayesian Optimal Experimental Design with language models to elicit user preferences in open-ended domains. An LM extracts natural-language features and verbalizes abstract pairwise queries. A particle-filter Bayesian linear model keeps a per-user posterior over feature weights and picks the next question by expected information gain. In a Prolific study on news-article recommendation (about 40 users per condition), OPEN beats LM-only and BOED-only baselines on time-integrated delta accuracy, with similar reported mental demand. It is limited to pairwise queries, one domain, a fixed 10-feature space and single sessions, with no transfer or drift evaluation.
user_evidence: User answers to natural-language preference questions
usil_relation: OPEN learns an individual Bayesian belief over each user's preferences from pairwise answers and picks the next question by expected information gain, which is a user-specific elicitation mechanism. This overlaps with USIL's learning from sparse user evidence and its asking decisions.
open_question: The learned user model captures preferences over content features, not procedural preferences. How would a BOED-style policy extend to deciding whether to ask, confirm, or defer, with per-user tolerance for questions, and persist across sessions and tasks?
evaluation_scale: About 40 Prolific participants per condition (39-48), each with a 5-minute elicitation and 15 pairwise news-article test comparisons.

title: When Users Change Their Mind: Evaluating Interruptible Agents in Long-Horizon Web Navigation
authors: Henry Peng Zou, Chunyu Miao, Wei-Chieh Huang, et al.
summary: InterruptBench is a benchmark for how LLM web agents handle user interruptions mid-task in long-horizon, state-changing web navigation. Built from 165 WebArena-Lite tasks, it uses LLM-synthesized interruption messages (addition, revision, retraction) injected at a progress-relative point, including up to three interruptions. Six LLM backbones in the WebAgent-R1 scaffold are compared against matched no-interruption baselines using success rate, post-interruption success curves SR(k), and token and action overhead. Success rises quickly then plateaus. Token overhead dominates cost, and failed episodes incur the most. Interruption handling remains a bottleneck, and open-weight models gain less from added interruptions. The users are simulated and there is no personalization.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned by the paper. It is an evaluation benchmark measuring how fixed LLM web agents adapt in-context to mid-task user intent updates (addition, revision, retraction).
user_evidence: Mid-task user interruptions (goal additions, revisions, retractions)
usil_relation: InterruptBench evaluates agents reacting to mid-task user interruptions (add, revise, retract) in stateful WebArena tasks, and it measures adaptation cost and multi-interruption effects [temporal_adaptation][key_results]. That is close to takeover and intervention signals in USIL, but the interruptions are treated as task-intent updates, not as evidence about a user's interaction preferences.
open_question: Could InterruptBench-style interruptions be extended to real or persistent simulated users, so that interruption patterns (when and why a given user intervenes) are learned per user and used to change when the agent asks, confirms, or defers, with per-user results reported?
evaluation_scale: LLM-synthesized interruption messages on 165 human-verified WebArena-Lite tasks, six LLM backbones, 1–3 interruptions

title: STaR-GATE: Teaching Language Models to Ask Clarifying Questions
authors: Chinmaya Andukuri, Jan-Philipp Fränken, Tobias Gerstenberg, Noah D. Goodman
summary: STaR-GATE is an iterative self-improvement method that finetunes a language model to ask better clarifying questions. A simulated persona-playing roleplayer answers, and a GPT-4 oracle with persona access supplies gold responses. The model is trained on conversations whose questions raise the log-probability of the gold response, with answers masked from the loss and regularization on the model's own responses. After two iterations, responses win 72% of GPT-4 pairwise comparisons against the initial model, and gains transfer to other roleplayers. Users are entirely simulated, there is no persistent user model or cross-session adaptation, and when to ask versus stop is not learned.
user_evidence: simulated user answers
usil_relation: STaR-GATE trains a questioning policy rewarded by how well elicited persona info improves a personalized response, which is the 'ask/clarify' part of a user-conditioned interaction policy. The policy is conditioned only on in-context Q&A history, with a simulated persona as the user [user_representation][personalization].
open_question: Can the questioning policy be made individual, learning per real user across sessions when to ask versus act, and when to stop asking, instead of using uniformly random termination and a population-trained policy evaluated only on GPT-4-simulated personas?
evaluation_scale: 10 held-out GPT-4-generated personas x 50 held-out tasks, 10 simulated conversations per pair, using LLM roleplayers (mixtral, mistral, gemma) and a GPT-4 judge; no human users

title: Introspective Planning: Aligning Robots' Uncertainty with Inherent Task Ambiguity
authors: Kaiqu Liang, Zixu Zhang, Jaime Fernández Fisac
summary: Introspective planning aligns an LLM robot planner's uncertainty with the inherent ambiguity of a task. It retrieves LLM-generated rationales, post-hoc explanations of human-selected valid plans, from a knowledge base and combines them with conformal prediction. The robot acts when one option remains and asks for clarification otherwise, reducing overask and overstep while keeping statistical guarantees. The authors add a Safe Mobile Manipulation benchmark with safety-critical cases. Offline experiments with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on three datasets beat KnowNo and prompting baselines. There is no personalization, no real users and no adaptation over time; the work is about task-level ambiguity.
what_is_learned: No model is trained. The method builds a retrieval knowledge base of (task, candidate plans, rationale, valid options) entries, keyed by instruction embeddings. Conformal prediction calibrates a threshold q̂ so the planner asks for clarification when more than one option remains plausible. This is task-level uncertainty calibration, not a user-specific policy.
user_evidence: task ambiguity
usil_relation: It decides when to act versus ask for clarification using calibrated uncertainty with statistical guarantees. Overask and overstep rates quantify the interaction cost of that decision [interaction_decisions][interaction_costs]. This matches the USIL ask/act decision, but the policy is calibrated for task ambiguity across a population, not per user.
open_question: Could the introspective retrieval and conformal threshold be conditioned on an individual user's history so the ask/act boundary reflects that user's tolerance for clarification queries and their ambiguity preferences, rather than one global q̂ at an 85% target?

title: Tell Me More! Towards Implicit User Intention Understanding of Language Model Driven Agents
authors: Cheng Qian, Bingxiang He, Zhong Zhuang, et al.
summary: IN3 is a benchmark of vague and clear agent tasks annotated with missing details, built to test whether models can recognize vagueness and recover implicit user intentions. The authors fine-tune Mistral-7B on GPT-4-simulated assistant-user dialogues to produce Mistral-Interact, which judges vagueness, asks one query per round with suggested options, and summarizes the intentions into a clear goal. Evaluated with eight real users, it reaches 85% vagueness accuracy and 96% summary coverage, approaching GPT-4. As an upstream module for XAgent on ten tasks, it sharply reduces unnecessary subtasks. Personalization, memory and cross-session adaptation are explicitly left for future work.
user_evidence: User answers to clarifying questions about missing task details (simulated and human)
usil_relation: Mistral-Interact learns when to treat an instruction as vague and ask options-based clarifying questions before an agent (XAgent) acts. This is a learned procedural decision (ask vs. pass to execution) in the same family as USIL's P3, and real users answer its queries.
open_question: Can the vagueness-judgment and querying policy be conditioned on a persistent per-user history (e.g., a user's past answers, tolerance for questions, and domain expertise), so that it asks fewer or different questions for a given user across sessions, and does that beat the population-averaged Mistral-Interact on per-user effort and satisfaction?
evaluation_scale: 8 real undergraduate-level users over 108 IN3 test tasks, plus 10 tasks in XAgent; training data from GPT-4 simulated users (1,261 tasks)

title: Robots That Ask for Help: Uncertainty Alignment for Large Language Model Planners
authors: Allen Z. Ren et al.
summary: KNOWNO makes LLM robot planners know when they don't know. It applies conformal prediction to LLM multiple-choice next-step scores and calibrates a threshold on about 400 held-out scenarios, without fine-tuning. If the prediction set is a singleton, the robot acts. Otherwise it asks the human to choose among the options. The method gives single- and multi-step task-success guarantees at a user-specified level and reduces help by 10-24% versus baselines in simulation and on hardware. The human is simulated and assumed faithful, and there is no per-user modelling or adaptation over time, so this is a population-level asking policy.
user_evidence: task uncertainty
usil_relation: KNOWNO is a calibrated act-versus-ask policy that uses uncertainty to decide when to request clarification, with a user-specified success level (1−ϵ) controlling how much help is requested. This is the population-level asking policy that USIL would make per-user.
open_question: Could the conformal threshold ϵ and the calibration set be learned per user from that user's own help responses, so the ask/act boundary adapts to each user's tolerance for interruptions and to their preferences? Would coverage guarantees still hold with few, drifting per-user calibration samples?
evaluation_scale: Simulated faithful human; 400 calibration scenarios; 200 simulation trials per method; 50 hardware trials (UR5); 10 bimanual trials; mobile manipulator kitchen experiments.

title: Active Preference-Based Learning of Reward Functions
authors: Dorsa Sadigh, Anca D. Dragan, S. Shankar Sastry, Sanjit A. Seshia
summary: Actively selects comparison queries to learn a human's reward function efficiently.
user_evidence: pairwise comparisons
usil_relation: Query-efficient per-person learning; outcome rewards rather than interaction preferences.

title: RealWebAssist: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Web Assistance with Real-World Users
authors: Suyu Ye, Haojun Shi, Darren Shih, Hyokun Yun, Tanya Roosta, Tianmin Shu
summary: RealWebAssist is a benchmark for long-horizon web assistance with real users. Ten participants gave spoken, ambiguous, evolving instructions to a human operator across 107 shopping, travel and booking tasks. This yielded 1,885 annotated instructions with correct click regions. Offline evaluation covers GUI grounding models, VLMs and LRMs paired with grounders. The best system (o3 + GTA-1) reaches 14.0% task success against 93.4% for humans. Errors split between reasoning (56.7%) and grounding (43.3%). Finetuning on other participants gives marginal gains. User-specific routines and preferences are framed as open challenges, but personalization is not evaluated, and there is no dialogue or asking.
what_is_learned: No model is learned as the main contribution. It is a benchmark for grounding sequential real-user web instructions to GUI click actions. A side experiment finetunes GTA-1 with GRPO on 9 participants' data, which is not user-specific.
user_evidence: Real users' sequential, often ambiguous spoken/typed instructions and their evolving goals within a long session
usil_relation: RealWebAssist collects sequential spoken instructions from 10 real users. It names user-specific routines and preferences as challenges, such as repeated procedural abstractions and revealed preferences like seating, which fits USIL's interest in longitudinal user evidence [personalization][temporal_adaptation]. These remain framed as challenges and are not measured.
open_question: Can RealWebAssist's per-participant data be used to test whether an agent learns an individual's routines and instruction style (e.g., terse, referential) over repeated sessions, with results reported per user? The paper reports only aggregates and says dialogue and asking are future work.
evaluation_scale: 10 participants, 40-minute sessions, 107 tasks, 1,885 instructions, 66 websites; offline evaluation of models on recorded data

title: UserBench: An Interactive Gym Environment for User-Centric Agents
authors: Cheng Qian, Zuxin Liu, Akshara Prabhakar, et al.
summary: UserBench is a Gymnasium-based travel-planning environment for evaluating LLM agents with user-centric interaction. GPT-4o simulated users start with underspecified goals and reveal implicit preferences incrementally, either when asked or after stalled turns. Agents choose among search, clarifying action, and answer across flight, hotel, apartment, car rental, and restaurant tasks, with 4K+ scenarios and a 417-scenario test set. Across 11 LLMs, answers fully match all user intents only about 20% of the time, and even the best models elicit under 30% of preferences through active querying. More turns do not reliably help. The paper does not train agents, personalize across sessions, or test transfer.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned in this paper. It is a benchmark and gym environment for evaluating off-the-shelf LLM agents on inferring hidden, implicit user preferences within a conversation. Training on the environment is only proposed as future work.
user_evidence: Simulated user replies to clarifying questions; implicit preference cues
usil_relation: UserBench evaluates whether agents ask clarifying questions to elicit implicit preferences that a simulated user reveals incrementally across turns. This is the ask-versus-act decision that USIL cares about, and it is scored against hidden ground-truth preferences [user_evidence][interaction_decisions].
open_question: Can a UserBench-style environment be extended so that agents must learn per-user interaction preferences (how often to ask, how much to confirm) across multiple sessions with persistent simulated users whose procedural preferences differ and drift, and be validated against real human users?
evaluation_scale: 417 test scenarios (the paper also states 471) with a GPT-4o user simulator; 11 LLMs, single run at temperature 0, max 20 turns

title: SimulatorArena: Are User Simulators Reliable Proxies for Multi-Turn Evaluation of AI Assistants?
authors: Yao Dou, Michel Galley, Baolin Peng, et al.
summary: SimulatorArena asks whether LLM-simulated users can stand in for real users when evaluating multi-turn AI assistants. The authors collect 909 annotated human–LLM conversations (107 crowdworkers, 9 LLMs) on math tutoring and document creation. They score simulators on message realism and on agreement with human ratings of assistants. Prompted GPT-4o simulators conditioned on automatically extracted user profiles (knowledge or preferences, writing style, interaction style) raise Spearman correlation with human ratings from 0.61 to 0.77 in math tutoring and from 0.55 to 0.70 in document creation. Cost is under 3% of human evaluation. The paper then benchmarks 18 assistants. It covers a single session, with no training and no tested transfer.
user_evidence: Real human conversations and ratings; user profiles for conditioning simulators
usil_relation: It shows that profiles of individual users' interaction style (e.g. 17 interaction attributes in tutoring) make simulated users more realistic and better correlated with human ratings of assistants. This is evidence that individual-level interaction style matters for evaluating multi-turn assistants, and a possible testbed for USIL.
open_question: Can profiles of individual users' interaction style, extracted from single sessions, be learned persistently and used to drive per-user ask/confirm/defer policies. Do they transfer to unseen tasks and later sessions, rather than only reproducing user messages within one conversation?
evaluation_scale: 909 real human–LLM conversations from 107 MTurk participants with 9 LLMs, compared with GPT-4o-simulated users; 18 assistants benchmarked on 50 math problems and 51 document topics

title: CollabSkill: Evaluating Human-Agent Collaboration on Real-World Tasks
authors: Yijia Shao, Zora Zhiruo Wang, Neel Ahuja, Yicheng Wang, Bowen Liu, Diyi Yang
summary: CollabSkill is a framework for evaluating human-agent collaboration on real occupational tasks (GDPval, APEX, APEX-Agents). 93 Upwork workers were randomly paired with one of five agents, producing 386 sessions, rubric-graded deliverables, interaction logs, and pre/post surveys. A Bayesian additive skill model separates latent human and agent skill from scalar scores. Collaboration rankings diverge from autonomous benchmarks: Claude Code beats Codex, and Claude Cowork ranks first. Worker skill varies widely and correlates with LLM familiarity. The paper does not study personalization, adaptation, or agent interaction decisions; it contributes evaluation methodology and analysis of worker AI literacy.
user_evidence: human collaborators
usil_relation: It treats the individual human as a unit of evaluation, with a per-worker latent collaboration skill sH, and shows that human variability matters: top-quartile workers win 74% against solo agents versus 27% for the bottom quartile [key_results][user_representation]. This supports USIL's claim that averaging over users hides important structure, although the skill is only a scalar outcome-level quantity.
open_question: Could the per-human latent skill and the 11 coded AI-fluency behaviors in CollabSkill's logs be extended from a scalar outcome-skill into a per-user interaction-preference profile that conditions when an agent asks, confirms, or defers, and does that improve collaboration outcomes over repeated sessions? The paper leaves this open, and its model does not separate task skill from collaboration skill.
evaluation_scale: 93 US-based Upwork workers, 386 sessions, over 1,500 prompts, 5 agents, 10 O*NET sectors; 76 completed pre/post surveys

title: AutoLibra: Agent Metric Induction from Open-Ended Human Feedback
authors: Hao Zhu, Phil Cuvin, Xinkai Yu, Charlotte Ka Yee Yan, Jason Zhang, Diyi Yang
summary: AutoLibra turns open-ended human feedback on agent trajectories into interpretable evaluation metrics. An LLM pipeline grounds feedback into (behavior, feedback, sign) aspects, clusters them into metrics with definitions and good and bad examples, and scores trajectories with an LLM-as-a-judge. Two meta-metrics, coverage and redundancy, select the number of metrics. Across Sotopia, WebArena, WebVoyager, CoGym, Baba-Is-AI and MiniHack, coverage reaches 60–88% and human validation is about 0.9. Induced metrics expose behaviors that expert-designed ones miss. Using them to drive prompt optimization improves Baba-Is-AI success by over 20%, including on held-out tasks. Metrics are pooled, not personalized.
what_is_learned: A shared set of natural-language evaluation metrics (definition plus good and bad behavior examples) induced by LLM clustering of aspects extracted from open-ended feedback on agent trajectories; no user model or parameters are trained, and agents are improved via prompt optimization.
user_evidence: open-ended human feedback
usil_relation: It treats open-ended human feedback on agent behavior (including CoGym end-user comments) as the evidence for what to evaluate and optimize, and it iteratively updates the metric set as the agent develops new behaviors. This is close to USIL's use of feedback, but the metrics are pooled across annotators and tied to agent behavior, not to individual users or interaction policy.
open_question: Could AutoLibra-style induction be run on a single user's feedback (for example CoGym users) to yield per-user procedural metrics such as when to ask or confirm, and would those metrics predict that user's satisfaction better than pooled metrics?
evaluation_scale: CoGym end-user comments on 197 trajectories; authors annotating ~80–100 GPT-4 trajectories per dataset across 5 datasets; 40 sampled instances per step for human validation; improvement experiment on 6 of 40 Baba-Is-AI tasks over 3 stages

title: Do LLMs Recognize Your Preferences? Evaluating Personalized Preference Following in LLMs
authors: Siyan Zhao et al.
summary: PrefEval is a benchmark of 3,000 preference-query pairs across 20 topics. It tests whether LLMs infer, remember and follow a user's explicit or implicit preferences in long multi-session conversations of up to 300 distractor turns. Evaluating 10 LLMs with zero-shot, reminder, self-critic, CoT and RAG baselines, the authors find that zero-shot adherence collapses with context length, implicit preferences are harder, and RAG and reminders help but still degrade. SFT of Mistral-7B on PrefEval improves performance and generalizes to unseen topics and longer contexts. Preferences are synthetic and stated; interaction policy and real users are not studied.
user_evidence: stated preferences in conversation
usil_relation: PrefEval tests whether an LLM remembers and follows a user's stated preference across up to 300 distractor turns of multi-session conversation. This is close to USIL's memory and persistence questions, but it targets response content, not how the agent works.
open_question: Can PrefEval-style long-context preference tracking be extended to procedural preferences (when to ask, confirm, or defer), using real users' corrections and takeovers instead of synthetic stated preferences, with per-user results reported?
evaluation_scale: 3,000 synthetic preference-query pairs (1,000 used per evaluation), up to 300 distractor turns, 10 LLMs; no real users

title: PersonalLLM: Tailoring LLMs to Individual Preferences
authors: Thomas P. Zollo et al.
summary: PersonalLLM is an open-source benchmark for personalizing LLMs to individual preferences. It has 10K+ open-ended prompts, each with 8 high-quality responses from top LLMs. Simulated users are sampled as Dirichlet-weighted ensembles of 10 reward models, which gives more diverse preferences than persona prompting. Baselines use in-context learning with Llama3-8B-Instruct. Winning-only examples work best, and retrieving examples from similar historical users gives only a small gain over self-ICL. Users are simulated rather than real, preferences are static, and the focus is on output quality rather than interaction behavior.
user_evidence: simulated user preferences
usil_relation: PersonalLLM builds a benchmark with heterogeneous simulated users and sparse per-user preference feedback, and tests cross-user meta-learning with retrieval from 10,000 historical users. This is the outcome_individual cell that USIL contrasts with procedure_individual.
open_question: Can PersonalLLM's reward-ensemble user simulation be extended to heterogeneous interaction preferences, such as when a user wants to be asked, confirmed with, or left alone, and to drift over time, so that per-user interaction policies could be evaluated?
evaluation_scale: 1,000 simulated test users (α=0.05), each with one test prompt; historical database of 10,000 simulated users with 50 triplets each

title: WebArena: A Realistic Web Environment for Building Autonomous Agents
authors: Shuyan Zhou et al.
summary: WebArena is a self-hosted, reproducible web environment with four functional apps (e-commerce, Reddit-style forum, GitLab, CMS) plus a map and knowledge tools. It comes with an 812-task benchmark built from 241 templates and evaluated by programmatic functional-correctness checks. Few-shot LLM baselines perform poorly: the best GPT-4 agent reaches 14.41% success against 78.24% for humans. Agents often wrongly judge feasible tasks impossible when given an unachievable-task hint. The paper includes simulated user roles and histories, but no personalization, no user interaction, and no learning across sessions. It is mainly useful as infrastructure for agent evaluation.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned. WebArena is an environment and benchmark. Baselines are few-shot in-context LLM agents (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, text-bison-001) that predict browser actions.
user_evidence: n/a
usil_relation: The environment pre-logs fixed simulated user profiles (a customer with 35+ orders, a GitLab maintainer, a shop owner) and includes user-centric tasks tied to that profile, so role- and history-dependent tasks exist. Agents are not adapted to these profiles, and no user signals are used.
open_question: Could WebArena's role-based accounts and histories be extended to build simulated users with differing procedural preferences (when to confirm or ask, how much autonomy to take), so that per-user interaction policies can be evaluated beyond end-to-end task success?

title: Retrospective Learning from Interactions
authors: Zizhao Chen, Mustafa Omer Gul, Yiwei Chen, Gloria Geng, Anne Wu, Yoav Artzi
summary: RESPECT lets a deployed multimodal LLM learn from its own past interactions by decoding implicit feedback (rephrasing, approval, frustration, moves to the next target) in users' follow-up utterances, with no annotation or solicited feedback. In MULTIREF, a multi-turn tangram reference game, a live MTurk deployment with 33 workers over several rounds raises interaction success from 31% to 82% and cuts turns per game from 8.9 to 6.7. A redeployed control stays flat. Positive-only FFT beats RL and KTO. It is a population-level task-outcome learner. It has no personalization or interaction-decision learning, and the models do not generalize beyond the task.
user_evidence: implicit conversational feedback in follow-up turns (rephrasings, approval/frustration, task abandonment) during live deployment
usil_relation: It learns from implicit user evidence (rephrasing, frustration, approval, corrections in follow-up utterances) in real deployment interactions, with continual retraining over rounds, which matches USIL's evidence sources and longitudinal framing. It also reports interaction-level metrics such as turns per interaction.
open_question: Can the same retrospective decoding of implicit feedback be conditioned on individual users' history to learn per-user interaction policies (when to ask, confirm, or defer) rather than a single pooled task policy, and would it transfer beyond MULTIREF?
evaluation_scale: 33 expert MTurk workers; 7,230 interactions and 55,004 utterances over four weeks (~330 games per system per round); $11,180 cost

title: The Era of Real-World Human Interaction: RL from User Conversations
authors: Chuanyang Jin, Jing Xu, Bo Liu, et al. (incl. Tianmin Shu, Jason Weston)
venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2509.25137 (also an ICLR 2026 workshop poster)
summary: RLHI (Reinforcement Learning from Human Interaction) trains language models on organic WildChat conversations rather than expert annotations. Two methods, User-Guided Rewrites and User-Based Rewards, use users' follow-up feedback and LLM-summarized personas from long-term history, applying persona-conditioned DPO to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. They beat baselines on personalization (+24.3 for rewrites), instruction-following (77.9% AlpacaEval 2.0 LC for rewards), and reasoning when trained on simulated math feedback. A human study gives 72.6% and 74.0% win rates. Evaluation is offline, and the paper does not address interaction decisions such as asking or deferring or online continual adaptation.
user_evidence: natural follow-up messages (corrections, complaints, requests) and long-term per-user conversation history summarized as a persona
usil_relation: Learns from real users' natural follow-up messages (corrections, re-attempts, clarifications) and conditions on a per-user persona from conversation history, which is the evidence type USIL uses. It applies this to output quality, though, not to interaction policy.
open_question: Could persona-conditioned feedback learning extend from what the response says to how the assistant behaves (when to ask a clarifying question, confirm, or defer), given that the follow-up signals here already encode user reactions to the assistant's process? Would the personas capture procedural preferences, and would they hold up under drift in an online setting?
evaluation_scale: 100 held-out WildChat users judged by an o3 LLM judge; human study with 10 participants rating 50 turns each; simulated users for math reasoning training

title: Principled Fine-tuning of LLMs from User-Edits: A Medley of Preference, Supervision, and Reward
authors: Dipendra Misra, Aldo Pacchiano, Ta-Chung Chi, Ge Gao
summary: This paper gives a theoretical and empirical treatment of fine-tuning LLMs from user-edit deployment data (context, agent response, user edit). It shows that SFT on edits, DPO that prefers edits over responses, and RL on edit-distance cost have different trade-offs depending on user, data distribution and model class. It proposes a simple late ensemble that runs a UCB bandit over offline-trained policies, using edit cost as reward. Experiments use LLM-simulated users with latent preferences on email writing and summarization. The late ensemble gets the lowest worst-case suboptimality and holds up under a test-time user shift. There is no human study, and the RL variant is not implemented.
user_evidence: user edits to agent responses in writing-assistant settings
usil_relation: It treats user edits as the personalization signal, the same evidence class USIL names (edits and corrections). It unifies SFT, DPO and cost feedback from (context, response, edit) triples, and it adapts online at test time by using edit cost to choose among policies, with theory on trade-offs by user type (strong vs weak).
open_question: Can edit signals be used to learn per-user procedural preferences, such as when to ask, confirm or defer, rather than only what text to produce? And do the SFT/DPO/cost trade-offs hold for real users whose edit behavior drifts and differs from simulated Qwen/Llama users?
evaluation_scale: LLM-simulated strong/weak users (Qwen3-32B) with latent preference strings across 4 article domains each; 10,000-20,000 offline edits per user type, T=200 online rounds, 3 seeds; transfer test with a Llama-3.3-70B user

title: When to Show a Suggestion? Integrating Human Feedback in AI-Assisted Programming
authors: Hussein Mozannar, Gagan Bansal, Adam Fourney, Eric Horvitz
summary: This paper asks when an AI code assistant should show or hide a suggestion. It proposes a utility-theoretic framework and CDHF, a cascade of calibrated XGBoost acceptance models trained on Copilot accept/reject telemetry from 535 programmers. The cascade can skip generating suggestions or hide them, reducing latency and verification time. Retrospectively, it hides 25.3% of shown suggestions with 94.7% of them true rejects. Programmer ID adds a modest AUC gain (0.780 to 0.795). The authors also show that using acceptance as a reward favors very short suggestions. No user study was run and transfer was not tested.
user_evidence: accept/reject of suggestions, telemetry and context features (typing, latent programmer state)
usil_relation: CDHF learns from implicit accept/reject telemetry when a coding assistant should show or withhold a suggestion, which is an interaction decision. A programmer-ID feature gives small gains, so individual differences matter for this decision [personalization][interaction_decisions].
open_question: Does a per-programmer show/hide policy, learned online from accept/reject telemetry across sessions and evaluated with a live user study, outperform the population cascade with a one-hot ID? Can it adapt to drift and transfer to new users or tasks, and what does it cost in interruptions and trust?
evaluation_scale: Retrospective offline evaluation on Copilot telemetry from 535 Python programmers over two weeks (4,749 sessions, 168,807 shown suggestions); an earlier 21-programmer study was used for the latent-state analysis.

title: Position: Towards Bidirectional Human-AI Alignment
authors: Hua Shen et al.
summary: This NeurIPS 2025 position paper argues that AI alignment should be bidirectional: aligning AI with humans and aligning humans with AI, in a dynamic, co-evolving relationship. A PRISMA-style review of 411 papers (2019–Jan 2024; HCI, NLP, ML; mostly text LLMs) supports a framework with four research questions and an extended Schwartz-based value taxonomy. The review finds that work centers on explicit feedback and training-time methods. Underexplored areas include implicit feedback, inference-time and interactive customization for individuals, human-in-the-loop evaluation, AI literacy, and societal impacts. It ends with three challenges and recommendations. No model or user study is presented.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned. The paper offers a conceptual Bidirectional Human-AI Alignment framework, a value taxonomy extended from Schwartz, and literature coverage counts from a 411-paper review.
user_evidence: n/a
usil_relation: The paper identifies customizing AI to individuals or groups, implicit and interactive feedback, proactive conversational elicitation of evolving values, and dynamic co-evolution as underexplored. These gaps motivate USIL, but it covers value alignment rather than interaction policies [personalization] [temporal_adaptation] [interaction_decisions].
open_question: How can the 'Customizing AI for Individuals' and 'dynamic co-evolution' gaps be turned into per-user procedural policies (when to ask, act, or defer) that are learned from implicit signals and evaluated longitudinally, rather than only aligning outcome values?

title: Magentic-UI: Towards Human-in-the-loop Agentic Systems
authors: Hussein Mozannar, Gagan Bansal, Cheng Tan, et al.
summary: Magentic-UI is an open-source human-in-the-loop web and code agent interface from Microsoft with six low-cost interaction mechanisms: co-planning, co-tasking, action approval, answer verification, plan memory, and multi-tasking. It is evaluated on autonomous benchmarks (GAIA, AssistantBench, WebVoyager, WebGames), with simulated users (GAIA accuracy rises from 30.3% to 51.9% with a side-information user), in a 12-person study (SUS 74.58), and on adversarial safety tests. No user-specific learning occurs; memory only stores reusable plans and is not evaluated. The interaction policy is fixed for all users, so the paper provides a platform and motivating pain points for per-user interaction learning.
user_evidence: plan edits, co-tasking takeovers, action-guard approvals/rejections, simulated user feedback
usil_relation: Magentic-UI implements the interaction mechanisms USIL would personalize: co-planning, action approval, takeover, clarifying questions, and deference to the user. Its authors suggest that approval frequency could be learned as users develop trust [temporal_adaptation]. The policy is fixed, designed for an average user, and tuned through unstructured interaction.
open_question: Can approval, help-seeking, and plan-review thresholds in a system like Magentic-UI be learned per user from edits, approvals, and takeovers, and does that reduce the excessive approvals and verbosity that participants reported?
evaluation_scale: 12 participants in an hour-long qualitative study with SUS; LLM-simulated users on 162 GAIA validation tasks; 24 adversarial safety scenarios

title: Plan-Then-Execute: An Empirical Study of User Trust and Team Performance When Using LLM Agents As A Daily Assistant
authors: Gaole He, Gianluca Demartini, Ujwal Gadiraju
venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI 2025)
summary: This CHI 2025 study tests how user involvement in high-level planning and step-by-step execution of a GPT-3.5 plan-then-execute LLM agent affects calibrated trust and task performance. In a 2x2 between-subjects experiment on Prolific (N=248) with six daily tasks of varying risk and plan quality, involvement did not calibrate trust, because plausible but wrong plans and actions often went unnoticed. It helped in some tasks and hurt in others, and it raised cognitive load while lowering confidence. Plan quality was the strongest driver of execution accuracy. The authors suggest tailoring involvement to the task and the user, but nothing is personalized or learned.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned by the system. It is a between-subjects user study of how involvement in planning and execution affects calibrated trust, plan quality and execution accuracy with a fixed GPT-3.5 plan-then-execute agent.
user_evidence: plan edits, step-level execution approvals/corrections, trust ratings
usil_relation: It varies the level of user involvement (automatic vs user-involved planning and execution) in an LLM daily assistant, and shows that involvement helps in some tasks and hurts in others while raising cognitive load. This is population-level evidence on procedural autonomy and confirmation that USIL would individualize.
open_question: Could per-user histories of plan edits and Proceed/Feedback/Specify Action choices predict when each user should be involved, so that involvement is tailored to the user and not averaged, and could this improve calibrated trust?
evaluation_scale: 248 retained Prolific participants (347 recruited), each completing six tasks in a simulated environment, in a 2x2 between-subjects design

title: LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory
authors: Di Wu, Hongwei Wang, Wenhao Yu, Yuwei Zhang, Kai-Wei Chang, Dong Yu
summary: LongMemEval is a 500-question benchmark for long-term memory in chat assistants. It tests five abilities over scalable simulated multi-session histories (~115k to 1.5M tokens): information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention. Long-context LLMs lose 30-60% accuracy and commercial assistants perform poorly. The authors propose a unified indexing, retrieval, and reading framework and show that round-level values, fact-augmented keys, time-aware query expansion, and chain-of-note reading with JSON improve recall and accuracy. No model is trained, the data is simulated, and there is no interaction policy or per-user learning.
user_evidence: User-assistant chat histories, including user statements that later update earlier ones
usil_relation: Its memory benchmark over simulated multi-session user histories, including knowledge updates, temporal reasoning, and a preference-use question type, is closest to USIL's need to persist and use user-specific history across sessions. The memory stores factual and preference content, not procedural interaction preferences.
open_question: Can a LongMemEval-style memory of user facts be extended to store and retrieve procedural preferences (when this user wants to be asked, confirmed with, or left alone), and does such memory change ask/act/defer decisions rather than just QA accuracy?
evaluation_scale: 500 questions over simulated user histories (~115k tokens for S, ~1.5M tokens for M); a human study of commercial systems with 97 questions and 3-6-session histories

title: Agent Workflow Memory
authors: Zora Zhiruo Wang, Jiayuan Mao, Daniel Fried, Graham Neubig
summary: Agent Workflow Memory (AWM) induces reusable workflows, meaning NL-described step sequences abstracted from successful agent trajectories, and stores them as text memory to guide LM web agents. It works offline from training examples or online from a stream of test queries. On WebArena it reaches 35.5% success (a 51.1% relative gain over BrowserGym) with fewer steps, and on Mind2Web it improves step success and generalizes across tasks, websites, and domains, with online induction helping most under larger distribution gaps. There is no user modeling, user feedback, or interaction-decision learning; the contribution is task-level procedural memory rather than personalization.
user_evidence: None from users directly; the agent's own (self-judged) successful trajectories
usil_relation: AWM's online induce-integrate-utilize loop builds a growing procedural memory from the agent's own experience, with cross-task and cross-website transfer on WebArena and Mind2Web. This is the memory mechanism a USIL agent could use to store procedural routines, but here the routines are task workflows.
open_question: Could workflow induction be applied to user-specific signals (edits, takeovers, approvals) to build per-user procedural memory of when to ask, confirm, or defer, and would it transfer across a user's tasks, rather than just across websites?

title: In Prospect and Retrospect: Reflective Memory Management for Long-term Personalized Dialogue Agents
authors: Zhen Tan, Jun Yan, I-Hung Hsu, et al.
summary: RMM (Reflective Memory Management) is a framework for long-term personalized dialogue agents. Prospective Reflection summarizes dialogue by topic across utterance, turn, and session granularity into a per-user memory bank. Retrospective Reflection refines a lightweight reranker over frozen retriever outputs online with REINFORCE, using the LLM's citations of retrieved memories as binary rewards. On MSC and LongMemEval, RMM beats RAG, MemoryBank, and LD-Agent baselines, with over 10% accuracy gain over no memory management. It does not decide when to ask or act, does not test transfer to new users, and reports no per-user analysis.
user_evidence: Multi-session dialogue history; citation signals from the LLM's own responses
usil_relation: RMM builds a per-user memory bank across sessions and refines retrieval online from implicit LLM-citation feedback. That is the memory and adaptation machinery a USIL system could use. However, it personalizes what is retrieved and said, not how the agent interacts.
open_question: Could reflective memory and citation-style reward be extended to store and retrieve per-user procedural preferences (when to ask, confirm, or defer), using real user signals such as corrections or takeovers rather than the LLM's own citations? Is the reranker actually user-specific, and does adaptation help individual users?
evaluation_scale: Offline benchmarks MSC and LongMemEval with Gemini-1.5 generators, averaged over 3 runs; 100-instance human evaluation on MSC to check LLM-judge agreement.

title: Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents
authors: Adyasha Maharana, Dong-Ho Lee, Sergey Tulyakov, Mohit Bansal, Francesco Barbieri, Yuwei Fang
summary: LOCOMO is a dataset of 50 very long-term, multimodal conversations (about 300 turns, up to 35 sessions each) between LLM-simulated speakers grounded in personas and temporal event graphs, with human editing. The benchmark has three tasks: QA across five reasoning types, event summarization, and multimodal dialogue generation. Long-context LLMs and RAG over observations improve QA by 22-66% but lag humans by about 56%, and temporal reasoning is hardest. The 'users' are simulated and no real user signals or interaction policies are studied, so the paper is relevant mainly as a memory evaluation resource.
user_evidence: Long multi-session conversation history (persona facts, temporal events)
usil_relation: LOCOMO tests whether agents keep speaker-specific information (observations, session summaries) across up to 35 sessions, which is the memory and longitudinal-evaluation substrate USIL would build on. It evaluates only recall and persona consistency, not interaction decisions.
open_question: Can a LOCOMO-style long-horizon benchmark be extended with real users' corrections, approvals and takeovers, so memory is tested for procedural interaction preferences (when to ask, confirm or defer) and not only factual recall?
evaluation_scale: 50 LLM-generated conversations (about 300 turns, up to 35 sessions each) with 7,512 QA questions; human annotators edited the data and provided a human-performance reference for QA

title: ProPerSim: Developing Proactive and Personalized AI Assistants through User-Assistant Simulation
authors: Jiho Kim, Junseong Choi, Woosog Chay, et al.
summary: ProPerSim is a simulation task and benchmark for assistants that are both proactive and personalized. LLM user agents with Big Five personas and personalized rubrics live in a simulated home and rate the assistant's recommendations on preference, frequency, timing, and communication. ProPerAssistant, a LLaMA 3.3 70B model with retrieval memory and daily DPO, learns for each of 32 personas whether to intervene and what to say. Scores rise from about 2.2 to 3.3-3.4 out of 4 over 14 days, and recommendation frequency falls from about 24 to 6 per hour. Evaluation is fully simulated, with no real users, drift, or transfer tests, and the assistant cannot ask questions.
user_evidence: Simulated-user ratings of proactive suggestions over a longitudinal interaction
usil_relation: Learns a per-persona proactive intervention policy (whether and when to recommend, and how often) from feedback over simulated days. This is close to procedure_individual learning, although feedback is simulated and the action space is limited to recommend or stay silent.
open_question: Would per-user timing and frequency policies learned against LLM-simulated personas hold up with real users whose preferences drift, whose feedback is noisy or delayed, and where asking, confirming, or deferring are available actions? Do the policies transfer across personas or tasks?
evaluation_scale: 32 GPT-4o-generated personas simulated by LLM user agents over 14 days each; humans (10 students, 3 for evaluation reasonableness) only validated simulation realism

title: Proactive Agent: Shifting LLM Agents from Reactive Responses to Active Assistance
authors: Yaxi Lu, Shenzhi Yang, Cheng Qian, et al.
summary: This paper trains LLM agents to be proactive: to anticipate and propose useful tasks from observed user activity (keyboard, browser, clipboard) without explicit instructions, or to stay silent. It contributes ProactiveBench, a pipeline that generates 6,790 training events and a test split of 233 real-world events, plus a reward model that imitates human accept/reject judgments (91.8% F1) and acts as the automatic evaluator. Fine-tuned LLaMA-3.1-8B and Qwen2-7B reach about 66% F1 and beat GPT-4o. Personalization, longitudinal adaptation and live user evaluation are not studied, and false alarms remain high.
user_evidence: Annotator accept/reject labels on proposed proactive tasks given user activity traces
usil_relation: It learns when to initiate versus stay silent (null) from observed activity events, trained on human accept/reject judgments. This is a population-level version of USIL's ask/act/defer decision, with false alarms and a candidate-count cap modelling interruption cost [interaction_decisions][interaction_costs].
open_question: Can the accept/reject signal and the false-alarm tradeoff be learned per user, so that each person's tolerance for proactive suggestions is modelled over time instead of through a majority-vote reward model, and does that beat the averaged policy?
evaluation_scale: 233 real-world-derived test events judged by a reward model; the reward model was validated on 120 held-out human-annotated entries from three annotators; no live user study

title: Cooperative Inverse Reinforcement Learning
authors: Dylan Hadfield-Menell, Anca Dragan, Pieter Abbeel, Stuart Russell
summary: Cooperative Inverse Reinforcement Learning (CIRL) formalizes value alignment as a cooperative two-player game in which a human knows a hidden reward parameter θ and a robot must learn it while both act. The paper reduces computing optimal joint policies to a POMDP in which the robot's belief over θ is a sufficient statistic. It proves that demonstration-by-expert, the IRL assumption, is suboptimal, since optimal humans teach by sacrificing immediate reward. An approximate best-response algorithm for instructive demonstrations beats expert demonstration in simulated navigation (500 sampled θ) on regret and other measures. No real users, drift, or cross-session persistence are studied.
user_evidence: human actions
usil_relation: CIRL treats the human as a cooperative teacher whose demonstrations trade immediate reward for information, so the robot's inference over the human's hidden θ depends on how the human chooses to act. This is a formal ancestor of learning from user-specific interaction evidence. It still targets the reward function rather than a per-user interaction policy.
open_question: Can CIRL's teaching/active-learning game be extended so the robot learns a persistent per-user model of how that person teaches, asks and defers, using real human data rather than simulated best-responders with sampled θ and perfect coordination?
evaluation_scale: 500 randomly sampled reward parameters θ in a simulated 2D grid navigation task, 2x2 factorial design (H-policy x 3 or 10 features)

title: Language Model Personalization via Reward Factorization
authors: Idan Shenfeld, Felix Faltings, Pulkit Agrawal, Aldo Pacchiano
summary: PReF personalizes LLM responses by representing each user's reward as a linear combination of shared learned base reward functions. A new user's weight vector is inferred from about 10 actively selected pairwise comparisons, chosen to maximize uncertainty. Personalized outputs come from inference-time alignment without retraining the LLM. On synthetic (Attributes, PRISM-augmented) and real users (28 volunteers), PReF beats standard RLHF, needs about 25x less data than per-user models, and reaches a 67% human win rate against GPT-4o. It transfers to unseen users and prompts. Limitations: mostly simulated users, no temporal drift, and a focus on output style rather than interaction behavior.
user_evidence: A few pairwise preferences per user, actively selected
usil_relation: PReF learns a per-user low-dimensional vector λ over shared base rewards from about 10 active pairwise queries. This is the few-shot, per-user adaptation that USIL needs for interaction policies, and the active query selection is a user-specific elicitation mechanism [claimed_contribution][interaction_decisions].
open_question: Can a factorized per-user representation like λ over shared base functions capture procedural preferences (when to ask, confirm, or defer) rather than output style? Could it be updated over long horizons as preferences drift, rather than within one session?
evaluation_scale: Synthetic LLM-roleplayed users (84 in Attributes, 1.5K in augmented PRISM, 10 seeds) plus a human study with 28 volunteers (15 comparisons to learn, 15 to evaluate against GPT-4o).

title: Personalized Language Modeling from Personalized Human Feedback
authors: Xinyu Li, Ruiyang Zhou, Zachary C. Lipton, Liu Leqi
summary: P-RLHF personalizes LLMs from pairwise preference feedback tagged with user identifiers. A lightweight user model produces implicit embeddings (individual, offset from a generic embedding, or cluster-based) plus an explicit text embedding, prepended to a LoRA-tuned LLM as soft prompts. A personalized DPO objective trains both jointly. Experiments on TL;DR with simulated length preferences, P-SOUPS and PRISM show it beats vanilla DPO and approaches oracle prompting. Unseen users fall back to a generic embedding that behaves like vanilla DPO. It personalizes output content, not interaction behavior, and has no longitudinal adaptation.
user_evidence: Pairwise preference labels tagged with user identity and optional user information
usil_relation: P-RLHF learns per-user embeddings from user-tagged pairwise preferences, so the individual user is a unit of learning, with a user model z_u conditioning a shared LLM. This matches USIL's optional user representation g(h) and its handling of unseen users via a generic embedding. But it personalizes generated content (outcome_individual), not interaction behavior.
open_question: Could the P-RLHF user embedding be trained on procedural signals (takeovers, approvals/rejections, answers to questions) to condition when the agent asks, confirms or defers, and would it transfer to unseen users or tasks with few interactions?
evaluation_scale: TL;DR with simulated length preferences (top 10/40 workers); P-SOUPS with 6 GPT-4 preference profiles and 50 instructions; PRISM with 1,500 users, win-rates on 76 samples from 10 seen and 10 unseen users, judged by GPT-4/GPT-4o role-play

title: Distributional Preference Learning: Understanding and Accounting for Hidden Context in RLHF
authors: Anand Siththaranjan, Cassidy Laidlaw, Dylan Hadfield-Menell
summary: The paper studies RLHF when hidden context, such as annotator identity or objective, affects preference labels. It proves that Bradley-Terry-Luce preference learning implicitly aggregates hidden context via Borda count, with social-choice consequences such as incentives to misreport. It proposes distributional preference learning (DPL), which predicts a distribution of utilities per alternative, to detect hidden context and mitigate its effects. On HH-RLHF with LLaMA-2-7B, DPL's explained variance drops when helpfulness and harmlessness labels are mixed, and risk-averse optimization lowers the jailbreak rate from 25.1% to 13.4% with similar helpfulness. It does not personalize or study interaction decisions.
user_evidence: Pairwise preference comparisons from heterogeneous annotators with unobserved context
usil_relation: It treats unobserved annotator heterogeneity (hidden context) as a failure mode of averaged BTL/RLHF reward learning, showing BTL implicitly implements Borda count. This supports the claim that averaging across users is lossy, and DPL captures per-alternative utility variance without recording user identity [user_representation].
open_question: Can DPL-style utility variance be tied to individual users, so that high-variance (hidden-context) cases trigger per-user asking, confirming or deferring rather than only risk-averse quantile optimization over the population?
evaluation_scale: Synthetic 1-D experiment; HH-RLHF helpful/harmless/combined datasets (partly relabeled by GPT-3.5); 187 jailbreak response pairs; no human participants evaluated.

title: The PRISM Alignment Dataset: What Participatory, Representative and Individualised Human Feedback Reveals About the Subjective and Multicultural Alignment of Large Language Models
authors: Hannah Rose Kirk, Alexander Whitefield, Paul Röttger, et al.
summary: PRISM is a NeurIPS 2024 dataset linking sociodemographics and stated preferences of 1,500 participants from 75 countries to their ratings and fine-grained feedback in 8,011 live conversations with 21 LLMs. Samples include census-representative UK and US groups. Case studies show that prompts differ by identity, model rankings are sensitive to sample size, topic and region, and sampling choices change welfare for out-group participants. No single model wins majority preference. No personalised model is trained; the paper positions the data as a resource for personalised or steerable alignment, and the analysis stays at the level of outputs rather than interaction policies.
what_is_learned: No model is trained. The paper is a dataset with empirical analyses: topic regressions on identity, aggregate model rankings via Pairwise Rank Centrality, and simulated welfare under different sampling schemes. It releases individualised ratings linked to participant profiles that could later support output-preference or reward learning.
user_evidence: Per-user surveys (stated preferences, demographics) plus ratings and choices in live multi-turn conversations
usil_relation: PRISM links each participant's cardinal ratings and fine-grained feedback to a detailed profile, and shows no single LLM wins majority preference (max 45% MEANCHOICE). This supports the claim that averaging over users hides real preference variation, and the data could seed individual-level learning.
open_question: PRISM covers output preferences from a single-session task and groups participants by demographics. Do the same participants differ in procedural preferences such as when they want clarification, confirmation or autonomy, and can these be learned per user and predicted from the profile and rating history?
evaluation_scale: 1,500 participants from 75 countries, 8,011 live conversations with 21 LLMs; balanced subset of 1,246 participants and 6,669 conversations for ranking analyses

title: PAL: Sample-Efficient Personalized Reward Modeling for Pluralistic Alignment
authors: Daiwei Chen, Yi Chen, Aniket Rege, Zhi Wang, Ramya Korlakai Vinayak
summary: PAL reframes reward learning from pairwise comparisons as ideal-point/metric learning and models each user as a convex combination of K shared prototypes, moving beyond the universal Bradley-Terry-Luce assumption. It learns a shared latent preference space and fits only per-user weights to adapt to new users from few comparisons (few-shot) or from average weights (zero-shot). Small MLPs on frozen foundation-model embeddings are competitive with large reward models on Summary and Pick-a-Pic. They clearly beat homogeneous baselines on synthetic and semi-synthetic heterogeneous data (95.2% vs 75.4% on Pick-a-Filter). Gains from K>1 are small on real data. The paper addresses output preferences only and does not address interaction.
user_evidence: pairwise preferences
usil_relation: The per-user simplex weights over shared prototypes form a compact user representation z_u that can be fit few-shot for unseen users. This is the same decomposition USIL treats as optional, but PAL applies it to output preferences (reward) rather than to interaction behavior.
open_question: Could a prototype-mixture user representation like PAL's be learned from procedural signals (takeovers, confirmations, ask/act decisions) to capture per-user interaction policies, and would it handle users outside the convex hull of the prototypes or preferences that drift over time?
evaluation_scale: Offline held-out accuracy on synthetic users, persona-based synthetic users (5 repeats), Pick-a-Filter, Pick-a-Pic v2 (anonymous IDs) and Reddit TL;DR Summary (worker IDs); no live user study.

title: SynthesizeMe! Inducing Persona-Guided Prompts for Personalized Reward Models in LLMs
authors: Michael J. Ryan, Omar Shaikh, Aditri Bhagirath, Daniel Frees, William Held, Diyi Yang
summary: SynthesizeMe induces a natural-language persona and a small set of validated demonstrations for each user from only 5-15 pairwise preference judgments, then conditions an LLM judge or reward model on that prompt. The paper also introduces PersonalRewardBench, built from 854 Chatbot Arena and PRISM users. The method improves LLM-as-a-judge accuracy by up to 4.4%, outperforms demographic conditioning, and produces prompts that are interpretable and transferable across models. A finetuned Bradley-Terry reward model remains stronger, and gains over it are within confidence intervals. It studies outputs only: no interaction decisions, longitudinal adaptation, or user-burden measures.
user_evidence: user preference history
usil_relation: SynthesizeMe learns a per-user, interpretable natural-language persona and demonstrations from sparse pairwise feedback. This is the kind of user representation z_u = g(h) that a USIL policy could condition on, and it is evaluated on held-out users in a low-data regime.
open_question: Can a persona induced from pairwise output preferences also predict a user's procedural preferences, such as when they want to be asked, to confirm, or to take over? And can it be updated as those preferences drift over sessions, which this paper leaves as future longitudinal work?
evaluation_scale: 854 users from Chatbot Arena (131) and PRISM (~720); held-out test users split 40/10/50 and per-user preferences split temporally. These are logged human preference data, not a live user study.

title: Aligning Language Models with Demonstrated Feedback
authors: Omar Shaikh et al.
summary: DITTO (Demonstration ITerated Task Optimization) aligns an LLM to an individual or task from fewer than 10 user demonstrations. It treats demonstrations as preferred over samples from the current and earlier policies, building online comparison data for DPO-style training, derived from online imitation learning. A per-user LoRA Mistral 7B is evaluated on author-specific writing benchmarks (77% GPT-4 win rate) and a 16-person user study (68.8% vs 55.5% for SFT). Demonstrations were about an order of magnitude more sample-efficient than pairwise preferences. The paper addresses output style only: no interaction decisions, no drift or longitudinal adaptation, and no cross-user transfer.
user_evidence: few user demonstrations
usil_relation: DITTO learns from sparse user-specific evidence (edits and demonstrations) with one model per user, and shows that demonstrations are about 10x more sample-efficient than pairwise preferences [interaction_costs]. This matches the few-shot individual adaptation in P1. It targets what is written (outcome_individual), not how the agent interacts.
open_question: Could demonstration-based online imitation, with edits as the signal, learn per-user procedural preferences such as when to ask, confirm, or defer, and would these persist across sessions as preferences drift? DITTO tests neither cross-user transfer nor temporal adaptation.
evaluation_scale: 16 human participants gave 20 blinded pairwise preferences each (320 total); static benchmarks used 20 authors (10 each from CMCC and CCAT50) with GPT-4 judging over 3 runs.

title: Aligning LLMs with Individual Preferences via Interaction
authors: Shujin Wu, May Fung, Cheng Qian, et al.
summary: This paper trains LLMs to 'interact to align': implicitly infer a user's unspoken persona and preferences over multi-turn conversation and tailor later responses. The authors build a tree-structured multi-turn preference dataset from 3,310 synthetic personas using iterative persona generation and multi-LLM collaboration, then train four base models with SFT and DPO. They introduce the ALOE benchmark (100 distinct personas) with Alignment Level and Improvement Rate metrics judged by GPT-4o. Average alignment improves 32.0% relative, and the judge agrees with humans (kappa 0.789). Evaluation is fully simulated, limited to 10 turns, with no explicit interaction decisions and no cross-session adaptation.
user_evidence: Implicit cues in multi-turn conversation (simulated persona users)
usil_relation: ALOE trains LLMs to infer individual user personas from sparse multi-turn evidence and adapt later behavior. It measures within-conversation improvement with Alignment Level and Improvement Rate, which resembles USIL's individual-user, evolving-evidence framing. However, the adapted object is response content and style, not an interaction policy.
open_question: Could the interact-to-align recipe be extended so the inferred persona drives procedural decisions (when to ask, confirm, or defer) rather than only response style, and would it hold with real users whose preferences persist or drift across sessions?
evaluation_scale: 100 held-out synthetic personas, each role-played by GPT-4o for 10 turns and judged by GPT-4o. Training used 3,310 personas. Judge validated by human annotators on 50 samples each.

title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model Is Secretly a Reward Model
authors: Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma, Eric Mitchell, Stefano Ermon, Christopher D. Manning, Chelsea Finn
summary: DPO shows that the KL-constrained reward-maximization objective of RLHF can be optimized directly with a simple binary cross-entropy loss on preference pairs. It reparameterizes the reward in terms of the policy, so the language model is secretly an implicit reward model and no explicit reward model or RL loop is needed. On IMDb sentiment, Reddit TL;DR summarization and Anthropic HH dialogue, it matches or beats PPO-based RLHF, with some evidence of out-of-distribution generalization to CNN/DailyMail. It aggregates labelers into one policy, with no personalization, temporal adaptation or interaction decisions, so it is the outcome-averaged baseline for USIL.
user_evidence: pairwise preferences
usil_relation: DPO is the standard outcome-averaged preference-learning baseline that USIL contrasts with. Its policy-as-implicit-reward parameterization could be reused for per-user preference or interaction-policy learning, but the paper only fits one aggregate reward on static Reddit TL;DR, Anthropic HH and IMDb pairs [what_is_learned][user_evidence].
open_question: Can the DPO implicit-reward objective be conditioned on a user history h_u so it learns per-user interaction policies (when to ask, confirm or defer) from sparse, drifting, individual preference pairs, and does it transfer across tasks without a separate reward model?
evaluation_scale: Evaluation uses GPT-4 as a proxy judge on three offline tasks. A 25-volunteer human study (25 summaries each) validates GPT-4 agreement on TL;DR only.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences
authors: Paul F. Christiano, Jan Leike, Tom B. Brown, Miljan Martic, Shane Legg, Dario Amodei
summary: Christiano et al. scale reward learning from human preferences to deep RL. A reward-function ensemble is fit to non-expert pairwise comparisons of 1-2 second trajectory clips while a policy is trained concurrently with A2C/TRPO. Queries are chosen by ensemble disagreement, and label rate is annealed. With about 700 labels it nearly matches RL on true reward on MuJoCo tasks, and it makes progress on most Atari games. It also learns novel behaviors such as a backflip in about an hour of feedback. Feedback is population-level, with no personalization, no cross-session persistence and no transfer evaluation. It is a canonical outcome-averaged reward-learning baseline.
user_evidence: pairwise comparisons from crowd labelers
usil_relation: Learns from sparse human pairwise comparisons with active, uncertainty-based query selection and reports human-effort cost (3-5 s per query, 30 min to 5 h). This is the standard outcome-level preference-learning and active-querying baseline that USIL extends to per-user interaction policies.
open_question: Can ensemble-variance query selection be turned into a per-user decision of when to ask versus act, given that contractor inconsistency is treated as noise rather than as individual preference signal?
evaluation_scale: Contractors (and some authors) giving several hundred to several thousand comparisons per task, 30 min to 5 h of human time; real-human results are single runs, plus synthetic oracle runs averaged over 3-5 runs

title: User Preference Modeling for Conversational LLM Agents: Weak Rewards from Retrieval-Augmented Interaction
authors: Yuren Hao, Shuhaib Mehri, ChengXiang Zhai, Dilek Hakkani-Tür
summary: VARS is a frozen-backbone framework for multi-session LLM agents. It learns a per-user dual vector, long-term and short-term, from weak rewards derived from the user's next turn (sentiment keywords and topic coherence). The vector adds a bonus to a reranker over structured preference memory cards. On MultiSessionCollab with simulated users, VARS matches a Reflection baseline on success (55.2% vs 54.4%, not significant) but significantly reduces timeouts and user tokens. The vectors are interpretable and weakly track cross-user preference overlap. Limitations: a single benchmark, simulated users, a heuristic reward, and no transfer tests. It does not decide when to ask or act.
user_evidence: weak scalar feedback from multi-session interactions (simulated users)
usil_relation: VARS learns persistent per-user vectors online from implicit follow-up-turn feedback and measures interaction cost (user tokens, timeouts) over 60 sessions. This is close to USIL's user representation z_u and its longitudinal evaluation. The learned preferences are style preferences, and the vector only changes which memories are retrieved.
open_question: Could the dual-vector state also condition when to ask, confirm, or defer, rather than only which preference cards are retrieved? Would it hold up with real users whose feedback is not keyword-rich, and would it transfer to new tasks or new users?
evaluation_scale: 60 LLM-simulated user profiles × 60 sessions (≤10 turns) on MultiSessionCollab (3,600 sessions per method); ablation with 10 profiles × 15 sessions

title: Latent Preference Modeling for Multi-Session Personalized Tool Calling
authors: Yejin Yoon, Minseo Kim, Taeuk Kim
summary: The paper introduces MPT, a benchmark of 4,695 instances over 459 multi-session histories. It tests whether LLM agents can recall, induce and transfer a user's latent preferences to fill underspecified tool-call arguments. It also proposes PREFINE, a test-time memory that keeps one natural-language preference hypothesis and refines it through a generate–verify–refine loop. PREFINE beats full-history prompting, RAG, Mem0, LangMem and A-MEM on context-free queries (O-F1 60.55 vs 35.29), uses fewer memory tokens, and helps on unseen API functions. Preferences are assumed persistent, users are composed from corpora, and no interaction costs or real users are studied.
user_evidence: multi-session interaction history (past tool calls and choices)
usil_relation: PREFINE keeps a per-user natural-language preference memory, updated across sessions from implicit behavioral signals (past tool-call arguments). It tests transfer to unseen functions, which resembles USIL's z_u and cross-task generalization. However, it learns what argument values to fill (outcome), not how the agent interacts.
open_question: Can the generate–verify–refine hypothesis memory be extended from inferring tool-argument preferences to inferring procedural preferences, such as when this user wants to be asked or to confirm before a tool call, and can it handle shifting preferences with real users?
evaluation_scale: MPT benchmark: 4,695 instances over 459 synthetic multi-session user histories composed from SGD, DuRecDial 2.0 and HomeBench; five LLMs

title: Personalization of Large Language Models: A Survey
authors: Zhehao Zhang et al.
summary: A TMLR 2025 survey that unifies work on LLM personalization, spanning personalized text generation and downstream tasks such as recommendation. It formalizes personalized LLMs and proposes taxonomies of granularity (user, persona, global), techniques (RAG, prompting, representation learning, personalized RLHF), metrics, datasets and applications. It concludes that no single technique is universally best. Open problems include weak benchmarks and metrics, cold start, bias, privacy and multimodality. It runs no experiments, and temporal adaptation and transfer are only brief future directions. It does not treat interaction decisions such as asking, confirming or deferring.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned by the survey itself. It reviews personalization methods for LLMs (RAG, prompting, per-user PEFT and embeddings, personalized RLHF), which mostly target output preference and user modeling.
user_evidence: n/a
usil_relation: The three-level granularity (user, persona, global) and the taxonomy of user representations (retrieved documents, per-user PEFT, user embeddings, personalized-reward RLHF) correspond to USIL's z_u. The survey's focus is on the outcome side, i.e. personalized text generation and downstream tasks.
open_question: The survey identifies no work on learning per-user decisions about when to ask, act, confirm or defer. Can its representation taxonomy (PEFT, embeddings, profiles) be reused for per-user interaction policies, and what benchmarks would measure them beyond LaMP-style output fidelity?

title: Structured Uncertainty guided Clarification for LLM Agents
authors: Manan Suri, Puneet Mathur, Nedim Lipka, et al.
summary: The paper proposes a structured-uncertainty formulation for clarification in tool-calling LLM agents. It keeps a belief over tool-call candidates, factored over parameters, and picks questions by expected value of perfect information minus a redundancy penalty. The agent stops asking when the net gain is low. The formulation is used for inference-time question selection (SAGE-Agent) and for uncertainty-weighted GRPO reward training. It also introduces ClarifyBench, a 716-sample multi-turn disambiguation benchmark with a simulated user. SAGE-Agent improves coverage with fewer questions than baselines, and the weighted GRPO raises When2Call accuracy. Nothing is personalized per user or across sessions, and no real users take part.
user_evidence: Simulated user answers to clarifying questions about tool arguments
usil_relation: Learns when to ask a clarifying question versus execute a tool call, using EVPI with a redundancy-cost penalty on repeated questions and a certainty-weighted GRPO reward. This is the procedure_averaged counterpart of USIL's ask/act decision, evaluated on ClarifyBench with LLM-simulated users.
open_question: Can the EVPI redundancy cost λ and stopping threshold α be made user-conditioned, learned from an individual's answers and takeovers across sessions, so one user gets fewer questions and another more? Would the gains hold with real users whose tolerance for questions differs?
evaluation_scale: ClarifyBench: 716 samples over 5 domains and 3 query types with an LLM user simulator; When2Call single-turn evaluation; GRPO trained on 9K When2Call examples; no real users

title: Ask Early, Ask Late, Ask Right: When Does Clarification Timing Matter for Long-Horizon Agents?
authors: Anmol Gulati, Hariom Gupta, Elias Lumer, et al.
summary: The paper measures how the value of a clarification depends on when it arrives in a long-horizon agent's trajectory and on which kind of information is missing. Using a forced-injection protocol on 84 underspecified LHAW variants from MCP-Atlas, TheAgentCompany and SWE-Bench Pro (6,000+ runs), it produces the first empirical VOI curves. Goal clarification loses nearly all value after about 10% of execution, input clarification stays useful to about 50%, and wasted compute grows with delay. Natural asking by GPT-5.2, Claude and Gemini does not match the optimal windows. Users are simulated, nothing is personalized, and no policy is learned.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned. The paper empirically measures value-of-information curves for clarification timing, as pass@3 against injection point, across four missing-information dimensions (goal, input, constraint, context). It compares these with the natural asking behavior of three frontier models.
user_evidence: Injected ground-truth clarifications; 300 unscripted agent sessions
usil_relation: It gives population-level empirical VOI curves for when a long-horizon agent should ask for clarification (goal info is front-loaded, input info is recoverable to ~50%) and shows that models' natural ask rates and timing diverge from the optimal windows (GPT-5.2 asks in 52% of sessions, Gemini never). This is the procedure_averaged baseline that USIL would individualize.
open_question: Do optimal clarification timing and ask rates differ per user (for example by expertise, interruption tolerance, or past answers), and can a timing-aware ask policy learn these from real users' interaction history rather than from synthetic ground-truth injections?
evaluation_scale: 84 LHAW-derived underspecified task variants, 7 conditions x 3 trials x 3-4 frontier models (6,000+ runs), plus a 300-session natural-ask study on TAC with a simulated user

title: Unified Learning from Demonstrations, Corrections, and Preferences during Physical Human-Robot Interaction
authors: Shaunak A. Mehta, Dylan P. Losey
summary: This paper introduces a unified formalism for robot arms to learn a reward model from scratch from any mix of physical demonstrations, corrections, and preferences.
