A single loss trains an ensemble of three neural reward networks to rank human inputs above perturbed alternatives, and trajectories come from constrained optimization. Optional active preference queries maximize information gain. In simulation (up to 500 simulated humans) and a 15-person study, it matches feature-based methods when features are known and outperforms end-to-end baselines and feature-based methods when features are missing. It learns what the user wants done, not how the robot should interact, and no transfer or cross-session learning is studied.
usil_relation: It learns a per-user task reward from a mix of kinesthetic demonstrations, physical corrections, and ranked preferences. It also selects active preference queries by information gain, which is a user-specific elicitation decision. This is close to USIL's evidence types and to its 'when to ask' decision.
open_question: The learned reward only captures what the user wants produced. Could the same unified feedback stream, including corrections and takeovers, be used to learn how this user wants the robot to ask, confirm, or hand back control, with persistence across sessions and tasks?
evaluation_scale: 15 participants in a user study (5 per task, 6 interactions per method) plus simulated humans (15 to 500) with differing reward weightings

title: Offloading Score: Measuring AI Reliance Through Counterfactual Workflows
authors: Vishakh Padmakumar, Lujain Ibrahim, Zora Zhiruo Wang, Jennifer Wang, Q. Vera Liao, Diyi Yang
summary: The paper introduces offloading score, a reliance measure computed from interaction traces. An LLM induces the observed human-AI workflow, builds a human-only counterfactual for an average user, and reports the fraction of steps AI saved. It also adds descriptive labels for the process and for how outputs were used. In a 40-person study of freelance developers building web apps under 1-hour or 4-hour limits, the score separated the time-pressure conditions better than baselines such as interaction counts, code attribution and NASA-TLX. It correlated negatively with later system recall. The measure is not personalized; the authors list personalized counterfactuals as future work.
what_is_learned: No model is learned. An LLM (gpt-5.2) is prompted to induce workflows from interaction traces, generate human-only counterfactual workflows for an average user, and compute offloading score as the fraction of steps saved. This is a measurement construct for AI reliance, not a learned policy or user model.
user_evidence: workflow traces
usil_relation: It evaluates how work is divided between human and AI (procedure) rather than only outcomes, using interaction traces from 40 developers. It also suggests offloading score as a training signal against overreliance [interaction_decisions]. This touches USIL's call for evaluation beyond task success, but only at the averaged level.
open_question: Could offloading score be computed with per-user counterfactual workflows, so that each user's baseline reliance and calibration drift are tracked across sessions? Could it then drive a user-conditioned policy for when an agent acts, asks, or returns control?
evaluation_scale: 40 Upwork freelance developers, between-subjects, 4 web-app coding tasks, 1-hour vs 4-hour conditions (20 per condition)

title: PersonaLens: A Benchmark for Personalization Evaluation in Conversational AI Assistants
authors: Zheng Zhao, Clara Vania, Subhradeep Kayal, Naila Khan, Shay B. Cohen, Emine Yilmaz
summary: PersonaLens is a benchmark for evaluating personalization in task-oriented LLM assistants. It provides 1,500 semi-synthetic user profiles (PRISM demographics, LLM-generated preferences, and past-interaction summaries) and 111 tasks over 20 domains. An LLM user simulator converses with the assistant under test, and an LLM judge scores personalization (1-4), task completion, naturalness, and coherence. Judge agreement with humans is moderate to strong (personalization kappa 0.52). Seven LLMs score about 2/4 on personalization, multi-domain tasks are harder, and past-interaction summaries help most. It evaluates outcome personalization only, with no learning, no longitudinal adaptation, and no evaluation of interaction decisions.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned. This is an evaluation benchmark with LLM-generated user profiles (demographics, preferences, past-interaction summaries), tasks, and situational contexts. An LLM user simulator and an LLM judge score prompted assistants on personalization, task completion, naturalness, and coherence.
user_evidence: User profiles with detailed preferences plus past interaction histories
usil_relation: Each simulated user has a profile with past-interaction summaries, and the ablations show those summaries drive the largest personalization gain (2.13 to 2.59 on TSD). This is a profile-conditioned, individual-level evaluation of assistants, which is the closest overlap with the outcome_individual cell and with P4.
open_question: Can a benchmark like PersonaLens be extended so simulated users have procedural preferences (when to ask, confirm, or defer) that persist and drift across sessions? Could personalization then be scored on interaction behavior with user-effort costs, and not only on tailored content judged by an LLM?
evaluation_scale: 1,500 LLM-generated profiles, 50 sampled for experiments (3,283 single-domain and 813 multi-domain dialogues). 100 dialogues were rated by 3 human annotators for judge validation.

title: LaMP: When Large Language Models Meet Personalization
authors: Alireza Salemi, Sheshera Mysore, Michael Bendersky, Hamed Zamani
summary: LaMP is a benchmark of seven personalized text classification and generation tasks (citation identification, movie tagging, rating prediction, headline, title, email subject, and tweet paraphrasing) with user-based and time-based splits. Each user is represented by a profile of past input-output pairs. The authors propose retrieval-augmented personalization: relevant or recent profile items are placed in the prompt (IPA) or fused in the decoder (FiD). Fine-tuned FlanT5-base gains 23.5% relative on average, and zero-shot LLMs gain 12.2%. Retrieval quality matters. Evaluation is offline and automatic with single runs. The paper is about personalizing outputs, not interaction behavior or autonomy.
user_evidence: User profile of past authored items (documents, ratings, tweets, emails, titles)
usil_relation: LaMP conditions model behavior on an individual user's history (profile retrieval) and uses user-based and time-based splits to test personalization for new users and for future interactions of existing users. This is the outcome_individual cell that USIL contrasts itself with.
open_question: Can LaMP-style retrieval of per-user history be extended to condition interaction decisions (when to ask, confirm, or defer) rather than text outputs, and what benchmark would score that beyond ROUGE, accuracy, and MAE?

title: Appropriate Reliance on AI Advice: Conceptualization and the Effect of Explanations
authors: Max Schemmer, Niklas Kuehl, Carina Benz, Andrea Bartos, Gerhard Satzger
venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces
summary: The paper defines appropriate reliance (AR) on AI advice and proposes Appropriateness of Reliance (AoR), a two-dimensional metric combining relative AI reliance (RAIR) and relative self-reliance (RSR). In a 200-participant online experiment on deceptive hotel review classification, the authors compare AI advice with and without LIME feature-importance explanations. Explanations raised RAIR (29.6% to 38.9%) without significantly changing RSR, partly through increased confidence change, but had no effect on trust. Team performance did not exceed human accuracy, so AR was not achieved. Analysis is group-level, with a fixed advisor and no personalization or adaptation.
what_is_learned: No personalization model is learned. The paper defines a measurement concept, Appropriateness of Reliance (RAIR and RSR), and tests via SEM how explanations affect reliance, trust and confidence. The only trained component is a fixed SVM advisor with LIME explanations.
usil_relation: The AoR measurement (RAIR/RSR) quantifies how people rely on AI advice, using initial vs. revised decisions and confidence changes [user_signals]. This is a procedural, interaction-level outcome and could serve as a per-user signal for adaptive deference or return of control.
open_question: Could per-user RAIR/RSR and confidence-change trajectories be estimated over repeated sessions to learn individual reliance profiles, and used to decide when to show explanations or advice, given that the paper only compares control vs. explanation groups in a single session?
evaluation_scale: 200 Prolific participants (199 analyzed), between-subjects, 16 hotel review classifications each

title: SPRInG: Continual LLM Personalization via Selective Parametric Adaptation and Retrieval-Interpolated Generation
authors: Seoyeon Kim, Jaehyung Kim
summary: SPRInG is a semi-parametric framework for continual LLM personalization under preference drift. During training, a per-user LoRA adapter is updated only on high-drift-score interactions, and a bounded replay buffer keeps hard residual samples. At inference, relevance-gated BM25 retrieval is combined with the parametric model through token-level probability interpolation. On LongLaMP Abstract Generation and Review Writing (100 users each, five chronological periods), it beats continual-learning and personalization baselines on ROUGE across all periods. Gains also hold across backbones and on an extra Amazon dataset. It personalizes generated text only, not interaction behavior, and measures computational cost rather than user-facing cost.
user_evidence: stream of a user's historical interactions/documents
usil_relation: Per-user LoRA adapters updated sequentially across five chronological periods, with a drift score that separates real preference change from noise, mirror USIL's concern with online per-user adaptation and drift versus noise. Only generated text content and style are personalized.
open_question: Could drift-gated selective updating and replay be applied to user-specific interaction signals (corrections, takeovers, approvals) to adapt when an agent asks, confirms, or defers, and would the drift score distinguish a change in procedural preference from noise?
evaluation_scale: 100 users per task (Abstract Generation, Review Writing) from LongLaMP, with real historical data split into 5 chronological periods; offline replay, no live users

title: Learning on the Job: Continual Learning from Deployment Feedback for Frozen-Weights Agents
authors: Valentin Tablan, Scott Taylor, Kristoffer Bernhem
summary: The paper tests whether the feedback ordinary deployment already produces (a one-bit outcome verdict and a post-failure corrected action sequence) is enough for a frozen-weights agent to learn continually. The agent distills WHEN–THEN insights into a shared natural-language memory store (Spark). On τ-bench banking with a simulated customer, Mistral Large pass^1 rises from 0.064 to 0.170 in instruction mode, and Sonnet 5 replicates. Frozen stores transfer across models in both directions. Memory is shared across users and excludes customer-specific facts, so there is no personalization. The paper releases a protocol with a static-RAG control and metrics for success, reliability and retention. Limitations: single runs, one domain, perfectly reliable feedback.
user_evidence: outcome verdicts (one-bit) and after-the-fact corrections from operators
usil_relation: It learns continually from ordinary deployment feedback (outcome verdicts and after-the-fact corrections) into an external natural-language memory for a frozen agent, and it measures retention across repeated trials. This is the same mechanism a USIL agent could use for user-specific procedural memory.
open_question: Would the post-episode feedback-to-memory loop still work if rules were conditioned on an individual user's corrections and takeovers, with noisy and drifting real feedback? Could it learn per-user when-to-ask or when-to-confirm rules rather than shared task rules?
evaluation_scale: τ-bench banking, 97 tasks × 4 trials = 388 simulated conversations per condition; simulated customer GPT-5.2; agents Mistral Large 2512 and Claude Sonnet 5; single run per condition

title: Right Now, Wrong Then: Non-Stationary Direct Preference Optimization under Preference Drift
authors: Seongho Son, William Bankes, Sayak Ray Chowdhury, Brooks Paige, Ilija Bogunovic
summary: NS-DPO extends DPO to preference drift in offline, timestamped preference data. It uses a Dynamic Bradley-Terry model with an exponential discount γ that down-weights older comparisons, so the fine-tuned LLM reflects present preferences. The paper gives regret and estimation-error bounds for log-linear policies under drift, recovering O(n^-1/2) when drift vanishes. Experiments use synthetic drift built from reward-model switches and country preference distributions. NS-DPO beats DPO, IPO and tDPO by up to ~10% reward accuracy under gradual drift and matches DPO with no drift. It is population-level and offline, with no user modeling or interaction decisions.
user_evidence: timestamped pairwise preference comparisons
usil_relation: Treats temporal preference drift in offline preference data, which relates to USIL's concern with distinguishing drift from noise in evolving user evidence. NS-DPO down-weights old data with a single γ and gives theoretical guarantees [temporal_adaptation][claimed_contribution].
open_question: Can time-discounting be applied per user, with user-specific drift rates, to interaction preferences (when to ask or confirm) rather than a population-level output reward? NS-DPO also down-weights stationary preferences, since it cannot tell which preferences changed.
evaluation_scale: Synthetic non-stationary datasets (UltraFeedback-RM/LM, TV-HH, 2C NSGO) with 100 time steps, built from reward models or country preference distributions; Llama-2-7b-chat and Llama-3.2-1b; no real users.

title: Personalized Adaptation via In-Context Preference Learning
authors: Allison Lau, Younwoo Choi, Vahid Balazadeh, Keertana Chidambaram, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Rahul G. Krishnan
venue: NeurIPS 2024 Workshop on Adaptive Foundation Models; arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.14001
summary: The paper proposes the Preference Pretrained Transformer (PPT), a single history-dependent policy trained offline with a DPO-style loss on preference data stratified by group. At deployment the model generates two responses per prompt, the user ranks them, and the comparison is appended to context. This lets the model infer the user's preference profile without per-user training or model selection. In a small synthetic contextual bandit with simulated users from three groups and a mixed-preference user, PPT's rewards rise over 15 turns and beat Personalized Soups. The authors acknowledge there are no LLM experiments, and cross-session and real-user evaluations are absent.
user_evidence: online per-user preference feedback accumulated in context
usil_relation: PPT conditions a policy on a user's interaction history, as in pi_u(a|s,h^u), and adapts online from pairwise feedback without per-user weight updates. The learned object is the preferred response (outcome), not an interaction decision such as when to ask or defer.
open_question: Can in-context preference inference be extended from choosing which response a user prefers to choosing how the agent behaves, such as when to ask, confirm, or defer, with real users and real LLMs over multiple sessions and drifting preferences?
evaluation_scale: Simulated users from 3 subpopulations plus one mixed-preference user; 50 test contexts over 15 turns; Nc=500 and 1000 training contexts; synthetic contextual bandit with 4 actions.

title: Robot Learning on the Job: Human-in-the-Loop Autonomy and Learning During Deployment
authors: Huihan Liu, Soroush Nasiriany, Lance Zhang, Zhiyao Bao, Yuke Zhu
venue: Robotics: Science and Systems (RSS) 2023; arXiv preprint arXiv:2211.08416
summary: Sirius is a human-in-the-loop deployment framework for robot manipulation. A human supervises and intervenes through a SpaceMouse, and the robot policy is periodically retrained on the growing deployment data. Intervention-guided weighted behavioral cloning treats demonstrations and interventions as high quality and the robot samples just before an intervention as low quality. Memory management bounds the dataset size. Across two simulated and two real tasks on a Franka arm, Sirius beats IWR, BC-RNN and IQL, converges faster, uses less memory, and lowers the human intervention ratio over rounds. It is not personalized to the user, and evaluation used a single operator.
user_evidence: human takeovers/interventions and corrective demonstrations during deployment
usil_relation: Sirius treats takeover and handback timing as implicit signals of human trust, and uses them to continually update the policy across deployment rounds while human workload falls. This is the kind of evidence USIL would learn from, though here it improves the task policy rather than a per-user interaction policy.
open_question: Could intervention and handback patterns like Sirius's be used to learn each operator's own intervention thresholds and autonomy preferences, so the robot decides when to seek help or hand back control? Does that differ across operators with different skill and risk tolerance, given that Sirius used only one operator per task?
evaluation_scale: A single human operator per task across 4 tasks (2 simulated, 2 real) over 3 deployment rounds. Simulation used 3 seeds with 100 trials per checkpoint. Real-world evaluation used 1 seed with 32 trials.

title: Physical interaction as communication: Learning robot objectives online from human corrections
authors: Dylan P. Losey, A. Bajcsy, M. O'Malley, A. Dragan
summary: This paper formalizes physical human-robot interaction as a POMDP in which human forces are observations about a hidden reward weight vector θ. The robot uses real-time approximations (QMDP, MAP, trajectory-level online gradient descent) to update θ after each correction and replan the rest of the task. A one-at-a-time update rule reduces unintended learning. In simulation and in two user studies on a 7-DoF arm (N=10 and N=12), learning cut effort, interaction time and cost versus impedance control and deformation baselines. Objectives were assigned by experimenters, features are assumed known, and neither cross-session nor cross-task transfer is tested.
usil_relation: Learns a reward from physical corrections online within a task, so the user's corrections steer the robot's behavior. It is a close precursor for adapting to corrections as evidence, though it learns what the robot optimizes rather than how it interacts.
open_question: Can physical corrections also serve as evidence about a user's procedural preferences (when to take over, how much autonomy to grant), persisting across sessions, when the experimenter does not assign the objective and the user's own preferences are elicited?
evaluation_scale: Simulated optimal and noisy humans with a 2-DoF point robot; two within-subjects studies with 10 and 12 UC Berkeley participants on a 7-DoF JACO2 arm

title: Learning from interventions: Human-robot interaction as both explicit and implicit feedback
authors: Jonathan Spencer, Sanjiban Choudhury, Matt Barnes, Matt Schmittle, Mung Chiang, P. Ramadge, S. Srinivasa
summary: Expert Intervention Learning (EIL) is a no-regret online algorithm that learns from human-gated interventions. It treats non-intervention as implicit approval, the moments before an intervention as bad, and expert actions as demonstrations, converting these into constraints on a linear action-value function over 64 motion primitives. In simulation with a scripted expert, EIL beats BC, DAgger and HG-DAgger on expert and total samples. On a real MuSHR car, HG-DAgger needs fewer samples but yields jerkier policies. It does not model individual users, preference drift, or transfer, and a user study is left to future work.
usil_relation: EIL treats the timing of human takeover and handback as implicit feedback, which is the kind of signal USIL would use to learn how an agent exercises autonomy. In this paper, though, it only trains a driving cost function for a single (simulated or unspecified) expert.
open_question: Can intervention and non-intervention timing be used to learn an individual user's interaction policy, such as when to hand back control or how autonomous to be, and does it adapt as that user's intervention style changes (which the paper lists as future work) or transfers across tasks?
evaluation_scale: Scripted simulated expert in MuSHR simulation; a human expert on a real 1/10-scale MuSHR car over 24 iterations of T=70 steps (number of participants not reported).

title: The Role of Adaptation in Collective Human–AI Teaming
authors: Michelle Zhao; Reid Simmons; Henny Admoni
summary: The paper proposes a feature-agnostic formalism for robot-to-human adaptation in human–AI teams, treating adaptation as a two-process cycle: learning a component of the human's POMDP, then influencing the collaboration through the AI's behavior. A case study in a search-and-rescue gridworld adapts navigation instruction complexity to each participant's inferred map knowledge using goal-prediction probability as a proxy. A user study with 100 participants compared adaptive and static instructors. Adaptation produced no significant gains in performance or preference, only engagement benefits for participants whose knowledge was misaligned with the complexity. The case study is limited to a single session and one parameter.
usil_relation: It formalizes per-human adaptation of how an AI teammate communicates (instruction complexity) as learning a component of the human's POMDP and then influencing the collaboration. The adaptive instructor individualizes complexity from each participant's behavior, tested with 100 participants in a user study. This is the closest match to procedure-level personalization.
open_question: Can the adaptation parameter be extended from instruction complexity to decisions such as when to ask, confirm, or defer, and persist and transfer across sessions and tasks, given that the adaptive instructor here gave no significant performance or preference benefit?
evaluation_scale: 108 Prolific participants (100 retained) in a mixed-design study with two 4-minute rounds each (static vs adaptive instructor)

title: Human-robot mutual adaptation in collaborative tasks: Models and experiments
authors: Stefanos Z. Nikolaidis, David Hsu, Siddhartha S Srinivasa
venue: The International Journal of Robotics Research
summary: The paper proposes the Bounded-Memory Adaptation Model (BAM), a probabilistic finite-state model of how humans adapt to a robot partner, embedded in a MOMDP where the human's adaptability α is a latent variable. The robot infers α online from the human's action choices and either guides adaptable people toward a better collaboration strategy or complies with non-adaptable ones. In online between-subjects studies (n=69 plus follow-ups), 57% of participants adapted under mutual adaptation versus 26% under cross-training, and trust was higher than with a fixed robot. Adaptability transferred weakly across tasks. Model structure is hand-specified and the belief is reset between tasks.
usil_relation: The robot infers a per-person adaptability α online and uses the belief to decide whether to pursue its own goal or defer to the human's preference. This is an individual-level procedural policy, and the paper tests cross-task transfer of adaptability from table-carrying to hallway-crossing.
open_question: Can adaptability be carried across sessions, rather than reset to a uniform belief, and extended to a learned, richer user model that also covers when to ask, confirm, or return control? Transfer of α was only weakly predictive (R²=11.9%), so what actually transfers remains open.
evaluation_scale: Online between-subjects MTurk studies: n=69 main study, plus follow-ups with n=43 (repeated table-carrying), n=65 (hallway), n=58 (table then hallway)

title: Programming by Chat: A Large-Scale Behavioral Analysis of 11,579 Real-World AI-Assisted IDE Sessions
authors: Ningzhi Tang, Chaoran Chen, Zihan Fang, et al.
summary: This observational study analyzes 74,998 developer messages from 11,579 real IDE chat sessions (Cursor, Copilot) across 1,300 public repositories and 899 developers. It builds a 7-category, 20-subcategory behavioral intent taxonomy, classifies messages with a prompted GPT-5 mini (macro F1 0.80 against 400 human-labeled messages), and clusters sessions into six archetypes. Findings: iterative modification dominates new implementation, failure reporting is common, validation is rare, sessions are short, intents are self-reinforcing, and opening turns differ from later ones. It does no personalization or per-user modeling, but it offers a population-level baseline of procedural interaction behavior.
what_is_learned: No model is trained. The paper derives a behavioral intent taxonomy by abductive coding, labels messages with a prompted GPT-5 mini classifier, and finds session archetypes via K-Medoids over intent sequences. These are descriptive findings about developer behavior.
user_evidence: real-world chat logs, refinements/corrections, user-written persistent plans and rules files
usil_relation: It is a large-scale observational analysis of how developers interact procedurally with IDE assistants, covering behavior specification, constraining AI autonomy, delegating diagnosis and validation, and session-opening framing. This is the kind of user-side interaction evidence USIL would learn from [interaction_decisions][user_evidence]. Its intent taxonomy and session archetypes could define the procedural preference space.
open_question: Do the intent distributions and archetypes vary systematically across the 899 developers, so that individual developers show stable procedural styles? Could per-developer intent sequences, such as constraint-setting or validation habits, predict when each developer wants confirmation or autonomy?

title: Future of Work with AI Agents: Auditing Automation and Augmentation Potential across the U.S. Workforce
authors: Yijia Shao, Humishka Zope, Yucheng Jiang, et al.
summary: The paper introduces an auditing framework and the WORKBank database to assess which occupational tasks workers want AI agents to automate or augment, and how this compares with expert-rated technical capability. It surveys 1,500 workers and 52 AI experts across 844 tasks in 104 occupations. It introduces the five-level Human Agency Scale (H1–H5). Tasks fall into four desire–capability zones. Workers want automation for 46.1% of tasks, H3 (equal partnership) is the most common preferred level, and workers prefer more agency than experts deem necessary. The results are averaged per task, with no learning, personalization, or longitudinal adaptation.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned. The paper builds a descriptive audit database (WORKBank) of aggregated worker ratings (automation desire, desired Human Agency Scale level) and expert ratings (capability, feasible HAS level) per occupational task.
user_evidence: worker survey and audio-enhanced interview responses on desired level of human involvement
usil_relation: The Human Agency Scale (H1–H5) is a population-level measure of how much autonomy versus human involvement workers want per task. This is the procedural dimension of USIL (autonomy, collaboration), but it is averaged across workers [claimed_contribution][user_representation]. The paper also notes that H3 agents need coordination with humans [interaction_decisions].
open_question: Do individual workers' desired HAS levels for the same task differ systematically (beyond the average and the demographic ICC), and can an agent learn each person's preferred agency level from behavior instead of surveys?
evaluation_scale: 1,500 workers across 104 occupations (7,016 task ratings from 1,678 participants), plus 52 AI experts rating 844 tasks

title: Intuitive Programming, Adaptive Task Planning, and Dynamic Role Allocation in Human–Robot Collaboration
authors: Marta Lagomarsino, Elena Merlo, Andrea Pupa, T. Birr, F. Krebs, Cristian Secchi, T. Asfour, A. Ajoudani
venue: Annual Review of Control Robotics and Autonomous Systems
summary: A narrative, non-systematic review of human-robot collaboration that frames it as bidirectional information flow. It links intuitive programming (multimodal input, learning task models from demonstrations), adaptive task planning (single and hierarchical planners, foundation models) and dynamic role allocation, which it categorizes by decision criterion and strategy. Surveyed works use physiological, gaze, gesture and language signals, and model human state through trust, fatigue and cognitive load. The authors call for personalized, co-evolving partner models and online co-adaptation. The paper has no experiments, and it notes that real-world integration and validation remain early.
what_is_learned: As a narrative review it learns nothing itself. It surveys learning of task models from demonstrations, foundation-model planning, and data-driven role allocation (learned trust models, preference costs), and calls for personalized evolving partner models.
usil_relation: Section 4 surveys dynamic role allocation: who leads or follows, whether to take over or wait, and clarifying questions as POMDP actions. It also covers learned trust and a preference cost that rises with repeated task rejections, which are per-user procedural adaptations. The conclusion calls for personalized, evolving partner models.
open_question: Can role-allocation and communication policies in HRC be learned per individual from sparse signals such as task rejections, corrections and trust shifts, and do they transfer across tasks and sessions? The review reports no such evaluation and only calls for it.

title: Human-aware AI —A foundational framework for human–AI interaction
authors: Sarath Sreedharan
summary: This talk abstract introduces Human-Aware AI (HAAI), a framework for human–AI interaction that tackles the asymmetry between AI systems and their users. It models the human's beliefs about the system and their cognitive capabilities, and accounts for three asymmetries: knowledge, inferential capability and vocabulary. The authors say it has already yielded effective explanation generation methods, though no results or data are given. Future directions include human advising of AI and value alignment. The paper is conceptual and gives no evidence of per-user learning, temporal adaptation, transfer or evaluation, so it contributes little to USIL beyond its mental-model framing.
what_is_learned: Nothing learned is established. The framework is conceptual: it models the human's mental model of the AI (beliefs, cognitive capabilities) to drive explanation generation. Human advising of AI and value alignment are proposed as future work.
usil_relation: The framework models the user's beliefs about the AI (M^R_h) and three asymmetries (knowledge, inference, vocabulary) to shape explanations. This is a conceptual precursor to a user representation z_u that conditions how an agent communicates [user_representation].
open_question: How could HAAI's human mental model M^R_h be learned per individual from sparse, evolving interaction evidence (corrections, advice) and used to decide when to explain, ask, or defer, rather than being assumed or averaged?

title: Effect of Adapting to Human Preferences on Trust in Human-Robot Teaming
authors: Shreyas Bhat, Joseph B. Lyons, Cong Shi, X. Jessie Yang
summary: The paper tests whether a robot that adapts to a human's learned preferences earns more trust in a human-robot search task. It combines a trust-aware MDP, a Beta-distribution trust model and Bayesian IRL over the human's health-vs-time reward weight, updated from accept/reject choices. In a within-subjects study with 12 participants and three strategies (non-learner, non-adaptive learner, adaptive learner), the adaptive strategy gained the highest post-mission Muir trust and the most agreement with recommendations. Limits: a two-component reward, an uninformed prior, a small sample, one task, and adaptation only within a single mission, with no cross-session or transfer evaluation.
usil_relation: Per-user online Bayesian IRL from accept/reject choices on robot recommendations, with a trust model feeding a policy that is personalized and evaluated against non-learning and non-adaptive baselines with trust as the outcome. This is close to USIL's idea of a user-conditioned policy.
open_question: The adapted element is the recommendation policy over a two-weight task reward (health vs. time), not procedural choices such as when to ask or defer. Would the approach learn per-user interaction preferences (ask/confirm/defer) over longer horizons, across sessions, and across tasks, rather than trust in a single 40-site task?
evaluation_scale: 12 university engineering students, within-subjects, 3 missions of 40 search sites each, Latin-square counterbalanced

title: A Systematic Review of Personalized Collaborative Systems
authors: Thomas Neumayr, Mirjam Augstein
summary: This 2020 systematic review surveys personalized collaborative systems (PCS) in the ACM Digital Library. From 344 retrieved results it identifies 36 relevant papers (2007–2018), and offers a general PCS definition, eight thematic clusters, an analysis of the data used for personalization (user, usage, environment), study-type coding, and a co-located vs. remote taxonomy. It finds PCS to be a young, niche, scattered field with a shift toward human-centered evaluation and calls for more user modeling for collaboration. The review itself learns nothing and does not analyze interaction-policy decisions, temporal adaptation, or transfer.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned; this is a systematic literature review of 36 ACM DL papers on personalized collaborative systems. It catalogs what reviewed systems personalize to and how (user models, recommenders, UI adaptation).
usil_relation: It catalogs personalization in collaborative systems (adaptability vs. adaptivity, user/usage/environment data, user modeling for collaboration) and concludes more user modeling effort is needed [user_representation][user_evidence]; this touches USIL's user-evidence and personalization themes in a pre-LLM, group-oriented setting.
open_question: The review does not analyze whether any of the 36 collaborative systems adapt procedural behavior (when to ask, act, or defer) per individual over time; how would USIL's per-user interaction policies apply in group collaboration, where individual and group preferences conflict?

title: Comparing Robot and Human guided Personalization: Adaptive Exercise Robots are Perceived as more Competent and Trustworthy
authors: Sebastian Schneider; Franz Kummert
summary: Long-term HRI personalization and user evaluations; check exact learned behaviors
usil_relation: It compares autonomous adaptation by online preference learning (DTS) against user-controlled adaptation in a 40-person between-subjects SAR exercise study. This is a Level-of-Automation question about who drives personalization, and it measures competence, warmth and alliance as relational outcomes.
open_question: Does the learned adaptation cover procedural aspects such as when the robot asks, confirms or defers, rather than only behavior parameters? Do the benefits persist across sessions and for individual users, given that only group-level comparisons are reported?
evaluation_scale: 40 participants, between-subjects (adaptable vs adaptive robot), exercise scenario with a socially assistive robot

title: Balancing Shared Autonomy with Human-Robot Communication
authors: Rosario Scalise et al.
summary: This 2018 paper frames human-robot language as shared autonomy and studies how people trade off plan efficiency against cognitive load when instructing a robot butler (HERB) in a table-clearing task. Crowdworker studies (a 9-person pilot and two n=50 experiments) compare untrained, robot-capability-trained, and language-phrasing-trained conditions. Untrained users give vague goal-level language. After training they shift to repetitive absolute orderings, which speed planning but raise mental demand. Partial-ordering or grouping language gives large planner gains at lower demand. In a 24-object scene users keep high-level language, and satisfaction drops. No model is learned, results are population-level, and transfer is only claimed.
what_is_learned: No model is learned; the paper empirically characterizes how humans' instruction language, mental demand and resulting plan efficiency change with robot-capability and language training and with task complexity.
usil_relation: It treats human instruction language as a shared-autonomy tradeoff between plan efficiency and human cognitive load, measured with NASA-TLX-style ratings. It also shows that training on robot capabilities shifts user language from natural to programmatic. This is procedural (how people communicate) and uses within-study training as a proxy for online learning [temporal_adaptation][interaction_costs].
open_question: Do individual users differ stably in their efficiency-versus-effort tradeoffs (e.g. absolute ordering vs. high-level instructions), such that a robot could learn per-user when to press for input or ask for help? The paper reports only aggregate results and treats this as future work [personalization][interaction_decisions].
evaluation_scale: 9-person preliminary study plus two disjoint AMT experiments with n=50 each (native English speakers); table-clearing with 3-7 objects (Exp I) and 24 objects (Exp II)

title: Collaborative Planning with Encoding of Users’ High-Level Strategies
authors: Joseph Kim, Christopher J. Banks, Julie A. Shah
summary: User high-level strategy preferences shape collaboration planning
usil_relation: Users give high-level strategies as soft preferences to steer a planner, which is a form of human-in-the-loop guidance. It is a weak precursor to eliciting user-specific procedural input, but the strategies are task guidance rather than interaction preferences.
open_question: Could user-supplied strategies be treated as persistent per-user evidence, so a planner learns how each user prefers to guide or delegate and decides when to request strategies versus plan autonomously?
evaluation_scale: Human subject experiments; number of participants not given in the abstract

title: How to be Helpful? Supportive Behaviors and Personalization for Human-Robot Collaboration
authors: Olivier Mangin; Alessandro Roncone; Brian Scassellati
venue: Frontiers in Robotics and AI (2022), volume 8
summary: The paper presents a framework that automatically converts a shared hierarchical task model into a POMDP and solves it online with POMCP. A Baxter robot can then proactively choose supportive actions (wait, hold, bring, clean-up) during collaborative table assembly. The robot keeps a belief over a hidden binary user preference for being held, updated from sparse error signals and the absence of negative feedback. In simulation it matches or beats hand-coded and always-hold/never-hold policies. A live study with four participants showed a 13.2% completion-time reduction under full support. Adaptation happens within one task only. Code and the task model set are released.
usil_relation: A per-user, within-task belief over a hidden procedural preference (whether the robot should hold parts) drives a POMDP policy for when to offer proactive support, which is a small instance of a user-conditioned interaction policy. The robot learns from sparse negative feedback (error button presses) and the absence of it, and sometimes takes information-gathering hold actions.
open_question: Can preferences about proactive support persist across sessions, transfer to new tasks or users, and be learned rather than hand-specified, given that this paper models only one binary preference inside a single task, with hand-set rewards and 4 participants?
evaluation_scale: 4 participants in a within-subjects live Baxter study, plus 6,000 simulated interactions and 100 episodes per task structure over 3 HTM structures

title: MemToolAgent: Leveraging Memory for Tool Using Agents Based on Environment and User Feedback
authors: Suleyman Armagan Er, Danilo Ribeiro, Yogesh Virkar, et al.
summary: MemToolAgent is a training-free memory framework for LLM tool-using agents. It stores past user-agent experiences (query, tool calls, binary user feedback, reflection) in a unified entry format. A reflection-based extractor turns failures and environment/user feedback into critiques and preference statements. A retrieval module picks how many entries to use from the similarity distribution. It reports relative gains of 29%, 80% and 17% on WorkBench, NESTFUL and PEToolBench, including personalized tool orchestration versus A-MEM and Mem0. Feedback is simulated and single-turn, with a single run. It makes no interaction decisions such as asking or deferring, and tests no preference drift.
user_evidence: User feedback on tool-execution outcomes; environment feedback on failures
usil_relation: Experience memory built from binary user feedback plus environment feedback, with reflection that distills failed executions into critiques and user preferences such as 'User prefers tools under API_X'. It is evaluated on PEToolBench, where per-user histories of 80-100 rated queries resolve tool ambiguity. This is a memory-based user-specific signal, but it targets what tool is chosen, not how the agent interacts.
open_question: Could the reflection-based memory of binary approvals and rejections be extended to distill per-user interaction preferences (when to ask, confirm, or defer) in multi-turn settings, and would it still hold up when preferences drift or when evaluated with real users rather than simulated feedback?
evaluation_scale: Offline benchmarks with simulated binary feedback: WorkBench (one query per template as memory), NESTFUL (500 test, 500 memory), PEToolBench (591 test queries, 50-query subset for A-MEM/Mem0 comparison); Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet, single run.

title: Memp: Exploring Agent Procedural Memory
authors: Runnan Fang, Yuan Liang, Xiaobin Wang, et al.
summary: Memp studies how LLM agents can build, retrieve and update a lifelong procedural memory from past trajectories. It compares storing verbatim trajectories, abstract scripts, or both (proceduralization), different retrieval keys, and update strategies: vanilla addition, validation filtering, and reflection-based adjustment. On TravelPlanner and ALFWorld with GPT-4o, Claude and Qwen, all memory variants beat no memory, proceduralization works best, and reflection-based updating improves results over sequential task groups. Memory built by a strong model also helps a weaker one. The signals are benchmark rewards, not users, so personalization and interaction decisions are not addressed.
user_evidence: None from users; the agent's own trajectories and task outcomes
usil_relation: Memp builds a lifelong, updatable procedural memory from past trajectories, with online update by validation filtering or reflection. This is the memory mechanism a per-user interaction policy could reuse. It also shows script-style abstractions generalize better than verbatim trajectories to new tasks.
open_question: Could Memp-style procedural memory be built from user-specific signals (takeovers, corrections, approvals) so that it stores per-user procedures for when to ask, confirm or defer, rather than task-solving procedures from benchmark rewards?

title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
authors: Charles Packer, Sarah Wooders, Kevin Lin, et al.
summary: MemGPT treats an LLM as an operating system with virtual context management. A tiered memory (main context with system instructions, working context and a FIFO queue, plus external recall and archival storage) is edited through self-directed function calls. Event-based control flow and function chaining let the agent page data in and out and decide when to return control to the user. No parameters are trained. On Multi-Session Chat, MemGPT raises deep memory retrieval accuracy from about 32% to over 92% with GPT-4 and produces engaging conversation openers. It also helps in long-document QA and nested key-value retrieval. Evaluation is offline with simulated personas. Code and data are released.
user_evidence: Multi-session conversation history (facts users state about themselves); no explicit corrections or approvals
usil_relation: MemGPT's working context stores user facts and preferences as editable text, and the agent decides on its own when to write, search or evict memory and when to yield control. That is a memory substrate for z_u and some self-directed autonomy over memory operations [personalization][interaction_decisions].
open_question: Can an OS-style memory hierarchy like MemGPT's store procedural interaction preferences (when a given user wants questions, confirmations, or handoffs) rather than only declarative facts, and can it do so for real users whose preferences drift? The paper has no real-user data and no quantitative drift test.
evaluation_scale: Multi-Session Chat persona logs (human labelers playing personas) with synthetic DMR QA pairs; 50 NaturalQuestions document-QA questions; nested KV with 140 UUID pairs. No real users.

title: Collaborative Interface Agents
authors: Yezdi Lashkari; Max Metral; Pattie Maes
summary: This 1994 paper presents a framework and protocol for collaboration among personal email learning agents. Each agent uses memory-based reasoning to learn its user's email handling as situation-action pairs, and users set tell-me and do-it thresholds that control suggestion versus autonomous action. When uncertain or exploring, an agent asks peer agents for predictions and learns per-situation-class trust in each peer from how well their predictions match its own user's actions. In a prototype on two graduate students' real email, a new user's agent reached higher-confidence correct predictions faster with an experienced peer's help. The evaluation is a single small scenario with no user-burden measurement.
usil_relation: Each user's email agent learns from that user's own actions. Per-user tell-me and do-it thresholds govern suggest-versus-act autonomy, and the agent decides when to ask peer agents. This is close to a user-conditioned interaction policy with cross-user transfer. The evidence does not show that the thresholds are learned; they are set by the user.
open_question: Can the tell-me and do-it thresholds, and the decision to ask peers, be learned per user from corrections and takeovers rather than set manually? Does this hold beyond a single two-user, three-day scenario with no preference drift and no per-user interaction metrics?
evaluation_scale: Real email of two graduate students (one new, one experienced), about 100 messages each over three days; a single scenario

title: Towards Adjustable Autonomy for the Real World
authors: P. Scerri, D. Pynadath, Milind Tambe
summary: The paper presents a transfer-of-control strategy approach to adjustable autonomy for agent-human teams. A strategy is a conditional sequence of control transfers and coordination-change actions such as delaying a meeting. It comes with an expected-utility model and an MDP operationalization solved by value iteration. The MDP replaced an earlier C4.5 decision-tree approach that made catastrophic errors in the E-Elves system, which ten users at ISI ran for about 7 months. Users could add constraints that forbid or require actions, and these cut policy-generation time by 28-53%. The policy is not learned or personalized per user, and evaluation is mostly qualitative and simulated.
usil_relation: The paper treats when to transfer control to the user as an expected-utility decision over time-dependent response probabilities, wait costs, and communication costs. It was deployed with ten E-Elves users for about 7 months and includes user-specified constraints, which is early evidence for adaptive autonomy in a real setting [interaction_decisions][interaction_costs][user_evidence].
open_question: Could the hand-specified response-probability distributions, communication costs, and decision-quality parameters be learned per user from takeovers, delays, and responses over the 7-month deployment, and would per-user policies beat the shared MDP and the user constraints?
evaluation_scale: 10 users in a research group at ISI over about 7 months of live E-Elves deployment, plus simulations and parameter sweeps over a 2800-state MDP

title: Learning to Defer to a Population: A Meta-Learning Approach
authors: Dharmesh Tailor, Aditya Patra, Rajeev Verma, Putra Manggala, Eric Nalisnick
venue: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS 2024), PMLR 238
summary: Extends learning-to-defer to experts never seen in training. The system meta-learns a deferral policy that adapts at test time from a small context set describing the current expert, and an attention-based variant finds context examples similar to the test input to estimate the expert's ability more precisely.
what_is_learned: interaction policy (deferral) conditioned on a latent per-expert model
user_evidence: Small context set of the specific human expert's past decisions/labels
usil_relation: It offers a formal few-shot recipe for conditioning a defer/act policy on one human's evidence. Remaining question: it models the human's competence rather than their *preference* for control, so it is unclear how it extends to sequential agent tasks.

title: Semi-Autonomous Systems with Contextual Competence Awareness
authors: Saaduddin Mahmud, Connor Basich, Shlomo Zilberstein
venue: International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems (AAMAS 2023)
summary: This paper extends competence-aware semi-autonomous systems to a Contextual Competence Aware System (CoCAS). CoCAS has a stochastic operator model, conditioned on Markovian operator state and context, that can represent multiple operators. The agent learns the autonomy profile and operator-model components, choosing domain actions and levels of autonomy (no autonomy, verified, supervised, full) jointly. It keeps CAS's convergence guarantees and generalizes CAS and fully observable SO-SAS. In simulated UAV surveillance and AV delivery domains it beats CAS and shared-autonomy baselines, with 100% level-optimality versus 78% for CAS, lower human cost, and about half the queries. It assumes full observability, simulated operators and no transfer evaluation.
user_evidence: Operator approvals, overrides and interventions at different autonomy levels
usil_relation: CoCAS learns a state-, operator- and context-conditioned level of autonomy from approval, disapproval and override feedback. This is an adaptive-autonomy policy conditioned on operator identity and state, and it is the closest match to USIL's procedural adaptation of when to act or defer [what_is_learned][personalization].
open_question: Can CoCAS-style autonomy learning work with a single real user whose preferences are latent and only partially observed, instead of with fully observable simulated operator states? Does a learned per-user autonomy profile transfer across tasks and contexts?
evaluation_scale: Two simulated domains: a UAV surveillance domain with one operator of varying availability, and an AV delivery domain with a local and a global operator over 8 routes and 200 learning episodes.

title: SARI: Shared Autonomy across Repeated Interaction
authors: Ananth Jonnavittula, Shaunak A. Mehta, Dylan P. Losey
summary: SARI is a shared-autonomy algorithm for assistive robot arms that learns assistance from scratch by exploiting the fact that users repeat important tasks. From the user's own teleoperation commands and robot states, it learns an encoder that infers a latent task, a policy that replicates similar past demonstrations, and a discriminator that sets the arbitration weight so control returns to the human when behavior is unfamiliar. It is retrained between interactions. The paper adds an error-bound analysis, simulations against DAgger variants, and three user studies (including one disabled participant), showing reduced effort and a preference for SARI over CASA in 9 of 10 users.
user_evidence: Repeated teleoperation demonstrations by the same user
usil_relation: SARI learns shared autonomy from a single user's repeated teleoperation, retrains between interactions, and uses a learned confidence discriminator to decide between acting and returning control. This is close to a user-conditioned arbitration policy, though the learning signal is task demonstrations rather than interaction preferences.
open_question: Does SARI's confidence-based return-of-control reflect individual users' preferences about autonomy (for example, how much a given user wants to be handed control) rather than just task familiarity? Do the learned models transfer across users, or can they handle user co-adaptation and preference drift, given that only 10 and 10 non-disabled users plus 1 disabled pilot participant were tested and per-user results were not shown?
notes: evaluates_transfer: new tasks not anticipated a priori
evaluation_scale: Simulations with noisy simulated humans on Franka and UR10 arms; Study 1: 10 non-disabled participants; Study 2: 10 non-disabled participants (No Assist vs CASA vs SARI); Study 3: remote pilot with 1 disabled participant

title: Report on the 1st Workshop on Human-Centered Proactive and Personalized Agents for Interactive Information Access at CHIIR 2026
authors: Kirandeep Kaur, Vinayak Gupta, Tanya Roosta, Madhura Raju, Grace Hui Yang, Chirag Shah
summary: This report summarizes the 1st Workshop on Human-Centered Proactive and Personalized Agents for Interactive Information Access at CHIIR 2026. It describes accepted contributions and themes: proactivity as calibrated initiative, memory and implicit personalization with privacy and dependence risks, user control and contestability, and evaluation beyond accuracy. It proposes a six-point research agenda covering when to stay passive, clarify, recommend, warn or act, plus temporal memory updating and longitudinal evaluation. There are no experiments, methods or learned components. The report is explicitly not a settled consensus. Its value for USIL is as a framing of proactive-agent decisions and open evaluation needs.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned; this is a workshop report. It only summarizes accepted papers that discuss memory, user models and calibrated initiative, and it sets out a research agenda.
user_evidence: n/a
usil_relation: It frames proactivity as calibrated initiative (when to stay passive, clarify, recommend, warn or act) with user control through why-now explanations, interruption budgets and permission ladders. This matches USIL's procedural decisions and its call for longitudinal evaluation. It stays at the level of themes and agenda, not per-user learning.
open_question: How can per-user proactivity and interruption thresholds, such as the interruption budgets and permission ladders proposed here, be learned from a user's corrections and refusals and evaluated longitudinally, rather than set as population-level design principles?

title: Shared Autonomy via Hindsight Optimization
authors: Shervin Javdani, Siddhartha S. Srinivasa, J. Andrew Bagnell
summary: The paper formulates shared autonomy for robot teleoperation as a POMDP with uncertainty over the user's goal. It infers a goal distribution from joystick inputs using MaxEnt IOC and selects robot actions via hindsight optimization, so it assists for the full distribution rather than one predicted goal. A 10-person within-subjects study against predict-then-blend found faster grasps and less user input, but users felt less in control and trended toward preferring blend. The model is not personalized and uses hand-specified costs. The authors flag user-specific policies and personalized cost learning as future work.
user_evidence: Real-time user control inputs
usil_relation: It infers the user's latent goal online from continuous joystick inputs and uses that belief to set how much the robot acts versus defers to the user. This is an early example of a user-conditioned assistance policy. The user's inputs also affect the robot's control authority, which is the interaction-level behavior USIL cares about.
open_question: Could the goal posterior and cost functions be learned per user, so that assistance level and control authority adapt to individual preferences (e.g., users who felt a loss of control with the policy method vs. those who preferred it) across sessions and over practice?
evaluation_scale: 10 participants (9 male, 1 female), all with robotics experience, within-subjects teleoperation study grasping three objects with two systems

title: To Help or Not to Help?: An Expanded Framework for Deciding Socially Appropriate Robot Assistance
authors: Rebecca Ramnauth, Dražen Brščić, Brian Scassellati
summary: The paper proposes a theoretical framework for deciding when a robot should offer help, treating social appropriateness as the point where task utility, a function of human and robot skill, exceeds a skill-independent social cost. A within-subjects Prolific vignette study (215 participants, 48 scenarios) supports the predictions: robot skill, human skill, utility type, and task type all predict appropriateness, and an extended linear model with a robot-skill weight fits best. The model is hand-specified, with no learning, personalization, or longitudinal adaptation. The authors discuss extensions for uncertainty, offering versus doing, and learning user-specific helping preferences as future work.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned by an agent. A hand-specified utility-versus-cost threshold model of when offering help is socially appropriate, given human and robot skill. The only fitting is linear regression of utility models to participant vignette ratings, including a flexible model with a robot-skill weight α_r.
usil_relation: It models when a robot should offer help (versus not offer or act directly) as a threshold on utility versus social cost, using task-specific human skill as a scalar user representation. This is a procedural, mixed-initiative decision of the kind USIL wants to learn per user [interaction_decisions][user_representation].
open_question: Can the skill-based utility-versus-cost threshold, including the α_r weighting, be learned per user from real interaction signals (accepted or declined offers, takeovers) and shown to match individual helping preferences better than the population-level ratings used here, and does it hold as preferences and skill change over time?
evaluation_scale: 215 Prolific participants rating 48 vignettes (2,580 evaluations), as third-person judgments

title: Navigating autonomy and control in human-AI delegation: User responses to technology- versus user-invoked task allocation
authors: Martin Adam, Christopher Diebel, Marc Goutier, Alexander Benlian
summary: This Decision Support Systems paper examines how software developers respond when an AI coding assistant proactively offers to take over code writing (IS-invoked delegation) versus when the developer requests it (user-invoked). In two online vignette experiments with U.S. developers (N=95 and N=194), IS-invoked delegation raised perceived self-threat and so lowered willingness to accept delegation. The effect was stronger when the delegation left the user with less perceived control, such as when the system also made the final decision. Nothing is learned or personalized, the encounters are one-time, and only averaged effects are reported. The paper is a theory-driven account of the psychology of delegation.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned. The paper tests a theory-driven causal model (invocation type → self-threat → willingness to accept delegation, moderated by perceived control) using vignette experiments, OLS regressions and bootstrapped mediation.
usil_relation: It tests how agent-initiated versus user-initiated delegation of code writing to an AI coding assistant, and the amount of control retained (execution only vs. execution plus final decision), change developers' self-threat and willingness to accept [interaction_decisions][key_results]. This is the population-level evidence on autonomy and initiative that a user-specific policy would need to account for.
open_question: Do developers differ systematically in how they react to AI-invoked delegation (for example by need for control or self-efficacy), and can an agent learn each developer's thresholds for offering delegation and for retaining decision rights from repeated acceptances, declines and takeovers rather than one-time vignette responses?
evaluation_scale: Two online between-subjects vignette experiments with U.S. software developers: 95 analyzed participants in Study 1 and 194 in Study 2 (2×2 design).

title: Personal assistants: Direct manipulation vs. mixed initiative interfaces
authors: Marcelo G. Armentano, D. Godoy, A. Amandi
summary: This 2005 study asks how presenting a personal Web-search agent, PersonalSearcher, through a direct-manipulation interface versus an explicit mixed-initiative agent interface changes users' perception of it. PersonalSearcher learns a hierarchical interest profile by unsupervised clustering of browsing behaviour and suggests pages above an adjustable relevance threshold. In a between-subjects study, 42 students used one of the two versions for 3 weeks and then completed a survey. Mixed-initiative users were more critical and noticed improvement over time, while satisfaction and preference did not clearly differ. Results are group percentages with no significance tests, and the interaction style is fixed by condition rather than learned per user.
usil_relation: The agent keeps a per-user interest profile that is updated from browsing behaviour and approval of suggestions over 3 weeks [personalization][temporal_adaptation]. The study also compares mixed-initiative with direct-manipulation interaction styles, a procedural dimension, and examines the cost of explicit feedback [interaction_costs].
open_question: Could the choice between lamp-signalled and automatic suggestions, and the feedback burden, be learned per user from their approvals and ignored suggestions, instead of being fixed by interface condition and compared as group averages?
evaluation_scale: 42 students in a between-subjects study, two groups of 21, using the agent for 3 weeks, followed by a multiple-choice survey

title: Models of attention in computing and communication: from principles to applications
authors: Eric Horvitz, Carl Kadie, Tim Paek, David Hovel
summary: This 2003 overview from the Attentional User Interface project argues that human attention should be a central construct in computing and communication systems. It reviews Bayesian and temporal models that infer a user's attentional state, workload and location from sensed signals, calendar and device activity. Decision-theoretic and economic analysis then trades the value of information against attention-sensitive disruption costs. Applications include the Notification Platform, Priorities (email urgency), DeepListener and Quartet. Preference profiles are user-specific but adjusted manually. The paper reports no new experiments, baselines or transfer tests, and it is a review of the authors' own work.
usil_relation: The Notification Platform and DeepListener make expected-utility decisions about whether, when and how to interrupt, and whether to act or clarify, using cost-of-disruption preferences stored in a user profile [interaction_decisions][personalization]. This is close to a user-conditioned interaction policy.
open_question: Can the per-user disruption-cost profiles, which are hand-set via sliders over defaults, be learned from a user's implicit signals such as dismissals, deferrals and takeovers, and do they transfer across tasks and devices and track drift over time? The paper reports no such evaluation.

title: Inferring the Unspoken: Aligning Embodied Agents with Implicit Preferences
authors: Manjie Xu, Xinyi Yang, Wei Liang, Chi Zhang, Yixin Zhu
summary: The paper introduces PBP, an OmniGibson benchmark with 290 implicit household preferences, to test whether embodied agents can infer unspoken user preferences from three unlabeled demonstrations. It finds a preference acquisition gap: planning is easy with the ground-truth preference but hard without it. InTU, a prompted two-stage method, verbalizes the inferred preference as a natural-language rule before planning and roughly halves end-to-end error. Verbalized preferences transfer across visually distinct scenes for symbolic LLMs, and removing demonstrations collapses accuracy. Evaluation is offline and synthetic. It does not study interaction decisions, drift, or real users.
usil_relation: InTU infers an explicit natural-language user preference from a few behavioral demonstrations and uses it in-context. This is close to USIL's user representation z_u built from user-specific history, and the paper tests cross-scene transfer of that representation [personalization][user_representation][transfer].
open_question: Can the verbalize-then-plan approach recover procedural preferences (when to ask, confirm, or defer) from real users' demonstrations, takeovers, or corrections, and does it stay stable as preferences drift across sessions? The paper covers only static task-content preferences from simulated rule-planner demonstrations.
notes: previously titled: Learning to Plan with Personalized Preferences
evaluation_scale: 5,000 synthetic evaluation groups across 50 scenes in OmniGibson, 290 preferences, 3 demonstrations per group, three runs per experiment

title: Capturing Individual Human Preferences with Reward Features
authors: André Barreto, Vincent Dumoulin, Yiran Mao, et al.
summary: The paper formalises learning a reward model that can be specialised to an individual user, including users outside the training raters. It derives a PAC bound showing that approximation error depends on both the number of examples and the number of raters. It proposes the Reward-Feature Model (RFM): shared reward features are learned from multi-rater pairwise preferences, and a new user is then adapted by fitting only a linear coefficient vector with logistic regression. With Gemma on UltraFeedback and PersonalLLM, RFM adapts from about 30 examples and beats linear, non-linear and in-context LLM baselines. Users are synthetic or reward models, not real humans, and no interaction policy is studied.
user_evidence: Pairwise preferences from individual raters, with few examples for new raters
usil_relation: RFM's per-user coefficient vector w over frozen shared reward features is a low-dimensional user representation that adapts quickly from a few dozen pairwise rankings and generalizes to held-out users. This is a close outcome_individual analogue of z_u = g(h), and its PAC analysis of examples versus raters is directly relevant to few-shot user adaptation.
open_question: Could reward-feature-style decomposition be applied to procedural signals (takeovers, confirmations, question answers) to learn per-user ask/act/defer policies, and would the shared features transfer across tasks and real users rather than synthetic or reward-model raters?
evaluation_scale: Synthetic feature-based users (±1 vectors over 13 features) with 500 held-out users, 5 runs with 99% CIs; reward-model-as-user leave-one-out on UltraFeedback and PersonalLLM; VPL protocol comparison

title: Group Preference Optimization: Few-Shot Alignment of Large Language Models
authors: Siyan Zhao, John Dang, Aditya Grover
summary: Group Preference Optimization (GPO) is a few-shot method for aligning LLMs to the opinions of specific groups. A transformer module is meta-trained across many groups to predict preference scores for LLM prompt-response embeddings from a few in-context (embedding, preference) pairs. At test time it adapts to unseen demographic groups, countries and individuals without fine-tuning the base LLM. On OpinionQA and GlobalOpinionQA it beats in-context steering, few-shot prompting, per-group SFT and in-context finetuning by 7-8%, using less compute. Evaluation is offline on survey data with multiple-choice questions, with no interaction decisions, temporal adaptation or user study.
user_evidence: A small number of labeled preference examples (survey responses) per group
usil_relation: GPO is few-shot, inference-time adaptation to an unseen group or individual from a handful of preference examples, with no base-model fine-tuning. It is the outcome-side, individual-conditioned analogue of USIL's few-shot user adaptation (P1) and implicit in-context user representation (P2).
open_question: Can an in-context meta-learned preference module like GPO predict procedural preferences (when a user wants to be asked, to confirm, or to have the agent act autonomously) from a few interaction traces, rather than opinion scores on multiple-choice survey answers? Does it track preference drift across sessions?
evaluation_scale: Offline survey data: 22 US demographic groups (OpinionQA), 14 countries (GlobalOpinionQA), and 100 individual participants per survey across 15 topics; 3 seeds; Alpaca-7B and Llama2-13B-chat.

title: Diverging Preferences: When do Annotators Disagree and do Models Know?
authors: Michael JQ Zhang, Zhilin Wang, Jena D. Hwang, et al.
summary: The paper asks when human annotators disagree on LLM response preferences and whether reward models and LLM-as-Judge account for it. It gives a taxonomy of ten disagreement causes in four classes and releases individual annotations for MultiPref and HelpSteer2. Over 30% of examples show diverging preferences. Standard Bradley-Terry/MSE reward models and LLM-as-Judge fail to detect them, performing at or below chance on Diverging ID AUROC. The authors propose distributional reward models (Mean-Var, Likert classification) that predict variance across annotators and identify divisive examples, which they use to filter WildBench. The work does no per-user personalization.
user_evidence: Multiple annotators' pairwise preference labels per example
usil_relation: It shows that single-value reward models and LLM-as-Judge ignore annotator disagreement, and it releases per-annotator labels (MultiPref, HelpSteer2). This supports USIL's argument that averaging across users hides individual differences, and the distributional reward is a population-level step toward individual modeling [claimed_contribution][user_representation].
open_question: Can per-annotator labels be used to learn individual-conditioned reward or interaction policies, for example when to ask for clarification on underspecified prompts, rather than only a population variance? Would predicted variance transfer into decisions to ask or defer?

title: Personalized Soups: Personalized Large Language Model Alignment via Post-hoc Parameter Merging
authors: Joel Jang, Seungone Kim, Bill Yuchen Lin, et al.
summary: Personalized Soups frames personalized LLM alignment (RLPHF) as multi-objective RL over declared preferences along three dimensions: expertise, informativeness, and style. Instead of jointly optimizing all preference combinations, it trains one PPO/LoRA policy per single preference and merges their parameters by weighted averaging at inference. This scales linearly in the number of preferences rather than exponentially. Evaluated on simulated users with GPT-4 feedback and 24 crowdworkers, it matches or beats a strong Prompted-MORL baseline, generalizes to unseen combinations, and supports adding new preferences modularly. Personalization is declarative and output-focused; interaction policy is not addressed.
user_evidence: Pairwise preference feedback along declared preference dimensions (e.g., concise vs. elaborate, friendly vs. unfriendly)
usil_relation: Personalized Soups composes per-preference policies on the fly from a user's declared preference vector, so personalization lives in parameter space and can be added modularly [what_is_learned][user_representation]. It also tests adding two new Style preferences without retraining the old policies [temporal_adaptation]. This is the nearest outcome_individual counterpart to a USIL user representation z_u, but it covers response style only.
open_question: Could the modular merge-by-preference approach be applied to procedural preferences (how often to ask, confirm, or defer) and have its weights inferred from user edits, approvals, and takeovers rather than declared up front? Would merging still work when the preference dimensions are learned from behavior and drift over time?
evaluation_scale: 8 (16 in scaling experiment) simulated preference combinations, 50 Koala prompts, GPT-4 as simulated annotator and judge, plus 24 crowdworkers for human evaluation

title: Modular Pluralism: Pluralistic Alignment via Multi-LLM Collaboration
authors: Shangbin Feng, Taylor Sorensen, Yuhan Liu, Jillian Fisher, Chan Young Park, Yejin Choi, Yulia Tsvetkov
summary: Modular Pluralism plugs a pool of smaller community LMs, finetuned with LoRA on community corpora such as news slants and cultural texts, into a frozen, possibly black-box base LLM. It supports three pluralism modes: Overton (summarizing diverse comments), steerable (selecting the comment matching a requested attribute), and distributional (aggregating community-conditioned answer distributions). Across six LLMs and four datasets it improves value coverage by 68.5% on average, plus steerability and distributional fit. Adding new community LMs patches underrepresented cultures. Personalization is group- or attribute-level, with no individual histories, no temporal adaptation, and no interactive decisions.
user_evidence: community corpora
usil_relation: Steerable pluralism conditions outputs on a user-stated value, demographic attribute or country. The modular pool of community LMs plugged into a black-box LLM is a group-level analogue of conditioning on a user representation.
open_question: Could the modular community-LM pattern be adapted to individual-level interaction preferences (when to ask, confirm, or defer) learned from a single user's corrections, rather than group-level content perspectives?
evaluation_scale: Offline evaluation on 4 English datasets (6 tasks) with 6 LLMs; 5 human annotators judged 100 Overton pairs and GPT-4 judged 600 pairs; no live user study.

title: Learning and Reasoning about Interruption
authors: Eric Horvitz, Johnson Apacible
summary: The paper presents methods and the Interruption Workbench for learning per-user Bayesian models that infer a user's current cost of interruption and forecast future interruptability from desktop activity, calendar, acoustic and visual sensing. Subjects tag their own recorded office activity, including dollar willingness-to-pay costs. Personalized models beat marginal baselines (for example 0.73 vs 0.53 accuracy for S1), and combining perceptual and calendar features helps most. Models transferred between users perform poorly, and composite models only partly close the gap. The alert-mediation decisions are described but not evaluated, and the study covers only two subjects, offline.
usil_relation: It learns individualized models of when a particular user can be interrupted from desktop, calendar, audio and visual signals. These models feed alerting decisions (whether, when and how to interrupt), which is the procedural, per-user adaptation that USIL targets. It also shows that cross-user transfer performs worse than personalized models.
open_question: Can per-user interruptibility models be learned online from natural implicit signals (dismissed alerts, takeovers) instead of video-assisted self-tagging, adapt as a user's routines drift, and improve actual alerting outcomes in a deployed, longitudinal evaluation with many users?
evaluation_scale: 2 subjects evaluated (about 5 hours each; 9,384 and 8,048 two-second cases), with a third subject contributing to composite models

title: Learning Next Action Predictors from Human-Computer Interaction
authors: Omar Shaikh et al.
summary: The paper formalizes next action prediction (NAP): predicting a user's next computer actions from multimodal interaction history. It contributes NAPsack, a passive VLM pipeline that labels naturalistic behavior (about 360K actions from 20 users' month-long phone screenshots), and LongNAP, a Qwen-2.5-VL-7B policy trained with GRPO to reason, retrieve from a per-user memory of traces, and predict the next 8 actions. Per-user models reach 0.38 on an LLM-judge score versus 0.21 for SFT and 0.27 for the best baseline, with 79% human win rate. Transfer to unseen users is modest (+13%). Proactive assistance is proposed, not evaluated.
user_evidence: interaction traces
usil_relation: It trains a separate model and memory per user from longitudinal, passively recorded interaction history, using a temporal split within each user. This is the individual-user, across-time data and representation setup USIL needs, but it is applied to predicting what the user does next rather than how the agent should act.
open_question: Could LongNAP's per-user reasoning traces and next-action predictions be used to decide when an assistant such as SleepWalk should act, ask, confirm, or defer, for example by using prediction confidence (intra-cluster variance) as a trigger? Would this beat population-level thresholds in a study with real users?
evaluation_scale: 20 Screenomics users, one month of phone use each (~360K actions, ~1,800 hours); offline evaluation plus a 300-comparison pairwise human judgment study

title: Large Language Models Empowered Personalized Web Agents
authors: Hongru Cai, Yongqi Li, Wenjie Wang, Fengbin Zhu, Xiaoyu Shen, Wenjie Li, Tat-Seng Chua
summary: The paper formulates LLM-empowered personalized Web agents and introduces PersonalWAB, a benchmark of 1,000 users built from Amazon review histories. It covers personalized search, recommendation and review generation, with single-turn and multi-turn (LLM-simulated user) tracks. It proposes PUMA, which retrieves task-specific behaviors from a per-user memory bank and fine-tunes LLaMA-2-7B with SFT and DPO to produce function calls and parameters. PUMA outperforms ReAct, Reflexion, RecMind and InteRecAgent baselines and is faster. Limits: shopping-only scope, no preference drift, full PUMA not evaluated multi-turn, LLM-generated profiles and instructions, and results averaged over users.
user_evidence: user profile, historical web behaviors (e.g., purchases, reviews)
usil_relation: PUMA conditions Web agent function calling on a per-user memory of Amazon histories, which is a per-user memory-based representation. PersonalWAB's multi-turn track also includes a 'respond' action for clarification, which touches on ask decisions.
open_question: Can per-user memory be extended to learn when an individual user wants the agent to ask, confirm, or act in Web tasks, given that the full PUMA was never evaluated in multi-turn, the agent could not use later feedback, and users and profiles are LLM-simulated rather than real?
