evaluation_scale: 1,000 users built from Amazon review histories; 6,896 train and 2,174 test instructions; LLM user simulator in multi-turn track

title: PersonaAgent: Bridging Memory and Action for Personalized LLM Agents
authors: Weizhi Zhang, Xinyang Zhang, Chenwei Zhang, et al.
venue: NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Multi-Turn Interactions in LLMs (as 'PersonaAgent: When Large Language Model Agents Meet Personalization at Test Time'); arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.06254
summary: PersonaAgent personalizes an LLM agent through a per-user persona system prompt that links episodic and semantic memory with tool-using actions. At test time, the persona is optimized with textual-gradient feedback by simulating recent interactions and minimizing the discrepancy from ground-truth user responses, with no model fine-tuning. On time-ordered LaMP tasks (citation, movie tagging, news categorization, product rating, plus generation) with 100 users, it beats prompting, ICL, RAG, PAG, ReAct and MemoryBank, and ablations show each component matters. Personas are distinct per user. The agent never decides when to ask or defer, and no real-user study was run.
user_evidence: user interaction history (recent interactions replayed at test time)
usil_relation: The per-user persona prompt that combines memory with tool-use instructions, updated asynchronously after each session from recent interaction feedback, is a concrete mechanism for per-user adaptation of agent behavior (tool and query selection) over time. This is the nearest thing to a user-conditioned policy z_u, but it is trained for output accuracy.
open_question: Can a persona-optimization loop like this learn procedural preferences such as when to ask, confirm, or defer, using signals such as takeovers, corrections and approvals instead of LaMP ground-truth labels? And do the learned personas transfer across tasks or drift gracefully when preferences change?
evaluation_scale: 100 LaMP users with the longest histories, offline, single run, Claude-3.5 Sonnet backbone, plus a cold-start resample with 10 interactions per user

title: Toward Personalized LLM-Powered Agents: Foundations, Evaluation, and Future Directions
authors: Yue Xu, Qian Chen, Zizhan Ma, et al.
summary: A survey of personalized LLM-powered agents that proposes a capability-oriented taxonomy covering profile modeling, memory management, planning, and action execution. It frames personalization as a user-conditioned policy over a per-user preference representation, and reviews user-centric data, preference types, and representations (reward vectors, embeddings, NL profiles, memory stores). It organizes evaluation into five goals (Effectiveness, Adaptivity, Generalization, Robustness, Risk) and benchmark families (interactive alignment, user substitution), and surveys applications. Open problems include temporal dynamics, generalization, synthetic-user benchmarks, privacy, and efficiency. It touches on clarification decisions (SAGE-Agent) but runs no experiments.
what_is_learned: Survey; no model learned. It synthesizes how surveyed methods learn user profiles, preference representations, memory update and retrieval policies, and personalized planning and tool-use policies, framed as a user-conditioned policy pi(a_t|s_t,h_t,p_u).
user_evidence: various (surveyed)
usil_relation: Defines a user-conditioned policy pi(a_t|s_t,h_t,p_u) that mirrors USIL's central object, and covers selective clarification (SAGE-Agent) and an Interaction Efficiency metric. However, it is organized around personalizing outputs and capabilities (profile, memory, planning, action), not per-user interaction policies.
open_question: The survey treats personalization mostly as outcome/content alignment. It does not establish how to learn and evaluate per-user procedural policies (when to ask, confirm, defer, or return control) from edits, takeovers, and approvals over time, or whether such policies transfer across tasks and contexts.

title: TidyBot: Personalized Robot Assistance with Large Language Models
authors: Jimmy Wu, Rika Antonova, Adam Kan, et al. (incl. Shuran Song, Jeannette Bohg, Thomas Funkhouser)
summary: TidyBot personalizes household tidying by prompting an off-the-shelf LLM with a user's few example placements. The LLM summarizes them into generalized natural-language rules, which choose receptacles and manipulation primitives (pick-and-place or pick-and-toss) for unseen objects. On a 96-scenario text benchmark, summarization reaches 91.2% unseen accuracy, beating examples-only, WordNet, RoBERTa and CLIP baselines. A 40-participant study prefers it over the CLIP baseline, and a real mobile manipulator places 85% of objects correctly. It needs no training and is interpretable. It learns what to produce, not how to interact, and drift, asking policies and cross-session persistence are not studied.
user_evidence: a few demonstrations or examples of the user's preferred object placements
usil_relation: TidyBot shows few-shot per-user personalization with an interpretable natural-language summary as the user representation, evaluated on a real mobile manipulator. This resembles USIL's z_u as a natural-language profile, but it is used for outcome preferences (object placement and primitive choice).
open_question: Can LLM summarization of a user's examples capture procedural preferences, such as when the robot should ask, confirm, or defer, and update them as the user corrects it across sessions?
evaluation_scale: 96 benchmark scenarios with scenario-defined (simulated) users, 672 seen and 672 unseen placements; a 40-participant study judging outputs (960 evaluations); 8 real-world robot scenarios with 10 objects each and 3 runs (240 objects).

title: After Talking with 1,000 Personas: Learning Preference-Aligned Proactive Assistants from Large-Scale Simulated Persona Interactions
authors: Ziyi Xuan, Yiwen Wu, Zhaoyang Yan, Vinod Namboodiri, Yu Yang
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive Mobile Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies
summary: The paper proposes a population-to-individual pipeline for preference-aligned proactive smartphone assistants. Stage 1 fine-tunes a 3B Llama with LoRA on about 100,000 synthetic interactions from 1,000 census-aligned LLM personas, organized by a five-dimension preference schema (scheduling, domain, autonomy, communication style, context). Stage 2 adapts on-device with per-user, per-category activation steering updated from accept/reject/ignore, ratings and text feedback. In simulation, timing appropriateness and interaction quality rise sharply, and steering approaches DPO. A 34-participant storyboard study favors personalization, though simulator variance and the small, short human study limit real-world claims.
usil_relation: Closest to USIL in learning a per-user, per-category steering state that adjusts proactive-assistant timing, initiative, detail and tone from accept/reject/ignore and rating feedback on top of a population-pretrained model. This is a population-to-individual pipeline for procedural preferences (when to intervene, how much autonomy), not only outputs.
open_question: Does per-user steering learned from lightweight accept/reject/ignore feedback hold up with real users over weeks, in real deployment rather than 10-interaction storyboard studies, and does it transfer across tasks and devices? Ignored suggestions are ambiguous, so can drift be told apart from noise? Do individual-level results beat population-tuned policies once per-user variance is reported?
evaluation_scale: 1,000 LLM-simulated census-aligned personas with 100 interactions each, plus 34 human participants (10-pair A/B detection study and 10-interaction Static/Adaptive/Mixed adaptation study on storyboards)

title: PersonalAlign: Hierarchical Implicit Intent Alignment for Personalized GUI Agent with Long-Term User-Centric Records
authors: Yibo Lyu, Gongwei Chen, Rui Shao, Wei-Li Guan, Liqiang Nie
venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
summary: PersonalAlign defines a GUI-agent task in which long-term user records are used to resolve omitted preferences in vague instructions and to anticipate routines for proactive suggestions. The authors build AndroidIntent (775 preference and 215 routine annotations from Fingertip20K, 91 users) and propose HIM-Agent, a non-parametric hierarchical memory. It aggregates record prototypes into Preference Intent Memory and Routine Intent Memory, with a state-based filter for proactive triggering. HIM-Agent improves execution and proactive performance by 15.7% and 7.3%, and false alarms drop relative to baselines. Evaluation is offline only, with no transfer tests, drift analysis, or real-user study.
usil_relation: HIM-Agent builds per-user memory from 91 users' long-term GUI logs (Fingertip20K) and uses it to decide when to proactively suggest. This is close to USIL's per-user history h_t^u and its act-versus-suggest decision. The state-based routine filter with false-alarm evaluation is a small instance of learning when to intervene.
open_question: Can per-user memory govern how the agent works (when to ask, confirm, or defer) rather than only what intent to infer? Does it adapt under real preference drift, and does it transfer across users, platforms, or tasks, given the fixed 80/20 offline split and Fingertip-only data?
evaluation_scale: Offline evaluation on logs of 91 users over about 2 months: 775 preference episodes, 215 routine episodes, 100 negative states; no live users.

title: Polite Personal Agents
authors: Silvia Schiaffino, Analı́a Amandi
summary: Historical work on individualized and polite proactive assistance.
usil_relation: The abstract frames personal agents as gradually learning a target individual's preferences and habits, like a human assistant, which resembles the persistent, per-user adaptation USIL assumes. Only the abstract is available, and it says nothing about interaction policy.
open_question: Does the 'polite' personal agent learn when to interrupt, ask, or act proactively for each individual user, or does it only learn content preferences and habits? The abstract does not say.

title: Resilient Chatbots: Repair Strategy Preferences for Conversational Breakdowns
authors: Z. Ashktorab, Mohit Jain, Q. Liao, Justin D. Weisz
venue: International Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
summary: This CHI 2019 study asks which repair strategies users prefer when a chatbot conversation breaks down. It defines eight strategies grounded in communication theory, including three novel explanation-based ones that expose the underlying model, and tests them in a scenario-based paired-comparison experiment with 203 MTurk workers. Options is the most preferred strategy, while Defer ranks last after successful repairs but second after failed ones. Preferences vary with social orientation, service frustration, chatbot experience, and repair outcome, but not with task context (shopping, banking, travel). No model is learned and no personalized system is built, but the findings motivate adapting repair behavior to individuals.
what_is_learned: No model is trained. The paper estimates population-level preference rankings of chatbot repair strategies with Bradley-Terry scores, and uses logistic regression to relate individual and task factors to strategy preference.
usil_relation: It shows that preferences for repair strategies (options, confirm, defer) are not universal and vary with social orientation, service frustration, and chatbot experience. This is empirical support for procedural, interaction-level individual differences, which is USIL's motivation.
open_question: Can per-user repair-strategy preferences (e.g., when to offer options, confirm, or defer after a low-confidence breakdown) be learned online from real interaction signals, and do they outperform the population-best strategy (Options) for individual users?
evaluation_scale: 203 MTurk participants (after filtering), 1,624 pairwise comparisons over 48 scripted scenarios

title: Interactive Policy Learning through Confidence-Based Autonomy
authors: Sonia Chernova, Manuela Veloso
summary: Confidence-Based Autonomy (CBA) is an interactive learning-from-demonstration algorithm in which the agent decides when to ask for a demonstration. Confident Execution requests help when classifier confidence or nearest-neighbor distance falls below automatically computed per-decision-boundary thresholds. Corrective Demonstration lets the teacher retroactively fix mistakes made during autonomous execution. In a simulated highway driving task with a single teacher (an author), CBA needed fewer demonstrations than teacher-selected ones (about 700 vs 1300) and caused fewer training collisions than corrective-only learning. There is no user model, no multi-user study, no transfer experiment, and no personalization across users.
usil_relation: CBA is a classic learned ask-vs-act policy: confidence thresholds, recalculated as data accumulates, decide when the agent requests a demonstration versus acts, and teacher corrections serve as retroactive feedback. This is the procedural decision USIL targets, but here it is tuned to one teacher's data without any per-user framing.
open_question: Can CBA-style confidence thresholds and correction policies be learned per user, so that ask/act boundaries adapt to different teachers' styles, consistency, and tolerance for interruptions, and do they carry across tasks and sessions?
evaluation_scale: 1 teacher (one of the authors) in a simulated five-lane highway driving domain

title: CowPilot: A Framework for Autonomous and Human-Agent Collaborative Web Navigation
authors: Faria Huq, Zora Zhiruo Wang, Frank F. Xu, Tian-Yue Ou, Shuyan Zhou, Jeffrey P. Bigham, Graham Neubig
venue: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
summary: CowPilot is a Chrome-extension framework for web navigation in which an LLM agent proposes each next action with a highlight and reasoning, auto-executes after five seconds, and lets the human pause, reject, take over, or resume. It adds metrics beyond task success: human, agent and total steps, intervention count, and agent-driven completion. On 27 WebArena tasks with three author-annotators, CoPilot with GPT-4o reached 95% accuracy versus 48% autonomous, with humans taking about 15% of steps. Nothing is learned or personalized; the paper notes that intervention patterns may vary by user. Only the extension package is released.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned about users. No model is trained; off-the-shelf LLMs (GPT-4o, Llama-3.1-8B) propose actions, and GPT-4o cleans human event logs into agent-space actions. The contribution is a collaboration framework and evaluation metrics.
usil_relation: CowPilot's pause/reject/resume mechanism with a 5-second auto-execute window is a concrete interface for logging user interventions and takeovers. It also reports intervention counts and human-step share as interaction-cost metrics. These are the kind of procedural signals USIL would learn from.
open_question: Could CowPilot's logged interventions (rejections, pauses, resumes) be used to learn per-user policies for when to auto-execute versus ask, and would that lower intervention counts for individual users compared with the fixed 5-second rule?
evaluation_scale: 3 authors acting as human agents on 27 WebArena tasks, with GPT-4o and Llama-3.1-8B, in autonomous, CoPilot and human-only modes

title: PrefDisco: Benchmarking Proactive Personalized Reasoning
authors: S. Li, Avinandan Bose, Faeze Brahman, S. Du, Pang Wei Koh, Maryam Fazel, Y. Tsvetkov
summary: PrefDisco turns static reasoning benchmarks (math, logic, science, medical, social) into interactive cold-start personalization tasks. Each simulated persona has a sparse, weighted preference profile that the model must discover by asking questions, within 5 turns, before adapting its response. The PREFALIGN rubric metric scores alignment, and Baseline, Discovery and Oracle conditions are compared across 21 frontier LLMs. In 29% of model-task pairs, discovery is worse than baseline, models ask few questions (about 1.4–1.5), and accuracy falls from 65.2% to 60.1%. Limitations include simulated users, no preference drift, and no cross-task transfer experiment.
what_is_learned: Nothing is trained. It is an evaluation benchmark for whether LLMs can infer a latent per-instance preference profile (attributes, values, weights) by asking questions and then adapt reasoning and responses. The closest category is user model, but only as an inference target within a session.
usil_relation: PrefDisco evaluates when and what to ask in order to elicit hidden per-persona preferences under a 5-turn budget, and it reports that models ask only about 1.4–1.5 questions and often do worse than baseline. This is a population-level evaluation of an elicitation policy (procedure_averaged) with individual-level outcome grading. The personas are simulated and the preferences concern communication style.
open_question: Do per-user elicitation and interaction policies, such as how many questions to ask and when to stop, persist and transfer across tasks and sessions with real users whose preferences drift? PrefDisco builds persona consistency but runs no transfer experiment and handles no preference evolution.
evaluation_scale: 10,000 scenarios: 100 LLM-generated personas and 100 problems per benchmark across 10 benchmarks, 21 frontier models, 5-turn limit

title: Users' Expectations and Practices with Agent Memory
authors: Brennan Jones, Kelsey Stemmler, Emily Su, Young-Ho Kim, Anastasia Kuzminykh
summary: This CHI extended abstract reports a preliminary qualitative study of how users understand and manage the memory of personalized AI tools. It combines semi-structured interviews with six regular users and a thematic analysis of 54 Reddit threads. Users have incomplete mental models of what is stored and are surprised by how much sensitive information is kept. They see memory as layered, from general facts to user, domain, project and task knowledge, and want it organized and controllable by task. Today they separate memories with chat threads, custom instructions, and separate accounts. The authors propose task-based memory organization and access control. No system is built or evaluated.
what_is_learned: Not a learning system; qualitative themes on users' mental models, expectations, and practices for agent memory: a layered memory hierarchy (factual, user, domain, project, task), temporal dependency of needs, and manual practices for separating memories.
usil_relation: Interviews with six users and 54 Reddit threads show users want to control and organize what an agent remembers by task, project and domain, and already use manual workarounds such as separate chats, custom instructions, and re-pasting prompts. These are user-specific procedural preferences about memory that a USIL system would need to learn and represent.
open_question: Can an agent learn each user's boundaries between task, project and domain memories, and when memory should carry over or stay disjoint, from implicit signals such as chat-switching, deletions and re-pasted context, rather than from explicit toggles? Would that also hold as needs shift over time and across task stages, which the interviews raise but no system tests?
evaluation_scale: 6 interview participants (ages 24–35, mostly ChatGPT users) with a brief survey, plus thematic analysis of 54 Reddit threads

title: PIRA-Bench: A Transition from Reactive GUI Agents to GUI-based Proactive Intent Recommendation Agents
authors: Yuxiang Chai, Shun-Ye Tang, Han Xiao, Rui Liu, Hongsheng Li
summary: PIRA-Bench introduces the Proactive Intent Recommendation task, in which a GUI agent watches a noisy, multi-threaded stream of mobile and desktop screenshots plus a textual user profile and predicts what the user will want to do next, staying idle on noise. The benchmark has 100 trajectories with 3 profiles each, scored by intent F1 times a false-positive score using an LLM judge. The PIRF baseline wraps MLLMs with a memory of intent threads and reflection-based deletion. PIRF improves scores modestly (best 28.05 vs 23.29), far below humans (90.35). Personalization is profile-conditioned only; no per-user learning or transfer is tested.
what_is_learned: No model is trained. PIRF is a prompting/memory architecture around off-the-shelf MLLMs that tracks intent threads (CREATE/RESUME/UPDATE/IDLE) and outputs sets of recommended intents conditioned on a static textual profile; the benchmark evaluates intent prediction.
usil_relation: PIRA-Bench rewards operational restraint (IDLE on noise, FPS metric) and conditions proactive intent recommendations on a textual user profile, which touches the question of when a proactive agent should act versus stay quiet [interaction_decisions][personalization].
open_question: Can proactive restraint be learned per user from signals such as accepted or dismissed recommendations over weeks, rather than set by a fixed noise-rejection rule and a static synthetic profile, and does it transfer across apps and tasks?
evaluation_scale: 100 trajectories (~32-33 screenshots each) with 3 synthetic profiles each; ground truth by majority vote of 3 human annotators; LLM judge (Gemini-3-flash); human reference baseline

title: FingerTip 20K: A Benchmark for Proactive and Personalized Mobile LLM Agents
authors: Qinglong Yang, Haoming Li, Hao Zhao, Xiao Yan, Jing-Tao Ding, Feng-Li Xu, Yong Li
summary: FingerTip 20K is a benchmark of 21,437 real mobile-use episodes from 95 users over about a month. It has two tracks: proactive task suggestion from context and past intents, and personalized task execution that follows each user's past action preferences. Evaluation covers prompted GUI agents, specialized models and a LoRA-tuned Qwen-2.5-VL-7B. Suggestion is hard: the best generalist reaches 12.8% success vs. 30.3% for humans. Prompted agents show no personalization (Sim2≈1), while the fine-tuned model improves Sim2 to 1.42 and generalizes modestly to unseen users and apps. The benchmark has no ask/defer decisions, online adaptation or preference drift.
usil_relation: FingerTip 20K uses real longitudinal data from 95 users and a Sim2 metric that compares action sequences with those of different-type users, which makes it a personalized benchmark for how a GUI agent executes tasks. Its proactive suggestion track also touches when to propose tasks without an instruction.
open_question: Can Sim2-style per-user action-preference evaluation be extended to interaction decisions such as when the agent should ask, confirm or hand back control, and learned online as a user's preferences drift? The benchmark covers neither, and prompted agents score Sim2≈1, i.e. no personalization.
evaluation_scale: 95 crowdsourced users over about one month (21,437 episodes, 506 apps); 20 human annotators on 400 episodes; user ratings for Sim2 validity

title: Personalized AI Scaffolds Synergistic Multi-Turn Collaboration in Creative Work
authors: Sean W. Kelley, D. De Cremer, Christoph Riedl
summary: A preregistered randomized online experiment (n=331) tests whether personalizing GPT-4o with users' psychometric profiles and AI-led interview summaries improves multi-turn collaboration on a creative marketing-campaign task. Personalization is profile-augmented prompting with no training. Personalized AI raised campaign quality (β=0.59) and, among top-quality campaigns, creativity. Mediation analysis shows effects run through attention and reasoning, not trust or (marginally) memory. Personalized responses concentrate in early turns, and personalized users produced more act and fewer coordinate turns. The profile is static, so long-term adaptation, interaction-policy learning and transfer are not studied. A partial condition tests mismatched profiles.
what_is_learned: No model is trained. Personalization is profile-augmented prompting: GPT-4o summarizes psychometric questionnaires and an AI-led interview into text placed in the assistant's system prompt. The study measures effects on outcomes and mechanisms (memory, attention, reasoning), not a learned policy.
usil_relation: The study personalizes an LLM assistant with an individual user's profile (psychometrics plus an AI-led interview summary) in multi-turn collaboration. It shows causal gains in quality and creativity and finds that personalization shifts act vs. coordinate turns, which is a procedural effect. This is close to outcome_individual personalization with a text user representation [personalization][user_representation].
open_question: Would a user-conditioned interaction policy learned from behavioral evidence (edits, takeovers, answers) over repeated sessions produce the same collaboration gains? Would it change when the agent asks, acts, or defers, rather than relying on a static psychometric profile given at the start? The paper gives no evidence on drift, longitudinal updating or transfer to other tasks [temporal_adaptation][transfer].
evaluation_scale: 331 analyzed Prolific US participants with marketing experience (116 generic, 114 personalized, 101 partial), single ~45-minute session; campaigns rated by an LLM judge validated against 200 human raters on 100 campaigns

title: Is More Autonomy Always Better? Exploring Preferences of Users with Mobility Impairments in Robot-assisted Feeding
authors: Tapomayukh Bhattacharjee, E. Gordon, Rosario Scalise, M. E. Cabrera, A. Caspi, Maya Cakmak, S. Srinivasa
venue: IEEE/ACM International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction
summary: This HRI 2020 user study asks what autonomy level, input modality, and speed people with mobility impairments prefer in robot-assisted feeding, given perceived error risk and dining context. Ten lab participants and eight online video participants rated fixed modes (low, partial, full autonomy; voice vs. web; slow vs. fast) with Likert and TAM items. Voice was preferred for individual dining and web for social dining. Autonomy levels did not differ significantly, so more autonomy was not always better, and participants with higher mobility limitation rated more favorably. Nothing is learned or personalized, but the results motivate user- and context-dependent interaction design.
what_is_learned: Nothing is learned. This is an empirical preference study of fixed autonomy modes, input modalities, and speeds in robot-assisted feeding, with no learned model.
usil_relation: It shows that preferred autonomy level and interface depend on context (individual vs. social dining) and on mobility-limitation group, which is evidence that procedural preferences vary across users. It also finds partial autonomy was not reliably preferred over low autonomy, so the best level of autonomy is not uniform.
open_question: Can a feeding robot learn each user's preferred autonomy split (acquisition, timing, transfer) and interface from a few meals, and adapt it as dining context and the user's fatigue or tolerance for errors change? This study only observes group-level trends in 10 users.
evaluation_scale: 10 participants with mobility impairments in two within-subject lab studies, plus 8 online video participants

title: Diagnosis, Feedback, Adaptation: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework for Test-Time Policy Adaptation
authors: Andi Peng, Aviv Netanyahu, Mark K. Ho, Tianmin Shu, Andreea Bobu, Julie Shah, Pulkit Agrawal
summary: DFA (Diagnosis, Feedback, Adaptation) is a human-in-the-loop framework for test-time adaptation of pretrained policies under distribution shift. It generates counterfactual demonstrations so users can identify which concepts are task-irrelevant for their own desired reward. Those concepts then drive data augmentation of the user's single demonstration for supervised finetuning. In a 20-person study across 2D Navigation, Minigrid and VIMA, counterfactuals significantly improved users' concept identification (p<.001), leading to more efficient finetuning and alignment with individual reward preferences. It personalizes task outcomes via per-user rewards rather than learning interaction policies, and does not address cross-session or cross-task transfer.
usil_relation: Per-user reward R′ determines which concepts users mark task-irrelevant, and the study shows their answers differ by assigned reward [personalization]. The system also queries the user for failure judgments, demonstrations and concept feedback [interaction_decisions]. This is individualized, feedback-driven adaptation from sparse evidence, but it adapts the policy's task behavior, not its interaction behavior.
open_question: Could the rule for when to show a counterfactual and query the user be learned per user, e.g., from their past accuracy and effort in judging concept relevance, and would per-user preferences about how much to be queried transfer across tasks and sessions?
evaluation_scale: 20 in-person participants giving 240 responses across 12 tasks, plus a 5-user pilot on VIMA; finetuning results use simulated augmentation at observed user accuracy rates.

title: Modeling and Predicting Trust Dynamics in Human–Robot Teaming: A Bayesian Inference Approach
authors: Yaohui Guo, X. Jessie Yang
summary: The paper presents a personalized Bayesian trust-dynamics model for human–robot teaming. Each user's trust is a Beta distribution with four parameters (prior attitude, success gain, failure gain), fit by MAP with a population prior from earlier users. It predicts trust from the robot's success/failure history and a few self-reported trust ratings. Leave-one-out testing on 39 participants in a drone surveillance task gives RMSE 0.072, beating ARMAV (0.101) and Optimo (0.139). Error drops with longer training and more frequent reports, and clustering reveals three trust-dynamics types. It does not learn interaction policies, assumes constant robot reliability, and does not test transfer to other tasks.
usil_relation: It builds a per-user model that adapts online from sparse self-reported trust, using a population prior for a new user. Such a trust estimate could feed autonomy and confirmation decisions. The paper only proposes that use as future work [interaction_decisions] [decision_context].
open_question: Could the per-user trust parameters (ws, wf, prior) drive a user-specific policy for when a robot asks, confirms, or defers, and does it beat a population-level policy? Would the parameters transfer to other tasks, robots, and varying reliability?
evaluation_scale: Offline leave-one-out on an existing dataset of 39 participants, 100 trials each, in a simulated drone surveillance task

title: Interactive and Explainable Robot Learning: A Comprehensive Review
authors: Esmaeil Seraj, Kin Man Lee, Zulfiqar Zaidi, Qingyu Xiao, Zhaoxin Li, Arthur Nascimento, Sanne van Waveren, Pradyumna Tambwekar, Rohan Paleja, Devleena Das, Matthew Gombolay
summary: This Foundations and Trends review surveys interactive and explainable robot learning, asking how non-expert users can teach robots and how robots can ask for help in ways users understand. It organizes what is learned (policies, rewards, transitions), the user signals used (demonstrations, preferences, corrections, language, implicit cues), and learning methods. It also covers personalization, long-term adaptation, feedback timing, trust and expertise modeling, active querying, evaluation metrics and benchmarks, and ethics. It runs no experiments of its own. Its main findings are gaps: explainable robot learning is rarely validated on real robots, explainability benchmarks are scarce, and perceived safety is not yet a learning criterion.
what_is_learned: As a survey, it organizes what robots learn in interactive settings: policies (states to actions), desired state transitions, and reward or objective functions. It also covers movement primitives, hierarchical task networks, policy versus reward explanations, and surveyed user models (trust, expertise, latent behavior embeddings).
usil_relation: Its personalization section (clustering demonstrations with IRL, latent behavior embeddings, FLAIR) and its coverage of robot-initiated queries, feedback timing and trust or expertise models are the closest match to USIL. They cover user-adaptive learning and when to ask or hand over, though mostly for task skills, not individualized interaction policies.
open_question: Can the surveyed pieces (personalized latent user models, trust and expertise inference, confidence-based asking, feedback timing) be combined into a per-user interaction policy that learns when a robot asks, explains, or defers, and be evaluated longitudinally on real robots with per-user results?
